statements.text: Many sampling interfaces treat T = 0 as a special case meaning "pick the highest-scoring token".
statements.explanation: Treating T = 0 as an argmax is a common convention.

statements.label: C
statements.text: As T grows very large, the distribution approaches a uniform one over the candidates.
statements.explanation: Dividing by a huge T shrinks all scaled scores toward 0, making the weights nearly equal.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Raising the temperature makes the model know more facts.
statements.explanation: Temperature rescales existing scores and adds no information.

statements.label: E
statements.text: As T approaches 0 from above, probability concentrates on the highest-scoring token, approaching greedy decoding.
statements.explanation: Dividing by a tiny T magnifies score gaps so one token takes nearly all the mass.

questions.source: Temperature is a concentration control, not a fact checker
questions.stem: Two tokens have scores that differ by 2 (token i has the higher score). With temperature T, the ratio of their probabilities is p_i / p_k = exp(2 / T). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: At T = 1 the ratio is e squared, about 7.39.
statements.explanation: exp(2 / 1) is about 7.389.

statements.label: B
statements.text: At T = 2 the ratio is about 14.8.
statements.explanation: At T = 2 the ratio is exp(1), about 2.72.

statements.label: C
statements.text: At T = 0.5 the ratio is about 5.46.
statements.explanation: At T = 0.5 the ratio is exp(4), about 54.6.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The ratio depends on the scores of all other tokens in the vocabulary.
statements.explanation: The normalizing total cancels in a ratio, leaving only the two scores and T.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Raising T increases the ratio between the two tokens.
statements.explanation: A larger T shrinks the exponent and moves the ratio toward 1.

questions.source: Temperature is a concentration control, not a fact checker
questions.stem: A model gives scores to three candidate answers to a factual question. Answer C has the highest score but is factually wrong. Answer A is correct and has the lowest score. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Raising the temperature is a reliable way to make the model correct.
statements.explanation: Flattening the distribution adds randomness, not correctness.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Lowering the temperature makes the model choose C more often.
statements.explanation: Lower temperature concentrates probability on the top-scoring candidate, which here is the wrong answer.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Some temperature setting reorders the candidates so that A ranks first.
statements.explanation: Dividing scores by any positive temperature preserves their order.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Raising the temperature a lot would make A get sampled more often because the model gains evidence that A is correct.
statements.explanation: A flatter distribution shifts mass toward low-scoring candidates indiscriminately, wrong ones included; no evidence is added.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Setting the temperature to its minimum guarantees a correct answer.
statements.explanation: Greedy-like decoding picks the top-scoring candidate, which here is wrong.

questions.source: Three scores are not yet three chances
questions.stem: Two programmers try to turn the scores [-1, 2, 3] into probabilities. One divides each score by the sum of the scores. The other uses a softmax with a temperature parameter that, by a bug, can be set negative. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A negative temperature is just a lower-temperature variant of the same sampling.
statements.explanation: A negative temperature inverts the preference order, which is not a gentler version of the same behavior.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A softmax with temperature -1 on [1, 2, 3] gives the largest probability to the score of 1, reversing the ordering.
statements.explanation: Dividing by -1 reverses the sign of the scores, so the smallest score gets the largest weight.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Dividing by the sum fails outright for a list such as [1, -1], whose sum is 0.
statements.explanation: The sum is 0, so every division is by zero.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Dividing by the sum is a valid normalization for any list of scores.
statements.explanation: It breaks on negative scores and on any list that sums to zero.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Dividing by the sum (which is 4) gives [-0.25, 0.5, 0.75], which includes a negative probability.
statements.explanation: -1 / 4 is -0.25, and a probability cannot be negative.

questions.source: Temperature is a concentration control, not a fact checker
questions.stem: A next-token distribution over five tokens is [0.45, 0.30, 0.15, 0.06, 0.04]. A decoder applies truncation before sampling and then renormalizes the kept probabilities to sum to 1. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: After top-p with p = 0.8 and renormalizing, the most probable token has probability 0.5.
statements.explanation: 0.45 divided by the kept total of 0.90 is 0.5.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Top-k with k = 2 keeps two tokens, and after renormalizing they have probabilities 0.7 and 0.3.
statements.explanation: Renormalizing 0.45 and 0.30 by their sum, 0.75, gives 0.6 and 0.4.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Top-p (nucleus) sampling with p = 0.8 keeps the smallest set of top tokens whose cumulative probability reaches at least 0.8, which here is the top three.
statements.explanation: 0.45 + 0.30 = 0.75 falls short of 0.8, and adding 0.15 gives 0.90, which reaches it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Top-p always keeps the same number of tokens regardless of the shape of the distribution.
statements.explanation: The number kept varies: a peaked distribution keeps few tokens and a flat one keeps many.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Truncation moves the removed tokens' probability onto the least likely tokens that remain.
statements.explanation: Renormalization scales all kept tokens by the same factor, so it preserves their relative proportions.

questions.source: A distribution is not the sample you happened to see
questions.stem: A team compares greedy decoding (always take the highest-probability next token) with sampling at temperature 1. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Greedy decoding can fall into repetitive loops.
statements.explanation: A phrase that is highly likely after itself can repeat indefinitely.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Sampling at temperature 1 draws each token in proportion to the model's own distribution.
statements.explanation: Temperature 1 leaves the distribution unscaled, and sampling follows it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Greedy decoding is guaranteed to produce true statements because it chooses the most likely token.
statements.explanation: Likelihood given a corpus is not truth.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Greedy decoding returns the single most probable whole sequence.
statements.explanation: Choosing the best token at each step does not guarantee the best sequence, because an early choice can lock out a better continuation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Greedy decoding on the same input with the same model is deterministic, apart from numerical nondeterminism in the hardware.
statements.explanation: With no randomness in selection, the same input gives the same path.

questions.source: A distribution is not the sample you happened to see
questions.stem:
A developer writes this function to draw samples from a distribution.

```python
import random

def draw_many(probs, n, seed=7):
    out = []
    for _ in range(n):
        rng = random.Random(seed)
        out.append(rng.choices(range(len(probs)), probs)[0])
    return out
```

Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A test that only checks that two calls with the same seed return equal lists would reveal the bug.
statements.explanation: The buggy function is perfectly repeatable, so a repeatability test passes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Two calls with the same arguments return identical lists.
statements.explanation: The function is fully deterministic, which is what hides the problem from a repeatability check.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Every element of the returned list is the same index.
statements.explanation: Each loop iteration builds a fresh generator with the same seed, so each draw is the same first value.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A test comparing the observed proportions over 1,000 draws with probs = [0.2, 0.5, 0.3] would fail on this function.
statements.explanation: All 1,000 draws land on one index, so the observed proportions are 1, 0 and 0 and miss the target.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The function samples correctly from the distribution because the seed is fixed.
statements.explanation: Fixing a seed gives repeatability, not a correct sampling distribution.

questions.source: A distribution is not the sample you happened to see
questions.stem: A sampler assigns probability 0.5 to outcome X. In 1,000 independent draws, the count of X is a binomial variable with mean 500 and standard deviation about 15.8. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A count of 530 is within about 2 standard deviations of the expected count and is not alarming.
statements.explanation: 530 is 30 above 500, which is about 1.9 standard deviations.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Using 4,000 draws instead of 1,000 halves the standard deviation of the observed proportion.
statements.explanation: The standard deviation of a proportion scales as 1/sqrt(n), so quadrupling n halves it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The count must be exactly 500 for the sampler to be correct.
statements.explanation: Random counts scatter around the expectation; exact equality is not required and is not typical.

statements.label: D
statements.text: About 95% of such runs would give a count between roughly 468 and 532.
statements.explanation: Two standard deviations is about 31.6, so roughly 95% of counts fall between 468.4 and 531.6.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A count of 600 would be about 6 standard deviations above the expected count, strong evidence of a bug or of a wrong assumed probability.
statements.explanation: 600 is 100 above 500, about 6.3 standard deviations, which is vanishingly unlikely by chance.

questions.source: A distribution is not the sample you happened to see
questions.stem: The true probability of an outcome is p = 0.3. An experimenter estimates it as the observed fraction in n independent draws, whose standard error is sqrt(p(1 - p) / n). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For n = 10,000, the standard error is about 0.046.
statements.explanation: At n = 10,000 the standard error is about 0.0046, ten times smaller.

statements.label: B
statements.text: At n = 100, an observed fraction of 0.35 is strong evidence that the true probability is not 0.3.
statements.explanation: A gap of 0.05 is only a little more than one standard error at n = 100, which is ordinary sampling noise.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Multiplying n by 100 reduces the standard error by a factor of 100.
statements.explanation: Standard error falls as 1/sqrt(n), so a hundredfold increase in n gives a tenfold reduction.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A larger sample makes the observed fraction tend toward p but does not guarantee it equals p exactly.
statements.explanation: Convergence is statistical: the fraction approaches p without ever being guaranteed to hit it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: For n = 100, the standard error is about 0.046.

questions.source: A distribution is not the sample you happened to see
questions.stem: A sampler converts a uniform random number u in [0, 1) into an index using the cumulative sums of probabilities [0.2, 0.5, 0.3], which are 0.2, 0.7 and 1.0. It returns index 0 when u < 0.2, index 1 when 0.2 <= u < 0.7, and index 2 when u >= 0.7. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If u is uniform, index 1 is returned with probability 0.5.
statements.explanation: The interval [0.2, 0.7) has width 0.5, and a uniform u falls in it with that probability.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A draw of u = 0.95 returns index 1.
statements.explanation: 0.95 is at least 0.7, which is index 2.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the weights were the unnormalized list [2, 5, 3], comparing u in [0, 1) directly against their cumulative sums 2, 7 and 10 would still give correct results.
statements.explanation: Every u in [0, 1) is below 2, so index 0 would always be returned; the weights must be normalized or u scaled by their total.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A draw of u = 0.15 returns index 0.
statements.explanation: 0.15 is below 0.2.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A draw of u = 0.65 returns index 2.
statements.explanation: 0.65 lies in [0.2, 0.7), which is index 1.

questions.source: A distribution is not the sample you happened to see
questions.stem: A script counts how often each of three outcomes is drawn, using weights [0.90, 0.09, 0.01] and 20 draws. The counting step returns a dictionary that lists only the outcomes that actually appeared. Suppose the printed dictionary is {0: 18, 1: 2}. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The chance that an outcome with probability 0.01 never appears in 20 independent draws is below 5%.
statements.explanation: The chance is 0.99 to the power 20, about 0.82, so non-appearance is the typical result.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Outcome 2 is now impossible under the sampler.
statements.explanation: The sampler's probabilities did not change; the outcome was simply not drawn.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Outcome 2 was observed zero times in this run.
statements.explanation: A missing key means no recorded selections in this sample.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A report that needs a count for every outcome should treat a missing key as a count of 0.
statements.explanation: Reporting code must default absent outcomes to zero so the table covers all outcomes.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The absent key means the probability for outcome 2 was removed from the model.
statements.explanation: Not appearing in a sample says nothing about the model's assigned probabilities.

questions.source: A distribution is not the sample you happened to see
questions.stem: A team sets temperature to 0 on a hosted model API and sends the same prompt 100 times. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Temperature 0 usually means greedy decoding, always taking the highest-probability token.
statements.explanation: Zero temperature is conventionally implemented as an argmax over scores.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Pinning a dated model version is irrelevant to repeatability across weeks.
statements.explanation: Providers can change an unpinned alias to a newer model, so pinning a dated version reduces that source of drift.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Even so, outputs are not guaranteed to be byte-identical on hosted infrastructure, because of effects such as floating-point nondeterminism, batching and silent model updates.
statements.explanation: Providers commonly document that determinism is best-effort rather than guaranteed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If all 100 outputs happen to be identical, that proves the answer is correct.
statements.explanation: Repeatability says nothing about correctness: the same wrong answer can repeat indefinitely.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Identical outputs at temperature 0 are produced by the random seed.
statements.explanation: With greedy decoding no random draw is made, so a seed is not what produces the repetition.

questions.source: First prompts: the same experiment, one floor up
questions.stem: A tester asks the same factual question in four fresh conversations, in two forms: "Explain in one sentence..." and "Answer with one word only, no punctuation." The four one-word answers agree exactly, while the four one-sentence answers differ in wording. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The four one-sentence answers can differ in wording while making the same claim.
statements.explanation: Phrasing varies more than the underlying claim in free-form answers.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Agreement across the four one-word answers shows that the answer is correct.
statements.explanation: Agreement shows consistency, which is not the same as correctness.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Four agreeing answers prove that the model's distribution has no variance.
statements.explanation: Four samples cannot establish zero variance; a small sample can agree by chance.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Constraining the format has an effect like lowering the temperature, concentrating probability without a temperature control.
statements.explanation: Both make the distribution more concentrated, one by rescaling and one by restricting what is likely.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A tightly constrained format leaves fewer high-probability continuations, so the spread across runs shrinks.
statements.explanation: A narrow format makes most continuations invalid, concentrating probability on a few.

questions.source: Temperature is a concentration control, not a fact checker
questions.stem: An engineer compares two prompts. Prompt A is run at temperature 0.2 with seed 1, and prompt B at temperature 0.8 with seed 2. Prompt B yields more varied answers. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Running each configuration many times is better than running each once, because single draws are noisy.
statements.explanation: Repeated draws let you estimate a spread rather than relying on one random outcome.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Because prompt B gives more varied answers, B is the better prompt.
statements.explanation: More variety is a different property from better quality; it depends on what the task needs.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Recording the prompt, temperature, seed and model version of every run helps others reproduce the comparison.
statements.explanation: Without the settings on record, nobody can tell which condition produced which output.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A cleaner comparison would change only the prompt and hold temperature and seed fixed.
statements.explanation: Controlled comparisons vary one factor at a time.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The comparison changes prompt, temperature and seed at once, so the difference in variety cannot be attributed to the prompt.
statements.explanation: With three variables changed together, any of them could explain the result.

questions.source: Where the numbers come from
questions.stem: A model assigns the three tokens of a short reply the probabilities 0.9, 0.5 and 0.2, each conditioned on the tokens before it. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The sequence probability equals the average of the three token probabilities, which is about 0.53.
statements.explanation: Sequence probability is the product of the conditional probabilities, not their mean.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Adding another token whose probability is below 1 can raise the sequence probability.
statements.explanation: Multiplying by a factor below 1 always reduces the product.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The sum of the natural logs of the three token probabilities is about -0.80.
statements.explanation: The sum is ln 0.9 + ln 0.5 + ln 0.2, which is about -2.41; -0.80 is the per-token average.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A sequence probability of 0.09 means the reply is 9% likely to be factually true.
statements.explanation: The number is a probability of the text under the model, not of its truth.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The probability of the whole three-token sequence is 0.09.
statements.explanation: By the chain rule, 0.9 x 0.5 x 0.2 = 0.09.

questions.source: Where the numbers come from
questions.stem: Perplexity is the exponential of the average negative natural log probability per token. A model assigns probabilities 0.5, 0.25, 0.125 and 0.125 to the four tokens of a test sentence. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A model that assigns probability 1 to every token has a perplexity of 1.
statements.explanation: The average negative log probability is 0, and exp(0) = 1.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The perplexity on this sentence is about 4.76.
statements.explanation: The average negative log2 probability is (1 + 2 + 3 + 3) / 4 = 2.25 bits, and 2 to the power 2.25 is about 4.76.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A model that spreads probability uniformly over a 50,000-token vocabulary has a perplexity of 50,000.
statements.explanation: Each token has probability 1/50,000, so the effective number of choices is 50,000.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Perplexity measures the factual accuracy of what the model says.
statements.explanation: It measures how well the model predicts the given text, not whether the text is true.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A lower perplexity on held-out text indicates better next-token prediction on that text.
statements.explanation: Perplexity is the effective number of equally likely choices per token, so lower means sharper predictions of the actual text.

questions.source: First prompts: the same experiment, one floor up
questions.stem: A model is asked for a citation and then to "rate your confidence from 0 to 100 that this citation is real". It answers "Confidence: 95". Separately, the first token of its answer had a probability of 0.95. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Whether a model's stated or implied confidence is well calibrated has to be measured against labeled outcomes.
statements.explanation: Calibration is an empirical property assessed across many cases with known ground truth.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If this particular citation turns out to exist, the stated confidence was therefore well calibrated.
statements.explanation: One correct case cannot establish calibration; the stated number must match the hit rate across many cases.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A token probability of 0.95 means that 95% of citations the model produces are real.
statements.explanation: The token probability describes the model's distribution over next tokens, not the real-world rate of correct citations.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Looking the citation up in an independent source is a valid way to check it.
statements.explanation: An external record is independent of the process that generated the citation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The stated 95 is generated text; it was not computed by checking a bibliographic database.
statements.explanation: A verbalized confidence is produced the way any other text is produced.

questions.source: First prompts: the same experiment, one floor up
questions.stem: A model produces a citation with authors, a year, a journal name and an exact statistic for "a study on spaced repetition". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A specific, well-formed citation is not evidence that the paper exists.
statements.explanation: Models generate plausible citation-shaped text whether or not a matching source exists.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the paper is found, the quoted statistic still needs to be checked against the paper's text.
statements.explanation: A real paper can still be misquoted or misattributed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Language models sometimes produce citations that do correspond to real papers.
statements.explanation: Models do reproduce real citations, especially famous ones, but not reliably, so a match still has to be checked.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Searching a bibliographic database or the publisher's site for the exact title and authors is an independent check.
statements.explanation: An external index does not depend on the model's generation process.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Asking the same model "is this citation real?" gives an independent check.
statements.explanation: The process that produced the citation would be vouching for itself, so errors can be correlated.

questions.source: Stochastic parrots
questions.stem: Critics argue that language models stitch together sequences of linguistic form from training data without access to meaning, a position often called the "stochastic parrot" argument. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The question of whether language models understand meaning is settled in the research literature.
statements.explanation: The debate is active and unresolved.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The phrase "it's just autocomplete" is a more precise statement of the argument than the original claim.
statements.explanation: "Just autocomplete" is a weaker slogan; the argument is more specific about meaning and grounding.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Critics of the argument cite probing studies suggesting that internal representations track structure beyond surface word order, while defenders reply that internal structure is not the same as grounded reference.
statements.explanation: Both sides of this exchange exist in the literature.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The argument has a conceptual part (form alone cannot yield meaning) and an empirical part (costs, unauditable corpora, harms of unearned trust), and the two can be assessed separately.
statements.explanation: The conceptual claim about meaning and the empirical claims about consequences are different kinds of claim with different evidence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Models can produce sensible text for strings that never appeared in training, which a pure replay of observed sequences could not do.
statements.explanation: Generalization to novel strings shows that behavior is not mere lookup of memorized sequences.

questions.source: Ship It: a report that survives a skeptical reader
questions.stem: A sampling report states: "Outcome 2 was selected in 849 of 1,000 draws at temperature 0.5, so outcome 2 is the right answer." The three outcomes are labeled candidate answers with fixed scores that the programmer chose in a toy program, with no answer key involved. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Establishing correctness would require an answer key or a source check tied to a specific claim.
statements.explanation: Correctness needs a criterion external to the sampler, such as a reference answer.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The count 849 records how often an index was selected in a simulation and says nothing, by itself, about whether that candidate is correct.
statements.explanation: Selection frequency reflects the assigned probabilities, which were constructed independently of any truth.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A supportable claim is "at temperature 0.5 with this seed, the sampler selected outcome 2 in 849 of 1,000 draws".
statements.explanation: This statement reports exactly what was observed without extending it to truth.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A reviewer should accept the conclusion because the count is high.
statements.explanation: A large count shows concentration of probability, not correctness.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Rerunning with the same seed and obtaining 849 again shows that the procedure is repeatable.
statements.explanation: Identical results under a fixed seed demonstrate reproducibility.

questions.source: Build It: the baseline that lets you audit
questions.stem: A function intended to return softmax probabilities for a list of scores has a bug: it returns the correct set of probabilities but sorted into ascending order instead of in the order of the inputs. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A test that the returned probabilities sum to 1 would catch the bug.
statements.explanation: Sorting does not change the sum.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A test that the scores [3, 1, 2] give the largest probability at index 0 would catch the bug.
statements.explanation: The correct output puts the largest value first; the buggy output puts it last.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A test that equal scores give equal probabilities would catch the bug.
statements.explanation: Equal scores give equal values wherever they are placed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A test that the scores [1, 2, 3] give an ascending list of probabilities would catch the bug.
statements.explanation: The input is already ascending, so sorted output matches the correct output.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A test that every returned probability is nonnegative would catch the bug.
statements.explanation: Sorting does not change signs or magnitudes.

questions.source: The subtraction that changes nothing important
questions.stem: A unit test asserts that softmax([1000, 1000]) returns [0.5, 0.5]. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Passing the test shows that larger scores always receive larger probabilities.
statements.explanation: Both scores are equal, so the test says nothing about ordering.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Passing the test shows that the implementation does not overflow on large scores.
statements.explanation: A direct exp(1000) would overflow, so a correct result implies a stable computation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Passing the test shows that the scores [1000, 1] are also converted correctly.
statements.explanation: The test never exercises unequal scores, so it says nothing about them.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Passing the test proves the function is correct for every possible input.
statements.explanation: A single case can only show the function behaves correctly on that input.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Passing the test shows that invalid temperatures are rejected.
statements.explanation: The test never calls the function with an invalid temperature.

questions.source: The unfinished script
questions.stem: An application retrieves a policy document and places it in the prompt before asking the model to answer a question about late submissions. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Supplying the source makes an answer that matches it more likely, but not certain.
statements.explanation: Relevant context shifts probability toward answers consistent with it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Retrieval updates the model's weights for the duration of the conversation.
statements.explanation: Weights are fixed at inference time; only the context changes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The retrieved text enters as additional context tokens that the model conditions on; the model is still producing continuations of text.
statements.explanation: Retrieval changes the input, not the mechanism.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Once the source is in the prompt, the model is guaranteed to quote it faithfully.
statements.explanation: Models can still misread, omit or contradict supplied text.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If correctness matters, a check comparing the answer with the source is still needed.
statements.explanation: Independent verification catches the cases where the answer departs from the source.

questions.source: Where the numbers come from
questions.stem: A model's training data ends in a given month. A user asks about an event that happened after that month. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The model will always refuse to answer, because it knows exactly where its knowledge ends.
statements.explanation: Models often answer anyway, since refusing is just one possible continuation among many.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It may still produce a fluent, confident-sounding answer, because it continues text plausibly.
statements.explanation: Plausible continuation does not depend on the content being grounded.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The model has no training signal about that event.
statements.explanation: Anything after the cutoff was never in the training data.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Pasting a document about the event into the prompt would not help, because the model can only use what it saw in training.
statements.explanation: Text placed in the context can be used by the model whatever the training data contained.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Raising the temperature will make the model recall the event.
statements.explanation: Temperature rescales existing scores and cannot add knowledge that was never learned.

questions.source: Temperature is a concentration control, not a fact checker
questions.stem: A team chooses decoding settings for three tasks: extracting invoice numbers from scanned documents, brainstorming product names, and drafting a unit test for a given function. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Low temperature guarantees that an extracted invoice number is correct.
statements.explanation: A low temperature makes the output consistent, but a consistent output can still be wrong.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Low temperature or greedy decoding is usually appropriate for extraction, where the most likely output is wanted consistently.
statements.explanation: Extraction rewards the single most probable and repeatable output.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A higher temperature suits brainstorming, where diversity is the goal.
statements.explanation: A flatter distribution produces more varied candidates.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Sampling several candidate tests and keeping only those that pass an automated check is a reasonable way to use randomness for code generation.
statements.explanation: Generating diverse candidates and filtering them with an external check combines variety with verification.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Setting the temperature as high as possible is best for unit tests, because creativity finds more bugs.
statements.explanation: Extremely high temperature yields incoherent text and invalid code.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against your gate
questions.stem: A developer asks an AI coding assistant to implement a softmax-with-temperature function and also to write the tests for it. All the tests pass. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An AI model checking another AI model's work is always as good as an independent human review.
statements.explanation: Reviewers with correlated blind spots, or with no stake in the result, do not equal independent review.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Tests written by the same system that wrote the implementation may share its misunderstandings, so passing is weaker evidence than passing tests written independently.
statements.explanation: Correlated errors between author and checker let a shared mistake pass unnoticed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: All tests passing proves that the implementation has no bugs.
statements.explanation: Tests show only that the cases tried pass.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Asking the assistant to propose a deliberately wrong implementation and checking whether it also passes the tests is a way to judge how strong the tests are.
statements.explanation: A mutant that survives reveals a gap in the tests.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Writing the specification and the tests before requesting the code gives an independent standard to measure the result against.
statements.explanation: A specification fixed in advance cannot be bent to fit the code that was produced.

questions.source: One question, asked over and over
questions.stem: A model has a vocabulary of 50,000 tokens. At each step it produces a score for every token and a softmax converts the scores into probabilities. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Softmax automatically excludes tokens that would be ungrammatical.
statements.explanation: Grammaticality is encoded only through the scores the model learned, not through any rule in the softmax.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Every token receives a strictly positive probability, including absurd continuations.
statements.explanation: The exponential of any finite score is positive, so no token has zero probability.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Truncation methods such as top-k can set the probabilities of low-ranked tokens to zero.
statements.explanation: Top-k and top-p remove tokens explicitly after the softmax and renormalize.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Absurd continuations receive very small probabilities rather than being excluded.
statements.explanation: Softmax ranks candidates; it does not exclude any.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A token whose probability is 10^-9 can never be sampled.
statements.explanation: A tiny probability is still positive, so across many draws such a token can be sampled.

questions.source: A distribution is not the sample you happened to see
questions.stem: A model's scores yield a probability of 0.70 for the answer "approve". In 1,000 independent draws, "approve" is selected 690 times. A separate, independent audit of the case finds that the correct answer is "reject". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: 0.70 is the probability the sampler assigned and 0.69 is the frequency observed in this sample; they are different quantities.
statements.explanation: The assigned probability describes the distribution; the observed frequency describes one sample from it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The observed frequency of 0.69 shows that "approve" is correct.
statements.explanation: Frequency of selection says how often the sampler chose a label, not whether it is right.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The 0.01 gap between them shows that the sampler is broken.
statements.explanation: The standard error at 1,000 draws is about 0.0145, so a gap of 0.01 is ordinary noise.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because the model assigned 0.70 to "approve", 70% of cases like this one truly deserve "approve".
statements.explanation: A probability assigned by a model is not the same as the real-world rate of correctness unless calibration has been established.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Whether "approve" is correct is settled by the audit against ground truth, not by the distribution.
statements.explanation: Correctness requires an external criterion such as an audited answer.

questions.source: A source identifier is an address, not an argument
questions.stem: A question-answering system must answer only from supplied documents. One supplied document, with identifier doc-A, reads: "The warehouse opens at 9:00." The consumer's validator checks only that the response is a JSON object with the keys answer and cites, that answer is a nonblank string, and that every entry in cites is a supplied document identifier. The model returns {"answer": "The warehouse opens at 7:00.", "cites": ["doc-A"]}. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The response is faithful to the document it cites.
statements.explanation: The document says 9:00 and the answer says 7:00, so the answer contradicts its source.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A check that compares the claim with the text of doc-A would reject this response.
statements.explanation: Only a content-level comparison of claim against source text can detect the contradiction.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Citing an identifier that exists shows the cited document supports the claim.
statements.explanation: An identifier is an address; whether the text at that address supports the claim is a separate question.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The response passes the validator.
statements.explanation: The object has the right keys, a nonblank answer, and a cited identifier that was supplied, so every implemented rule is satisfied.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Listing the allowed document identifiers as an enumeration inside a JSON schema would reject this response.
statements.explanation: The identifier doc-A is on the allowed list, so an identifier enumeration accepts the response.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.stem: A prompt tells a model: "Return only a JSON object with the keys name and age." The calling code runs json.loads on whatever comes back and passes the result to a function that reads both keys. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The instruction is enforced by the runtime once the model has read it, so replies conform.
statements.explanation: A prompt is text that conditions a sampler; nothing in the runtime forces the reply to follow it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A reply that parses as JSON will contain both keys.
statements.explanation: Valid JSON can be a list, a string, or an object with other keys; parsing says nothing about required keys.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Strengthening the wording of the instruction ("you MUST comply") makes the post-response check unnecessary.
statements.explanation: Emphatic wording lowers but does not remove the failure rate, and only a check detects the failures that remain.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Decoding constrained to a JSON schema also makes the value of age true.
statements.explanation: Constrained decoding enforces structure, but the truth of a value is beyond what a schema can enforce.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The model can ignore or misread the instruction, so the instruction alone does not guarantee conforming output.
statements.explanation: A prompt is a request to a probabilistic generator and can be disobeyed or misunderstood.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.stem: A downstream function unpacks exactly two fields, answer and sources, from each model response and raises an exception on any other field. Validator X requires exactly those two keys. Validator Y requires those two keys and ignores any extra keys. A model returns an object with answer, sources, and a plausible-looking extra key named confidence. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The better of the two validators can be chosen without knowing what the consumer does with the object.
statements.explanation: Strictness versus tolerance is a trade-off whose right answer depends on the downstream job.

statements.label: B
statements.text: For a consumer that crashes on unexpected fields, Validator Y is the safer choice.
statements.explanation: Y would pass the extra field through and the consumer would crash; X turns the surprise into a visible rejection.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Validator Y accepts the response.
statements.explanation: Y checks only that the required keys exist and is silent about additions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Validator X rejects the response.
statements.explanation: The key set is not exactly the two required keys, so X rejects.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Rejecting a response because of a reasonable-looking extra field only shows the validator is badly designed.
statements.explanation: For a consumer that crashes on unexpected fields, rejecting at the boundary is the protective behavior.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.stem: Two teams build a prompt that extracts invoice totals for a billing program. Team 1 writes down the required output object, the test cases, and what counts as correct before writing any prompt. Team 2 adjusts the prompt until the outputs look right to them, then writes a checker that accepts what the final prompt produces. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Team 1 should keep its criteria fixed even when outputs show them to be incomplete.
statements.explanation: Criteria can be revised when a gap appears, provided the change is recorded as a new version.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Team 2's checker risks encoding whatever the prompt happened to produce rather than what the billing program needs.
statements.explanation: A criterion written after tuning is a description of the outputs, so passing it is close to circular.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Team 2's pass rate on its own checker is strong evidence that the prompt meets the consumer's needs.
statements.explanation: Agreement with a checker built from the outputs measures consistency with those outputs, not fitness for the consumer.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Team 1's acceptance criterion exists independently of any particular output.
statements.explanation: A criterion fixed beforehand can fail an output; one fitted afterward cannot.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Writing criteria first removes the need for a separate held-out set.
statements.explanation: Fixing criteria early addresses a different problem from overfitting to the cases used while iterating.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.stem: A developer asks a coding assistant to implement a validator from one line: "the output must have an answer and a list of sources." The line does not say whether extra keys are allowed, whether the list may be empty, or what to do with a whitespace-only answer. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Tests written in advance for these edge cases would reveal which interpretation was chosen.
statements.explanation: Edge-case tests turn silent choices into observable pass or fail results.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Whatever interpretation it picks becomes the validator's behavior even though no one decided it.
statements.explanation: Unspecified behavior is still behavior, and it will be exercised in production.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Passing the developer's one happy-path example shows the unspecified cases are handled correctly.
statements.explanation: A happy-path example exercises none of the unspecified cases.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The assistant may silently pick an interpretation for each unspecified case.
statements.explanation: Generators fill gaps with something plausible rather than reliably flagging them.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The requester removes the ambiguity by stating the unspecified cases or by writing tests for them.
statements.explanation: Only the requester knows what the consumer needs, so closing the gaps in the specification is theirs to do.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.stem: A grounded question-answering contract requires every response to have a nonblank answer string and a nonempty list of supplied source identifiers, and nothing else. A user asks a question that the supplied sources do not address. The model replies {"answer": "The sources do not say.", "sources": ["doc-2"]}, where doc-2 is a supplied identifier. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The contract already gives the consumer a distinct signal whenever the system abstains.
statements.explanation: With no status field, an abstention and an assertion look identical to the consumer.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The validator cannot tell this honest non-answer apart from a factual assertion.
statements.explanation: The validator sees a nonblank string and a known identifier; it has no notion of what the sentence means.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The response is invalid because doc-2 does not contain the answer.
statements.explanation: Validity here is defined by the structural rules, which this response satisfies; support is a separate judgment.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Adding the line "be accurate" to the prompt supplies a refusal state in the output.
statements.explanation: An instruction to be accurate adds no output field, so the consumer still cannot see a refusal.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Adding an explicit status field to represent abstention would require changing the validator and its tests, a new version of the contract.
statements.explanation: A closed, exact-key contract rejects a new field until the contract itself is changed and retested.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.stem: Before any prompt is written for a feature whose output a program will consume, a team prepares a written acceptance plan. Check each statement that is true about what belongs in such a plan.

statements.label: A
statements.text: It should name wrong implementations or outputs the tests are expected to catch, including a well-formed but unsupported answer that structural tests cannot catch.
statements.explanation: Listing the failures to be caught keeps the plan honest about which defects tests cover and which need content review.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It defines in advance how a response will be judged supported by evidence, including a category for answers that cannot be judged.
statements.explanation: A pre-fixed evidence criterion, with an unknown outcome, prevents redefining success after seeing results.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It names the program that consumes the output and what that program needs from it.
statements.explanation: The consumer's needs are the only criterion that exists before any output does.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It can be left empty until the first outputs arrive, since the format cannot be known earlier.
statements.explanation: The required output shape comes from the consumer, not from observing the model.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It lists test cases and separates those used while iterating from those held back.
statements.explanation: A split fixed beforehand is what allows later measurement on untouched cases.

questions.source: Ship It: an experiment another person can audit
questions.stem: A strict consumer expects each raw response to be a JSON document. A model's reply is a Markdown code fence containing {"answer": "42", "sources": ["a"]}, introduced by one sentence of prose. A teammate deletes the sentence and the fence by hand and scores the cleaned string as a pass. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Whether the consumer should tolerate fenced replies is a contract decision to make before measuring.
statements.explanation: Tolerance changes what counts as acceptable, so it must be decided as part of the acceptance rule.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Scoring only the cleaned version measures something different from what the model produced.
statements.explanation: The cleaned string reflects a human repair, so its pass says nothing about unrepaired model output.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Keeping both the original and the cleaned text in the record lets a reader see what the model emitted.
statements.explanation: Preserving the original keeps the observation distinct from the transformation applied to it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Cleaning the reply is harmless to the measurement because the JSON inside is identical.
statements.explanation: The part that was removed is exactly what made the consumer's strict parse fail.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Running json.loads on the original reply raises an error.
statements.explanation: Prose and backticks are not valid JSON, so strict parsing fails.

questions.source: What each line of the validator promises
questions.stem: A validator checks sources with the Python expression mode(s in allowed for s in sources), where allowed = {"a", "b"} and mode is either all or any. It is called with sources = ["a", "zzz"] and, separately, with sources = []. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: With mode = all, the input ["a", "zzz"] is rejected.
statements.explanation: all requires every entry to be allowed, and "zzz" is not.

statements.label: B
statements.text: With mode = all, the input [] is accepted.
statements.explanation: all over an empty sequence is vacuously True, so an empty list passes unless something else rejects it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Using all makes a separate nonempty-list check unnecessary.
statements.explanation: Because all is True on an empty list, emptiness has to be rejected by a check of its own.

statements.label: D
statements.text: With mode = any, the input [] is accepted.
statements.explanation: any over an empty sequence is False, so an empty list is rejected by any.

statements.label: E
statements.text: With mode = any, the input ["a", "zzz"] is accepted.
statements.explanation: any returns True when at least one entry is allowed, and "a" is allowed.

questions.source: What each line of the validator promises
questions.stem: A validator enforces the contract "a JSON object with exactly the keys title (a nonblank string) and tags (a list of strings)". It receives three inputs. Input 1 is {"title": "Report", "tags": ["x"] with the closing brace missing. Input 2 is ["title", "tags"]. Input 3 is {"title": 7, "tags": ["x"]}. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Input 2 would be accepted by a check that only requires json.loads to succeed.
statements.explanation: A parse-only check accepts any syntactically valid JSON value, including a list.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Input 1 fails at parsing, so no field rule is applied to it.
statements.explanation: A syntax error stops processing at the parser, before any structural or field rule is reached.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Input 3 parses to an object with the right keys and fails on a field type.
statements.explanation: The keys match, but title must be a string and 7 is an integer.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The three failures are best described identically as "bad formatting" for the purpose of diagnosis.
statements.explanation: Parser, shape and type failures point to different repairs and should be distinguished.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Input 2 parses successfully but is the wrong kind of value for the contract.
statements.explanation: A list is valid JSON but not an object, so the shape rule rejects it.

questions.source: What each line of the validator promises
questions.stem: A validator treats a string field as nonblank when bool(value.strip()) is True in Python. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Without the strip() call, the value "   " would still be rejected.
statements.explanation: A string of spaces is a nonempty string and is truthy, so without strip() it would pass.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The value "n/a" fails the check because it is a placeholder.
statements.explanation: Any visible characters pass; the check does not recognize placeholders.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The value "   " (three spaces) fails the check.
statements.explanation: Stripping leaves an empty string, which is falsy.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Passing the check shows the answer is relevant to the question asked.
statements.explanation: Nonblank is a property of the characters, not of relevance, correctness or completeness.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The value "0" passes the check.
statements.explanation: The string "0" is nonempty after stripping, and nonempty strings are truthy even when they look like zero.

questions.source: What each line of the validator promises
questions.stem: A validator accepts a response only if it parses as a JSON object with exactly the keys answer and sources; answer is a nonblank string; sources is a nonempty list; and every entry of sources is a string in the allowed set {"a", "b"}. The test suite has five tests: (1) a valid object with sources ["a"]; (2) text that is not JSON; (3) answer equal to the integer 1; (4) sources equal to ["zzz"]; (5) an object with an additional key. Three mutated copies of the validator are made. M1 replaces "every entry" with "at least one entry". M2 deletes the nonblank part of the answer check but keeps the string-type check. M3 deletes the nonempty-list check but keeps the every-entry check. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: M1 still passes all five tests.
statements.explanation: Test 4 has a single unknown entry, which "at least one" also rejects, so the mutant is not exposed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: M2 still passes all five tests.
statements.explanation: No test supplies a blank answer, so deleting that check changes no test outcome.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Adding a test with sources ["a", "zzz"] would distinguish M1 from the original.
statements.explanation: The mixed list is accepted by "at least one" and rejected by "every entry", so the outcomes differ.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Passing all five tests shows the original validator implements the specification.
statements.explanation: Tests defend only the behaviors they exercise; three lines of the specification are undefended here.

statements.label: E
statements.text: M3 still passes all five tests.
statements.explanation: No test supplies an empty list, so the deletion goes unnoticed.

questions.source: What each line of the validator promises
questions.stem: A validator returns only True or False. A maintainer wants to understand why 30 of 200 responses failed. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A Boolean alone does not tell the maintainer which rule rejected a response.
statements.explanation: The Boolean collapses every rejection into one symbol, discarding the reason.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Adding reason codes means the validator now accepts a different set of responses.
statements.explanation: Labeling the reason for a rejection can leave the accept-or-reject decision untouched.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A Boolean is easy to aggregate into a pass rate.
statements.explanation: Summing True values and dividing by the count gives a rate directly.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Two failures that both count as zero in the pass rate call for the same repair, since the rate treats them alike.
statements.explanation: A non-JSON reply and a single bad identifier both score zero but are repaired differently.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Returning a reason such as parse error, key mismatch, wrong type or unknown source would let failures be tallied by category.
statements.explanation: A categorical reason preserves information a pass rate throws away.

questions.source: What each line of the validator promises
questions.stem: A validator must ensure that the field count is an integer, and implements this with isinstance(value, int) after parsing with json.loads. In Python, bool is a subclass of int. The inputs are {"count": true}, {"count": 3}, {"count": 3.0} and {"count": "3"}. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The input with "3" passes the isinstance check.
statements.explanation: A quoted number parses to a string.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Adding "and not isinstance(value, bool)" would reject the input with true.
statements.explanation: Excluding bool explicitly rejects True and False while still accepting ordinary integers.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The input with 3 passes the isinstance check.
statements.explanation: JSON 3 parses to the integer 3.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The input with true passes the isinstance check.
statements.explanation: A JSON true parses to Python True, which is an instance of int.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The input with 3.0 passes the isinstance check.
statements.explanation: JSON 3.0 parses to a float, which is not an instance of int.

questions.source: What each line of the validator promises
questions.stem: A validator relies on Python's json.loads with default settings to parse replies. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The bare token NaN is rejected as invalid.
statements.explanation: Python's parser accepts NaN and Infinity by default, an extension beyond the JSON standard.

statements.label: B
statements.text: For an object with a duplicated key, the later value silently replaces the earlier one.
statements.explanation: Python keeps the last occurrence of a duplicated key without any warning.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A reply consisting only of the number 7 parses successfully, so a separate shape check is still needed.
statements.explanation: Any JSON value parses, including a bare number, so shape must be checked after parsing.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A reply with a trailing comma inside an object raises a JSONDecodeError.
statements.explanation: Trailing commas are not permitted in JSON, and the standard parser raises an error.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A string quoted with single quotes is accepted as a JSON string.
statements.explanation: JSON strings must use double quotes; single quotes raise an error.

questions.source: What each line of the validator promises
questions.stem: A service asks a model for a JSON object with a long free-text answer field. About 6% of replies fail to parse. Inspection shows that each failing reply ends in the middle of a string, and the API response reports that generation stopped because the maximum output length was reached. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Rewording the schema description in the prompt is the only possible remedy.
statements.explanation: The cause is length, not wording, so changing the schema description may not help at all.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Truncation by the output limit is a plausible explanation for these parse failures.
statements.explanation: A reply cut off mid-string cannot be valid JSON, and the reported stop reason matches.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Recording the stop reason would let the pipeline separate truncation from other kinds of format failure.
statements.explanation: The stop reason distinguishes an incomplete reply from a complete but malformed one.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Raising the output limit or asking for shorter answers could reduce this failure.
statements.explanation: Giving the answer room, or shortening it, addresses the mechanism that is cutting the reply.

statements.label: E
statements.text: These failures show the model does not understand JSON.
statements.explanation: The same model produces valid JSON on shorter replies; the failure is mechanical, not conceptual.

questions.source: What a pass rate leaves out
questions.stem: A pipeline validates each response and, on failure, resends the request with the validator's error message appended, up to two further attempts. Over 100 requests, 70 pass on the first attempt, 20 of the 30 failures pass on a retry, and 10 still fail after the retries. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reporting only the final 90% fairly describes how reliably the model follows the contract in a single try.
statements.explanation: The final rate hides that 30% of single attempts failed; first-pass and final rates answer different questions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Retries add cost and latency.
statements.explanation: Each retry is another model call, so spend and wait time rise.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The final pass rate after retries is 80%.
statements.explanation: 70 first-attempt passes plus 20 recovered by retries gives 90 of 100, not 80.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A response that passes after a retry is thereby shown to be supported by its sources.
statements.explanation: The validator checks structure; passing after a retry says nothing about whether the content is supported.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The first-attempt pass rate is 70%.
statements.explanation: 70 of 100 requests passed without any retry.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.stem: A provider offers a "JSON mode", in which output is guaranteed to be syntactically valid JSON, and a schema-constrained mode, in which output is guaranteed to conform to a supplied JSON schema. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A rule such as "the quoted span must appear in the supplied source text" can be expressed directly in a JSON schema.
statements.explanation: A schema validates one document in isolation and cannot reference external source text.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Schema-constrained output cannot contain a wrong value in a correctly typed field.
statements.explanation: A schema constrains types and structure; a correctly typed field can still hold a false value.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Output that is syntactically valid JSON need not contain the keys the consumer requires.
statements.explanation: Valid syntax means the text parses; any object, list or scalar qualifies.

statements.label: D
statements.text: With schema-constrained output, the cited sources can be assumed to support the claims.
statements.explanation: Support is a relation between a claim and external text, which a schema does not model.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Using schema-constrained output makes held-out evaluation of answer quality unnecessary.
statements.explanation: Structure and quality are different properties, and quality still has to be measured on cases the prompt was not tuned on.

questions.source: Ship It: an experiment another person can audit
questions.stem: A response states two claims in one answer: (1) "The refund window is 30 days" and (2) "Refunds are paid in cash." It cites one supplied document, which reads: "Refunds can be requested within 30 days of purchase." The document says nothing about how refunds are paid. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Judging the answer requires comparing each claim with the cited text separately.
statements.explanation: A multi-claim answer needs a claim-by-claim comparison, because support can be partial.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Because the citation is valid for claim 1, the whole answer counts as supported.
statements.explanation: One correct citation cannot stand in for the support of every claim in the answer.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Claim 2 is not supported by the cited document.
statements.explanation: Nothing in the document mentions cash or any payment method.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because the document is about refunds, claim 2 is supported by implication.
statements.explanation: Topical relevance is not entailment; a document about refunds does not support an unstated payment method.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Claim 1 is supported by the cited document.
statements.explanation: The document states the 30-day window directly.

questions.source: A source identifier is an address, not an argument
questions.stem: To check a model's answer, a team sends the same model the answer and the source and asks "Is this answer supported by the source?" The model replies "Yes." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The reply is new model output that itself needs evaluation.
statements.explanation: A verdict from a model is another generation, not ground truth.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A model asked to review its own answer is as independent as a second reviewer would be.
statements.explanation: The same model shares its training and blind spots, so its review is not a second, independent opinion.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Only the model that wrote an answer is qualified to judge it, since only it knows what it meant.
statements.explanation: A judge is trusted because its agreement with a standard has been measured, and independence comes from a different failure profile, not from authorship.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because the model said yes, the error rate of this check is known to be zero.
statements.explanation: A single "yes" gives no information about how often such judgments are wrong.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A check built on a different mechanism, such as matching a quoted span against the source, a human reviewer, or a separately validated classifier, fails differently from the generator.
statements.explanation: Independence comes from a different failure profile, which is what makes a check informative.

questions.source: A source identifier is an address, not an argument
questions.stem: Evaluation methods are commonly grouped as code-graded (a program checks the output), model-graded (another model scores the output) and human-graded. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Model-graded evaluation can scale to open-ended outputs, but its agreement with human judgments needs to be checked.
statements.explanation: A model judge handles outputs no program can score, but it must be calibrated against human labels.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Checking that a response parses as JSON with the required keys is naturally code-graded.
statements.explanation: Structure and key presence are deterministic properties a program can test.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Exact string comparison with a reference is a good grader for free-form summaries.
statements.explanation: Many different wordings are equally good summaries, so exact match scores correct paraphrases as wrong.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Human grading is the cheapest and fastest of the three.
statements.explanation: Human review is typically the slowest and most expensive method.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Different methods are often combined, each used on a different aspect of the same output.
statements.explanation: Cheap programmatic checks for form, plus judged or human review for content, is a standard layering.

questions.source: A source identifier is an address, not an argument
questions.stem: A team uses a language model to choose the better of two candidate answers. Check each statement that is true about known risks of such judges.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Judge verdicts can vary from run to run when sampling is used, so repeated judging may be needed.
statements.explanation: Sampled judgments are not deterministic, so their variation should be measured.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Once the judge's scores look plausible, comparing them with human labels is unnecessary.
statements.explanation: Plausible-looking scores say nothing about agreement with the standard you care about, which has to be measured.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A judge can favor whichever answer is shown first, so swapping the order and checking consistency is a useful control.
statements.explanation: Position bias is documented, and order swapping exposes it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A judge can favor longer answers independent of their quality.
statements.explanation: Verbosity bias is a documented tendency of model judges.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A judge can rate text from its own model family more favorably.
statements.explanation: Self-preference has been observed and is a reason to use a judge from a different family or to calibrate.

questions.source: A prompt revision is a hypothesis
questions.stem: A team has 100 labelled questions and splits them into a development set and a held-out set. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Development cases may be inspected and used to revise the prompt.
statements.explanation: The point of a development set is to learn from it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A held-out score stays an unbiased estimate no matter how many prompt variants were chosen by comparing their held-out scores.
statements.explanation: Selecting among many variants using the held-out score biases it upward, which is a form of overfitting.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A held-out case is still held out after its failure has been used to decide a prompt change.
statements.explanation: Once a case has influenced a decision, it has become development evidence.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the held-out set has been used for tuning, relabeling it as untouched restores its status.
statements.explanation: Status depends on what influenced decisions, not on a label; only fresh data restores an untouched check.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Held-out cases should be shown to the prompt author early so they know what to optimize for.
statements.explanation: Seeing the cases early turns them into development data; they should stay unseen until the revision is frozen.

questions.source: A prompt revision is a hypothesis
questions.stem: A team adds three example input-output pairs to a prompt (few-shot prompting). Afterward they notice that one of the examples is also one of the 10 questions in their held-out set. The revised prompt scores 10/10 on the held-out set and the baseline prompt scores 7/10. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The 10/10 result cannot be taken as clean evidence that the revision helps.
statements.explanation: Part of the gain may come from the leaked item, and the size of that part is unknown.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Near-paraphrases of held-out questions placed in the prompt can also contaminate the held-out measurement.
statements.explanation: Overlap in content, not only identical items, can leak answers and inflate the score.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The three-question gap shows that the examples improved the model's format discipline.
statements.explanation: Nothing in the data attributes the gap to format discipline rather than to the leaked item or to noise.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Removing the leaked item and rescoring both prompts on the remaining 9 questions gives a cleaner, though smaller, comparison.
statements.explanation: Dropping contaminated items and rescoring both versions on the same remaining set restores a like-for-like comparison.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The prompt now contains the answer to one held-out question, so that item no longer measures generalization.
statements.explanation: An item whose answer is in the prompt tests recall of the prompt, not skill on unseen cases.

questions.source: A prompt revision is a hypothesis
questions.stem: Prompt v1 scored 5/10 on a question set and prompt v2 scored 8/10. Between the two runs, the developer added two examples, switched to a newer model version, rewrote the task description, and replaced several questions with easier ones. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A controlled comparison changes one identifiable feature and holds the rest fixed.
statements.explanation: Isolating one change is what lets an observed difference be attributed to it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Because the score rose, the added examples must be the cause.
statements.explanation: A rise accompanied by several simultaneous changes cannot be pinned on any one.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Changing the question set means 5/10 and 8/10 are not a like-for-like comparison.
statements.explanation: Easier questions raise scores on their own, independent of the prompt.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A written log of each change helps a later reader see what could explain the difference.
statements.explanation: A change log makes the candidate explanations visible and auditable.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It is not possible to tell which change produced the difference.
statements.explanation: Four changes overlap, so effects are confounded.

questions.source: A prompt revision is a hypothesis
questions.stem: Prompt A scores 7/10 and prompt B scores 8/10 on the same ten questions. Treat each question as an independent pass-or-fail trial. For a true pass probability of 0.75, the standard error of a proportion measured over n trials is sqrt(0.75 x 0.25 / n), which is about 0.137 for n = 10 and about 0.043 for n = 100. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The data show that B is reliably better than A.
statements.explanation: A difference smaller than the sampling noise cannot establish which prompt is better.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Evaluating on 100 questions at the same rate would shrink the standard error to about 1.4 percentage points.
statements.explanation: At n = 100 the standard error is about 4.3 points, a threefold reduction and not tenfold.

statements.label: C
statements.text: With ten questions, the standard error is roughly 14 percentage points.
statements.explanation: 0.137 is about 14 points.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Evaluating more questions would not change the standard error, which depends only on the pass probability.
statements.explanation: Standard error falls with the square root of the number of trials.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The one-question difference (10 percentage points) is larger than the standard error.
statements.explanation: Ten points is smaller than the standard error of about 14 points.

questions.source: A prompt revision is a hypothesis
questions.stem: A developer runs a prompt once at temperature 0.8 on ten questions and reports 9/10 correct. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A second run may produce different outputs and a different score.
statements.explanation: Sampling at non-zero temperature draws different tokens on different runs.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Run-to-run sampling noise is negligible compared with real prompt effects.
statements.explanation: On small sets, noise can be as large as the effects being compared.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Repeating the run several times adds no information beyond a single run.
statements.explanation: Repeated runs show how much of a score is sampling noise.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A single run suffices because output is a deterministic function of the prompt.
statements.explanation: At temperature above zero, the output is a random draw, not a fixed function of the prompt.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Setting the temperature to 0 makes the outputs of a hosted model identical on every run.
