statements.explanation: Greedy decoding reduces variation, but hosted systems do not promise bit-identical outputs.

questions.source: A prompt revision is a hypothesis
questions.stem: A teammate claims that starting a prompt with "You are an expert analyst" makes answers more accurate because experts are accurate. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An observed difference should be reported together with its conditions (cases, model, criterion) rather than credited to the role line.
statements.explanation: Reporting conditions tells a reader what the result does and does not cover.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The role line supplies new supporting facts that the model can use.
statements.explanation: A role label adds no source passages or facts.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The role line is an untested hypothesis until it is compared with the same prompt without it on fixed cases.
statements.explanation: Any prompt change is a hypothesis, and only a comparison on fixed cases can support it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If it helps on one test set, the improvement carries over to other tasks and models.
statements.explanation: Effects found on one set of cases, one model and one criterion need not transfer.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A persona line changes what a code validator checks about the output.
statements.explanation: A validator checks the returned object against fixed rules, whatever persona text produced it.

questions.source: A prompt revision is a hypothesis
questions.stem: After testing a revised prompt on 10 development cases, a developer's write-up lists only the 8 cases that improved and omits the other 2. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reporting failures harms credibility, so they should be left out.
statements.explanation: Disclosing failures is what makes the reported successes believable.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Showing only successes prevents readers from assessing which failure modes remain.
statements.explanation: Failures are where the remaining risk shows.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Omitting the cases that did not improve overstates the result.
statements.explanation: Selective reporting inflates apparent effectiveness.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A change-log entry that names the specific instruction changed, and why, lets a later reader reconstruct what differed.
statements.explanation: Specific entries make the candidate explanations for a difference visible.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A revision that fails to help is still an informative result when the trail is intact.
statements.explanation: A documented negative result tells others what not to repeat.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.stem: Two plans are proposed for judging whether answers are "supported" by their sources. Plan 1 fixes the definition of supported, including how to handle cases where the sources are insufficient, before any outputs are seen. Plan 2 defines it after seeing which prompt produced the more fluent answers. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A two-outcome criterion is more informative than one that adds a cannot-be-determined outcome, because it forces a decision.
statements.explanation: An unknown outcome keeps unverifiable answers from being forced into pass or fail.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Fixing the criterion before seeing outputs reduces the flexibility available to bias the conclusion.
statements.explanation: Committing in advance removes a source of unconscious or motivated adjustment.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Answers that cannot be determined should be counted as supported when they read fluently.
statements.explanation: Fluency is not evidence; unverified answers should be reported as unverified.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Plan 2 lets the definition drift toward whatever favors the preferred prompt.
statements.explanation: A threshold adjusted after seeing results can be tuned until the expected winner wins.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Plan 1 eliminates all disagreement between reviewers.
statements.explanation: A pre-fixed definition reduces ambiguity but reviewers can still read a case differently.

questions.source: Work through the three-response experiment
questions.stem: Reviewers tend to rate answers that read smoothly and confidently as more trustworthy. Check each statement that is true about this tendency and how to counter it.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Writing down the failure condition before reading any output helps counter it.
statements.explanation: A criterion fixed in advance resists being bent by how persuasive an answer reads.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A green result from an automated check removes the need for a content review.
statements.explanation: An automated check covers only what it tests; content support needs its own review.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A confident, well-formatted answer deserves more trust than a hesitant one.
statements.explanation: Confidence of presentation is not evidence of accuracy.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Fluency and factual correctness are separate properties of an output.
statements.explanation: Fluent text can be false, and awkward text can be right.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Verifying outputs costs more than producing them, so verification is often under-budgeted.
statements.explanation: Generation is cheap and checking is not, so checks that are not planned for tend not to happen.

questions.source: What a pass rate leaves out
questions.stem: A report says only: "The revised prompt achieved a higher pass rate." Check each statement that is true about what a reader cannot tell from that sentence.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A gain in format compliance could coincide with a loss of factual support, and the sentence would not reveal it.
statements.explanation: Aggregate pass rates compress different kinds of failure into one number.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The number of cases is irrelevant to interpreting the claim.
statements.explanation: A rate over 5 cases and a rate over 500 carry very different weight.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The reader cannot tell whether the baseline was run on the same cases.
statements.explanation: A comparison is only meaningful when both versions face the same cases.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The reader cannot tell what the pass criterion was.
statements.explanation: "Pass" depends entirely on which checks were applied.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The reader cannot tell whether the cases had been used while revising the prompt.
statements.explanation: Cases used for tuning inflate the result, so their status matters.

questions.source: Ship It: an experiment another person can audit
questions.stem: An experiment compared two prompts on the same 10 fixed cases. The format validator accepted 6 of 10 baseline responses and 10 of 10 revised responses. The team then reviewed support, claim by claim against the sources, for 4 of the 10 revised answers and found all 4 supported. Nothing else was checked, on one model on one date. Check each statement that the evidence justifies.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The 6 unreviewed revised answers can be reported as supported because they passed the validator.
statements.explanation: Passing a structural validator is not a support judgment, so those six remain unreviewed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The revised prompt is better than the baseline in general.
statements.explanation: Ten cases, one model and one date cannot support a general claim.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The 4 reviewed revised answers were supported by their sources.
statements.explanation: Those four were checked claim by claim and found supported.

statements.label: D
statements.text: On these 10 cases, the revised prompt passed the format validator more often than the baseline.
statements.explanation: 10 of 10 against 6 of 10 on the same cases is a recorded difference in validator acceptance.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The revised answers are accurate.
statements.explanation: Only four answers were reviewed, so accuracy of the set is not established.

questions.source: Computational Skepticism
questions.stem: To test robustness, a team writes three paraphrases of one question, keeping every fact and requirement the same, and runs each against the same prompt. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Answers that word the same facts differently show that the prompt is not robust.
statements.explanation: Many different wordings can satisfy the same task; what must hold fixed is the facts and obligations.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Comparing format validity, claim content and support separately shows which dimension moved.
statements.explanation: A change in format alone is a different finding from a change in claim content.

statements.label: C
statements.text: What must stay invariant under rewording can be decided after seeing the results.
statements.explanation: Deciding afterward lets the line be drawn to fit the observations.

statements.label: D
statements.text: After the paraphrase results are used to revise the prompt, those paraphrases remain untouched held-out evidence.
statements.explanation: Once results guide a revision, the cases have become development evidence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Differences in tone or sentence structure in the answers may be acceptable variation, while an altered fact is not.
statements.explanation: The invariant is the intended meaning and obligations, not the surface wording.

questions.source: From acceptable text to consequential action
questions.stem: An agent emits the tool call {"tool": "delete_file", "path": "/data/reports"} and the call validates against the tool-call schema. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Passing schema validation shows the call is well formed.
statements.explanation: The call has the expected fields and types.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Authorization should be enforced by permissions and allowlists outside the model's output.
statements.explanation: Least-privilege access and allowlists enforce limits whatever the model emits.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Passing schema validation does not establish that the agent is permitted to delete that path.
statements.explanation: A schema describes shape; permission is a separate policy question.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A schema-valid tool call is safe to execute.
statements.explanation: Well-formed and safe are different properties, and a well-formed call can still be destructive.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Even for a schema-valid call, destructive actions benefit from human confirmation or a reversible mechanism.
statements.explanation: Approval and undo mechanisms address consequences that no schema can judge.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against your gate
questions.stem: A developer gives an AI coding assistant a contract and a list of tests, but not the developer's own validator. The assistant returns an implementation, and the developer runs the developer's own tests on it. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Once an assistant is available, writing a baseline implementation first is wasted effort.
statements.explanation: A baseline written first gives an independent reference and shows what you understood before the assistant contributed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A failing test may reveal a gap in the contract or the tests, not only a defect in the assistant's code.
statements.explanation: The assistant works only from what it was given, so its mistakes can trace back to incomplete specifications.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Passing tests that the assistant wrote itself shows the developer's tests are redundant.
statements.explanation: Tests written by the same party share its assumptions and do not replace independent tests.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The assistant's own tests passing is sufficient evidence of correctness.
statements.explanation: Tests written by the same party that wrote the code share its assumptions.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The assistant can judge, from the same context, whether the tests are adequate, so no independent check is needed.
statements.explanation: Adequacy of the tests is the thing under question, and a system cannot be the only judge of tests on its own work.

questions.source: A prompt revision is a hypothesis
questions.stem: A team is building evaluation cases for a grounded question-answering feature, where answers must come only from supplied documents. Check each statement that is true about sound case design.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Adversarial boundary cases and a random sample of live traffic answer the same question, so their pass rates can be pooled freely.
statements.explanation: Boundary cases probe worst-case behavior while traffic samples estimate typical frequency; pooling them blurs both.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Dozens of near-duplicate cases carry as much information as the same number of diverse cases.
statements.explanation: Near-duplicates mostly repeat the same test and add little independent evidence.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A set drawn only from the very hardest cases estimates typical production behavior.
statements.explanation: Typical behavior requires a sample that resembles typical use, not only extremes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A set containing only easy, clean cases produces a flattering pass rate that may not predict real use.
statements.explanation: Case difficulty drives the rate, so easy cases overstate reliability.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Including questions the supplied documents cannot answer tests whether the system abstains instead of inventing.
statements.explanation: Unanswerable questions are the only way to observe abstention behavior.

questions.source: What a pass rate leaves out
questions.stem: A grounded question-answering test set has 20 answerable questions and 10 unanswerable ones. On the 20 answerable questions the system answers 17 correctly, wrongly abstains on 2, and answers 1 incorrectly. On the 10 unanswerable questions it abstains on 6 and gives a made-up answer on 4. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Overall, 23 of 30 cases (about 77%) show the intended behavior.
statements.explanation: 17 correct answers plus 6 correct abstentions is 23 of 30, which is 76.7%.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Accuracy on the answerable questions is 85%.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The system abstains correctly on 60% of the unanswerable questions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The single overall figure of about 77% would hide that 40% of the unanswerable questions received a fabricated answer.
statements.explanation: 4 of 10 unanswerable questions got fabricated answers, a fact the aggregate conceals.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The overall abstention rate across all 30 cases is 6 of 30, or 20%.
statements.explanation: Abstentions total 2 (wrongful) plus 6 (correct), which is 8 of 30, or about 27%.

questions.source: A source identifier is an address, not an argument
questions.stem: A grader scores a free-form summary as correct only when it exactly equals a reference summary string. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An exact-match accuracy of 0% proves the model's summaries are all factually wrong.
statements.explanation: Zero exact matches can occur when every summary is accurate but worded differently.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Rubric scoring by a trained human or a validated model grader is a more appropriate way to score summaries.
statements.explanation: Graders that tolerate paraphrase fit tasks with many acceptable outputs, provided they are validated.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Normalizing case and whitespace before comparing can change which responses count as matches.
statements.explanation: Normalization can turn a mismatch into a match, so it affects scores.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Exact matching suits closed-form outputs such as a label from a fixed set or a single number.
statements.explanation: When there is exactly one acceptable string, equality is a precise grader.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A correct paraphrase of the reference would be scored as wrong.
statements.explanation: Many distinct wordings convey the same content, and string equality accepts only one.

questions.source: Ship It: an experiment another person can audit
questions.stem: A team wants a prompt experiment that another person could audit. Check each statement that is true about what the record should contain.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The model's name alone is enough, because a model's behavior does not change over time.
statements.explanation: Hosted models are updated and aliases can be re-pointed, so the date and exact identifier matter.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Label hand-constructed test strings separately from responses actually returned by a model.
statements.explanation: The two kinds of data support different claims and must stay distinguishable.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Record the exact prompts, the source materials, the model identifier and the date.
statements.explanation: Without the inputs and conditions, a result cannot be reproduced or interpreted.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Preserve each raw response before any editing or repair.
statements.explanation: Edits made before saving destroy the observation that was actually made.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Overwrite the baseline prompt with each revision so that a single current file remains.
statements.explanation: An intact baseline is what each revision is compared against.

questions.source: Work through the three-response experiment
questions.stem: A team hand-writes 20 responses, some malformed and some contradicting their sources, to exercise a validator. The validator rejects 7. The report then states: "The model fails the format requirement 35% of the time." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The 35% describes the hand-written set, not the behavior of any model.
statements.explanation: No model produced these strings, so no model rate can be read from them.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the strings resemble real model outputs, the report may legitimately describe them as observed model outputs.
statements.explanation: Resemblance does not change provenance; presenting constructed text as observed output is misleading.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Hand-constructed test data has no value.
statements.explanation: Constructed cases are valuable for testing that a validator catches specific defects.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The 35% would be the same whichever mix of malformed and valid strings the person building the set chose.
statements.explanation: Whoever builds the set chooses how many malformed items to include, which sets the rate by design.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A defensible statement is that the model fails the format requirement 35% of the time.
statements.explanation: No model produced the strings; the supportable statement is that the validator rejected 7 of 20 constructed responses.

questions.source: A prompt revision is a hypothesis
questions.stem: A team iterates on a prompt for two weeks until their format validator accepts all 30 of their test cases. They report that output quality is now perfect. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A 100% rate on the cases used for iteration reliably predicts the rate on new inputs.
statements.explanation: Cases used for tuning will look good by construction.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A measure that becomes the sole target tends to stop being a good measure of the underlying goal.
statements.explanation: This is Goodhart's law, and it applies directly to optimizing against a single metric.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Testing on a set kept untouched during iteration would give a less biased estimate.
statements.explanation: Untouched data restores the independence a fair estimate needs.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The result shows that no unsupported answers can be present among the 30.
statements.explanation: A format validator says nothing about whether claims are supported.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Optimizing against a fixed validator cannot overfit, because the validator is deterministic.
statements.explanation: Repeated tuning finds prompts that satisfy the checker, whether or not they serve the underlying goal.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.stem: A team finds that its output contract has no way to express "insufficient evidence", so it adds a status field to the object and reruns its earlier cases. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The new version's pass rate can be compared with the old version's on the same cases without any caveat.
statements.explanation: The two versions apply different rules, so their rates measure different things.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Old tests passing validates the new behavior.
statements.explanation: Tests written for the earlier rules do not exercise the new field.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The change can be made silently if it raises the pass rate.
statements.explanation: Undisclosed changes make results impossible to interpret, whatever they do to the rate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The change should be recorded as a new version of the contract.
statements.explanation: Behavior has changed, so the contract is a different specification.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Cases that guided the redesign remain untouched held-out evidence.
statements.explanation: Cases that influenced a design decision have become development evidence.

questions.source: The driver's seat: what counts as acceptable
questions.stem: A team divides work on an evaluation between a human and an AI assistant. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Because an assistant can err, none of its work on an evaluation (drafts, code or tests) is of any use.
statements.explanation: Delegating drafting and computation while retaining judgment is a reasonable division.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Deciding what counts as acceptable depends on stakes and downstream costs that the assistant may not see.
statements.explanation: The consumer, the stakes and the cost of error usually live outside the files the assistant reads.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An assistant can draft test cases, implement a validator from a specification, and propose malformed inputs.
statements.explanation: Drafting and enumerating are tasks at which assistants are fast and useful.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because assistants write fluent explanations, their support judgments need no review.
statements.explanation: Fluency is not evidence, and an assistant's verdict is itself an output to check.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The assistant, not the person, should own the acceptance decision because it computes faster.
statements.explanation: Ownership follows who bears the consequences, not who computes fastest.

questions.source: A source identifier is an address, not an argument
questions.stem: To make answers inspectable, a team asks the model to add a short justification that quotes the supporting passage from the supplied source. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A quoted span can be checked mechanically for whether it appears verbatim in the source.
statements.explanation: Substring matching against the source is a deterministic check.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Asking for a quoted passage makes the answer easier to audit.
statements.explanation: A reviewer can go straight to the quoted location instead of searching the source.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A fluent justification is evidence of the model's actual internal reasoning process.
statements.explanation: A generated explanation is more text; it is not a window into the computation that produced the answer.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The justification is itself output that must be evaluated.
statements.explanation: A justification can be wrong, misleading or irrelevant like any other output.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A quote that appears in the source supports the claim it is attached to.
statements.explanation: A real quote can be taken out of context or be about something else.

questions.source: What a pass rate leaves out
questions.stem: A team cannot afford a human review of every accepted answer. From 1,000 accepted answers it reviews a random sample of 50 and finds 4 contradicted by their sources. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: With only 50 reviewed, the estimate is imprecise, with a standard error of roughly 4 percentage points.
statements.explanation: The standard error is sqrt(0.08 x 0.92 / 50), about 0.038.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The point estimate for the whole set is about 80 contradicted answers.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Reviewing a larger random sample would narrow the uncertainty of the estimate.
statements.explanation: Standard error shrinks as the sample grows.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because the validator accepted all 1,000, none of the unreviewed 950 can be contradicted.
statements.explanation: Acceptance by a structural validator carries no information about whether a claim is contradicted.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The sample proportion of contradicted answers is 8%.
statements.explanation: 4 divided by 50 is 0.08.

questions.source: What a pass rate leaves out
questions.stem: A prompt succeeds on any given trial with probability 0.9, and trials are independent. Evaluating its reliability on a workflow that must succeed on five consecutive runs, a team computes 0.9 x 0.9 x 0.9 x 0.9 x 0.9, which is about 0.59. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Independence of trials is an assumption that may fail for real workloads.
statements.explanation: Correlated failures, shared causes, or inputs that are hard in the same way break independence.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If success per run rose to 0.95, the chance of five in a row would be about 95%.
statements.explanation: 0.95 to the fifth power is about 0.77, not 0.95.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The 59% figure applies to any workflow with 5 steps regardless of whether the steps depend on each other.
statements.explanation: The calculation assumes independent steps with equal success probability; dependence changes the answer.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A 90% per-run success rate can look reliable on a single run and still be unreliable over a chain of runs.
statements.explanation: Failure probabilities compound across repeated or chained use.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The chance of five successes in a row is about 59%.
statements.explanation: 0.9 to the fifth power is 0.59.

questions.source: Work through the three-response experiment
questions.stem: A pipeline checks each model answer in layers: (1) the reply parses as JSON with the required keys; (2) every cited identifier belongs to the supplied set; (3) any quoted span appears verbatim in the cited source; (4) a model judge scores whether the claim follows from the source; (5) a human reviews a random sample of passing answers. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An answer that passes layers 1 through 4 has been established to be correct.
statements.explanation: Passing automated layers narrows risk without proving correctness.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Layer 4 covers meaning and, being a model, needs no calibration against human labels.
statements.explanation: A model judge's error rate has to be estimated against human labels.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Layer 3 can reject a fabricated quotation but cannot tell whether a genuine quotation was used in a misleading way.
statements.explanation: Verbatim matching verifies the quote exists, not that its use is fair.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Layer 5 is unnecessary once layer 4 exists, because two automated checks are as good as human review.
statements.explanation: A sampled human review is the independent check against which automated judges are calibrated.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Layers 1 and 2 are cheap and deterministic but cannot detect a claim that contradicts its source.
statements.explanation: Structure and identifier membership say nothing about content.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.stem: Two reviewers independently label 20 answers as "supported" or "contradicted" against their sources. They agree on 17 of the 20. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Disagreements often indicate the criterion for "supported" is ambiguous and needs sharpening.
statements.explanation: Systematic disagreement usually traces to an under-specified rule.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The raw agreement is 85%.

statements.label: C
statements.text: When two reviewers disagree, the correct label is whichever the more fluent reviewer chose.
statements.explanation: Disagreements are resolved by a defined procedure such as adjudication or a clearer criterion, not by style.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Cohen's kappa corrects observed agreement for agreement expected by chance.
statements.explanation: Kappa is defined as observed agreement minus chance agreement, scaled by the maximum possible beyond chance.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Raw agreement is the same quantity as chance-corrected agreement.
statements.explanation: With two labels, a substantial share of agreement can occur by chance alone, so the quantities differ.

questions.source: Work through the three-response experiment
questions.stem: On 200 responses, a structural validator accepted 140 and rejected 60. A careful reviewer then judged content for all 200. Among the 140 accepted, 21 were unsupported by their sources. Among the 60 rejected, 9 would have been supported had the format been acceptable. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The validator's acceptance rate of 70% (140 of 200) is a measure of the proportion of supported answers.
statements.explanation: Acceptance rate measures structural compliance; the supported share among accepted is a separate figure.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Of the 60 rejected responses, 40% had supported content.

statements.label: C
statements.text: 15% of the accepted responses were unsupported even though they passed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because the validator rejected some good content, it should be removed.
statements.explanation: A validator that guards the consumer's contract still has value; rejection of well-supported but malformed content is the cost of strictness and may be addressed by repair or retry.

statements.label: E
statements.text: 119 of the 140 accepted responses (85%) were supported.
statements.explanation: 140 minus 21 is 119, and 119 over 140 is 0.85.

questions.source: A source identifier is an address, not an argument
questions.stem: A contract asks the model to include a self-reported confidence number between 0 and 1 with each answer. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Confirming that the number lies between 0 and 1 checks the format but not whether it is calibrated.
statements.explanation: A range check confirms form, not meaning.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Language models' self-reported confidence can be overconfident.
statements.explanation: Overconfidence in model-reported probabilities is widely observed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Averaging the stated confidence over all answers and comparing it with overall accuracy gives a coarse calibration check.
statements.explanation: Mean stated confidence against overall accuracy is the simplest calibration comparison, though bins give more detail.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A stated confidence of 0.9 means the answer is correct about 90% of the time.
statements.explanation: A stated number carries that meaning only if it has been shown to be calibrated.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Calibration can be assessed by grouping answers by stated confidence and comparing each group's stated confidence with its observed accuracy.
statements.explanation: Reliability diagrams compare stated and observed accuracy within bins.

questions.source: Work through the three-response experiment
questions.stem: A baseline prompt produced responses where the format validator accepted 6 of 10, and 5 of those 6 were judged supported by their sources. A revision with examples was accepted on 9 of 10, and 6 of those 9 were judged supported. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reporting only the format acceptance rates would give the complete picture of the comparison.
statements.explanation: Two columns, format and support, tell a different story than either one alone.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The number of responses both accepted and supported fell from 6 to 5 of 10.
statements.explanation: Accepted-and-supported responses rose from 5 to 6 of 10.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The share of accepted responses that were supported fell from about 83% to about 67%.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Format acceptance rose from 60% to 90%.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The format gain alone shows the revision made answers more faithful to their sources.
statements.explanation: Format compliance is a different property; here the supported share among accepted fell.

questions.source: The gate: write the contract for the consumer first
questions.stem: For each held-out question, a team writes, before any model response exists, one sentence describing an answer that would pass its format validator and still fail its evidence criterion. Check each statement that is true about this practice.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If the sentence is written after seeing the response, it describes the output instead of testing the team's understanding.
statements.explanation: Hindsight descriptions are fitted to what happened and so test nothing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It forces the team to think about how its automated check could be fooled.
statements.explanation: Anticipating a passing-but-wrong answer exposes the gap between structure and content.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The sentence should be based on the model's actual response to that question.
statements.explanation: Basing it on the response defeats the purpose of writing it in advance.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Being unable to write the sentence suggests the team does not yet know what it is checking for.
statements.explanation: Not being able to imagine a failure means the evidence criterion is not yet understood.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The sentence is paperwork with no bearing on the quality of the evaluation.
statements.explanation: Pre-stated failures sharpen the evidence criterion and make the evaluation harder to game.

questions.source: What a pass rate leaves out
questions.stem: A report on 100 cases states that 90 pass. Among the 10 failures, 8 are cosmetic (a stray space in a field) and 2 are responses that tell a customer a wrong refund amount. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A single pass rate weights the cosmetic failures and the wrong-refund failures equally.
statements.explanation: Each failure subtracts one case regardless of its consequence.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A 90% pass rate means 90% of the answers were correct.
statements.explanation: Pass rate measures acceptance by the stated checks, not correctness.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Reporting failures by category lets readers see which failures matter.
statements.explanation: A breakdown shows that most failures here are harmless and two are consequential.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Equal weighting is a policy choice that can be replaced by severity weights.
statements.explanation: Which failures count most is a decision about stakes, not a discovered fact.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Severity weights should be chosen after seeing which prompt wins, so the better prompt is rewarded.
statements.explanation: Weights chosen after results can be fitted to favor an outcome and should be set beforehand.

questions.source: Work through the three-response experiment
questions.stem: A single constructed response is shown to pass a checker while violating the property the checker was meant to protect. Check each statement that is true about what such a constructed counterexample establishes.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A single such example is enough to refute the claim "passing this check implies the property."
statements.explanation: A universal implication is refuted by any single counterexample.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It shows that passing the checker does not by itself guarantee the property.
statements.explanation: The example proves the check is not sufficient for the property.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It shows how often the failure occurs in real use.
statements.explanation: One handpicked case carries no information about frequency.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It is a demonstration of a logical gap, not a frequency estimate.
statements.explanation: Its force is logical: one counterexample defeats a universal claim.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It shows the checker is broken, since a correct checker would have rejected such a response.
statements.explanation: The checker may perform exactly the job it was specified for; the error lies in over-reading what its pass means.

questions.source: Work through the three-response experiment
questions.stem: A function pass_rate(responses, validator) returns the number of accepted responses divided by the number of responses. Check each statement that is true about the input of an empty list.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Returning 1.0 could be misread as perfect performance.
statements.explanation: One implies tests were run and all passed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An experiment with zero cases has a pass rate of 100% by mathematical convention.
statements.explanation: A rate with an empty denominator is undefined; vacuous truth applies to universal statements, not to ratios.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Returning 0.0 could be misread as a tested system that failed every case.
statements.explanation: Zero implies tests were run and failed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Raising an error, or returning an explicit "undefined" value, signals that there is no evidence.
statements.explanation: An undefined result keeps "no data" from posing as a performance figure.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In Python, 0 / 0 evaluates to 0.0.
statements.explanation: Dividing zero by zero raises ZeroDivisionError in Python.

questions.source: What each line of the validator promises
questions.stem: A validator is written as follows: it parses the reply, then reads data["answer"] and data["sources"] directly, and only afterward checks that data is a dictionary. It is called with the reply [1, 2], then with "abc" (a JSON string), then with 5. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A validator that crashes on a malformed reply is behaving correctly, since a crash also signals rejection.
statements.explanation: A validator should return a rejection for any input; an unhandled exception can halt the pipeline or be mistaken for a different failure.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Reading data["answer"] from the string "abc" raises a TypeError in Python.
statements.explanation: Strings are indexed by integers, so a string key raises TypeError.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Reading data["answer"] from the list [1, 2] raises a TypeError in Python.
statements.explanation: Lists cannot be indexed with a string key.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Reading data["answer"] from the integer 5 returns None.
statements.explanation: Integers are not subscriptable, so the access raises TypeError.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Checking that the parsed value is a dictionary before indexing avoids these exceptions.
statements.explanation: A type check first lets the function return a rejection cleanly.

questions.source: Work through the three-response experiment
questions.stem: A reviewer checks 20 answers against their sources, using three outcomes: supported, contradicted, and cannot be determined. The counts are 12 supported, 5 contradicted and 3 cannot be determined. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Counting the 3 undetermined answers as supported is a neutral way to resolve them.
statements.explanation: Counting unknowns as supported inflates the result in the direction the reviewer may prefer.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The share of all 20 that were established as supported is 60%.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If every undetermined answer were later found supported, the share would be 75%.
statements.explanation: 12 plus 3 is 15 of 20, which is 0.75.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Reporting only the single supported percentage is as informative as reporting all three counts.
statements.explanation: The three counts show the established result and the size of the unresolved remainder.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If every undetermined answer were later found contradicted, the share would fall below 60%.
statements.explanation: The supported count would remain 12 of 20, so the share would stay at 60%.

questions.source: Ship It: an experiment another person can audit
questions.stem: A team ran the same prompt against a hosted model alias in March and again in June. Its validator acceptance rate on the same 40 cases was 36/40 in March and 31/40 in June. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A gap of five cases out of 40 can be dismissed as certainly meaningless.
statements.explanation: A 12.5-point gap on 40 cases is neither clearly noise nor clearly real, so it calls for investigation rather than dismissal.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The March rate was 90% and the June rate was 77.5%.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Recording only the model family name is enough to interpret such a difference.
statements.explanation: An exact model identifier and run date are needed to interpret changes over time.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because the prompt and cases were identical, any difference must be caused by random sampling alone.
statements.explanation: Model changes, infrastructure changes and sampling noise are all candidate explanations.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The 12.5-point difference proves that the provider degraded the model.
statements.explanation: The data are consistent with a model change, with sampling noise, or with both; they do not prove either.

questions.source: The driver's seat: what counts as acceptable
questions.stem: A team must choose which checks to run on model answers that will be shown to customers. Check each statement that is true about choosing checks by stakes.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Different consumers of the same output may reasonably set different acceptance rules.
statements.explanation: A hobby tool and a medical tool, for example, tolerate different risk.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The more costly a wrongly accepted answer is, the more independent content-level verification is justified.
statements.explanation: Verification effort should scale with the consequence of an error.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The acceptance threshold should be determined by whichever value makes the current pass rate look best.
statements.explanation: Choosing thresholds to flatter results defeats the purpose of having a threshold.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A strictness threshold such as "every claim must be supported" versus "most claims" is a decision about acceptable risk.
statements.explanation: How much unsupported content is tolerable is a risk judgment, not a technical fact.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A cheap structural check alone is adequate at any consequence level, since structural acceptance implies the answer is good.
statements.explanation: A structural check accepts well-formed false answers, which is dangerous when errors are costly.

questions.source: Work through the three-response experiment
questions.stem: A validator is run on three prepared strings: (1) text that is not JSON; (2) an object that parses, has the right keys and types, and cites an identifier that was not supplied; (3) an object that parses, has the right keys and types, and cites a supplied identifier but makes a claim that contradicts the source. It accepts only the third. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The validator accepts 1 of 3 strings, so the acceptance rate on this set is 1/3.
statements.explanation: One accepted out of three is a rate of 0.333.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The second string is rejected at the identifier-membership rule.
statements.explanation: Parsing, shape and types succeed, and the unsupplied identifier fails the membership rule.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The first string is rejected at parsing, before any field rule is applied.
statements.explanation: A syntax failure ends processing at the parser.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Calling 1/3 an accuracy score would misname what was measured.
statements.explanation: The rate measures acceptance by structural rules, which the contradicted claim passes.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The accepted string is the only one that is correct.
statements.explanation: The accepted string contradicts its source, so it is the one that is wrong in content.

questions.source: A prompt revision is a hypothesis
questions.stem: A prompt includes three example input-output pairs showing correctly formatted answers. Check each statement that is true about few-shot examples in an evaluation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Examples taken from the evaluation cases are harmless to the measurement.
statements.explanation: Examples drawn from the evaluation cases leak the answers and contaminate the result.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Examples can also anchor content, causing the model to copy details from an example into its answers.
statements.explanation: Models can reproduce surface features and facts from examples.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Higher format compliance implies the answers are more faithful to their sources.
statements.explanation: Format compliance and source faithfulness are independent properties.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The order and choice of examples can change the model's outputs.
statements.explanation: Sensitivity to example selection and order is well documented.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Whether examples raise format compliance is a hypothesis to be tested on fixed cases.
statements.explanation: Few-shot prompting is common practice but its benefit on a given task must be measured.

questions.source: Build It: your validator is the baseline
questions.stem: A team requires that each of its contract's rules have a test that fails if that rule is deleted. Check each statement that is true about this practice.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Deleting a rule in a scratch copy and rerunning the tests shows whether any test notices the deletion.
statements.explanation: Deliberately breaking code and observing the tests is the idea behind mutation testing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A test that passes both with and without a rule defends nothing about that rule.
statements.explanation: A test insensitive to a rule's presence provides no evidence about that rule.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Once every rule has such a test, the validator reflects what the consumer needs.
statements.explanation: The tests defend the contract as written; whether the contract matches the consumer's needs is a separate judgment.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It checks that tests defend each behavior the contract promises, not merely that tests exist.
statements.explanation: Coverage is measured per behavior, not by test count.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Coverage of the contract is measured by the number of tests.
statements.explanation: Many tests can exercise the same few behaviors and leave others undefended.

questions.source: A source identifier is an address, not an argument
questions.stem: A validator is given the set of allowed source identifiers but not the text of the sources. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: It can determine whether the cited text supports the answer.
statements.explanation: Without the source text, there is nothing to compare the answer against.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It can reject a citation of an identifier that was never supplied.
statements.explanation: Set membership is computable from the identifier list alone.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The inputs a check receives limit what it is able to decide.
statements.explanation: A function cannot decide on information it never receives.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Giving the validator the source text would be enough by itself to make it judge support, without any new comparison logic.
statements.explanation: Access to text is necessary but not sufficient; a comparison procedure such as quote matching or entailment judging is also required.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Membership in a registry of identifiers and support for a proposition are different relations.
statements.explanation: An identifier can exist while the text behind it says something else.

questions.source: Opening scenarios
questions.stem: A user asks an AI system to "fix the quarterly report". In run 1 the system lists which paragraphs should change. In run 2 it reads the report file and returns a rewritten version in the chat window. In run 3 it overwrites the report file on disk with a rewritten version. Every final message is fluent, polished prose. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Run 2's rewritten text and run 3's saved file are the same deliverable, because the wording is identical.
statements.explanation: A proposed revision shown in a window and a revision saved to storage are different deliverables: only the second changes stored state, and only the second can be checked as a before and after.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Only run 3 leaves a persistent change in the stored report.
statements.explanation: Runs 1 and 2 produce text that someone must still apply; run 3 mutates the file, so only it changes state that outlasts the conversation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Run 1 cannot influence any decision, because it changes no file.
statements.explanation: Advice can steer a decision (which paragraphs get cut, what is believed); lack of a state change does not make text inert.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The claim "the report on disk now contains the fix" needs evidence about the file, not just the final message.
statements.explanation: The evidence has to follow the object whose state is being claimed; a transcript supports a claim about what was said, not about what was stored.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The final message's wording reliably reveals which of the three runs took place.
statements.explanation: Polished prose can end all three runs, so the wording of the closing message does not identify what operation was performed.

questions.source: Opening scenarios
questions.stem: An assistant is told: "Summarize this document. Do not change any files." It reads the document, writes an excellent summary, and then also saves a tidied version over the original, because a file-saving function was enabled in its environment. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The overwrite breaks the instruction even if the tidied text is better than the original.
statements.explanation: The edit is outside the task; being good does not move an action inside the scope that was requested.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Because a file-saving function was enabled, the overwrite was authorized.
statements.explanation: An enabled function is a capability, not a grant of permission for a particular operation on a particular target.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A good outcome and an authorized action are separate judgments.
statements.explanation: One can be satisfied while the other is not; here only the quality judgment was ever applied, and nobody decided the system could write.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Withholding the write capability would have made no difference, because the instruction already forbade changes.
statements.explanation: An instruction is a request, not an enforcement mechanism; without a write capability the overwrite could not have happened at all.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The quality of the tidied text decides whether the write was in scope.
statements.explanation: Scope is set by what was asked and authorized, not by how good the unrequested result turns out to be.

questions.source: A response and a file are different kinds of result
questions.stem: "Fix this report" can mean four different things: explain what is wrong, propose a replacement, save a new version, or alter the original. Check each statement that is true about this request.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The four readings have different consequences for stored state.
statements.explanation: Explaining and proposing leave files untouched, saving a new version adds one, and altering the original destroys the previous version in place.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the requester does not say which reading is meant, the system effectively chooses one, possibly the most consequential.
statements.explanation: Ambiguity does not disappear; it is resolved by whatever the system does, so the requester should state the scope.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Saving a new version and altering the original carry the same risk, because both are writes.
statements.explanation: Overwriting the original removes the before state, while saving to a new file leaves the original available for comparison and rollback.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Asking which reading is intended is a reasonable response to an ambiguous request.
statements.explanation: A clarifying question is cheaper than an irreversible action taken on a guess.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Altering the original leaves no copy of the previous text unless a backup exists.
statements.explanation: An in-place overwrite replaces the before state, which is why it deserves a separate decision from saving a new file.

questions.source: A response and a file are different kinds of result
questions.stem: In a coding-assistant session, the only record of an edit is the assistant's closing message: "I updated settings.yaml and set timeout to 30." Nothing else was captured. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The message supports the claim that the assistant said it made the change.
statements.explanation: A transcript is good evidence about what was said, and nothing more.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The message establishes that settings.yaml now contains timeout: 30.
statements.explanation: The statement describes an action; whether it happened, and where, needs evidence about the file itself.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Reading the file afterward and comparing it with a copy taken beforehand would be independent evidence of the change.
statements.explanation: A before-and-after state comparison can fail in ways the narration cannot, for instance by showing no change.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A log entry recording that a write was requested is enough to report the write as completed.
statements.explanation: A request is an attempt; success needs a result from the runtime or an observation of the changed state.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the file is unchanged, the assistant's claim is still accurate provided it was worded confidently.
statements.explanation: Confidence is not accuracy; an unchanged file contradicts the claim whatever its tone.

questions.source: A response and a file are different kinds of result
questions.stem: Two runs of a document-summarizing assistant produce nearly the same summary. In run P the user pasted the document text into the chat. In run Q the assistant called a file-reading tool on the document. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In run P no file-read tool call is expected in a tool log.
statements.explanation: The text arrived through the conversation itself, so no new read operation took place.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Since the summary quotes details of the document, a read operation must have occurred.
statements.explanation: A model can use text already in its context window; an answer that sounds informed does not show how the information arrived.

statements.label: C
statements.text: How the source reached the model changes which observation records exist.
statements.explanation: Pasted text, an attachment and a tool read leave different traces, and a report should say which route was used.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The two runs can give similar answers while leaving different records.
statements.explanation: The output hides the route; the record does not.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A tool-call log is a more direct basis for "the file was read" than the fluency of the summary.
statements.explanation: Fluent output is compatible with many routes, while a recorded read operation is evidence of one.

questions.source: Capabilities as sets: the grant, written down
questions.stem: Three interfaces declare these capability sets: Z = {reason}, X = {reason, read}, Y = {reason, read, write}. A task requires {read, write, send_email}. The missing set for a surface is the required set minus the surface's declared set. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The missing set for X is {send_email, write}.
statements.explanation: Required minus {reason, read} leaves write and send_email.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The missing set for Z contains two elements.
statements.explanation: None of read, write or send_email is in {reason}, so all three are missing.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Y covers the task.
statements.explanation: send_email is required and absent from Y, so the missing set for Y is {send_email}, not empty.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If write were added to X's declared set, the missing set for X would be empty.
statements.explanation: send_email would still be missing, so the set would still have one element.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An empty missing set would show the task is authorized on that interface.
statements.explanation: The subtraction compares declared capabilities with declared requirements; it takes no permission input and says nothing about authorization.

questions.source: Capabilities as sets: the grant, written down

statements.label: A
statements.text: The result is ["write"].
statements.explanation: Converting the list to a set removes the duplicate read, and subtracting {reason, read} leaves only write.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The duplicate "read" entry causes "read" to appear twice in the output.
statements.explanation: Set conversion removes duplicate labels before the subtraction.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Sorting changes which capabilities are reported as missing.
statements.explanation: Sorting only fixes the order of the result; membership is decided by the set difference.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A requirement label that no surface declares, such as "deploy", would stay in the missing result.
statements.explanation: The function does not validate requirement labels, so an unfamiliar one is reported as not covered.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A correct result here shows the surface really lacks the ability to write.
statements.explanation: The function compares declared sets; if the declaration or the task description is wrong, the arithmetic is still correct-looking.

questions.source: Capabilities as sets: the grant, written down
questions.stem: A teaching model declares chat = {reason}, assistant = {reason, read} and agent = {reason, read, write}, so each set contains the one before it. Check each statement that is true about this nested design.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Any task covered by the smallest surface is also covered by the two larger ones.
statements.explanation: Containment means every capability of the smaller set appears in the larger sets.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Real products typically fit a single linear ladder of capabilities, so the nested model is a faithful picture of them.
statements.explanation: Real systems can combine capabilities in ways that fit no single ordering.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A task that requires only read is covered by the smallest surface in the ladder.
statements.explanation: The smallest surface declares only reason, so read is missing there.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because the sets are nested, the largest surface is the best choice for every task.
statements.explanation: Nesting gives an order, not a recommendation; a task that needs less should be given less.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A tool that can append to a log but cannot read files shows that the ladder is a design convenience.
statements.explanation: Such a write-without-read capability fits none of the nested sets.

questions.source: The gate: choose the autonomy before you grant the capability
questions.stem: A task needs a system only to read one source file and return a summary whose claims can be checked against that file. Check each statement that is true about choosing the interface.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A surface that declares reading but not writing covers the requirement without extra operations.
statements.explanation: The task's required set is {read} plus ordinary reasoning, and a write capability adds nothing it needs.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The widest surface should be avoided because systems with write access are untrustworthy.
statements.explanation: The reason to prefer the smaller grant is that the task does not need the extra operation, not a judgment of the system's character.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Every operation that is granted is one more thing to verify afterward.
statements.explanation: Review effort grows with the set of things the system could have done.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Least privilege means giving the smallest capability set that completes the task.
statements.explanation: It is a standard security principle: grant what the task needs and no more.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the task were extended to include saving a draft file, a read-only surface would no longer suffice.
statements.explanation: Saving is a write requirement, which a read-only surface lacks.

questions.source: The gate: choose the autonomy before you grant the capability
questions.stem: A requester is told that a read-only interface cannot produce a saved file. The task as written explicitly authorizes saving an output file in a named folder. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A read-only setup cannot complete the task as specified.
statements.explanation: The required set includes a write that the setup lacks.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Returning advice alone would satisfy a request that authorized a saved file.
statements.explanation: Advice is a proposal; the request asked for a persistent artifact, which is a different deliverable.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the scope is widened after seeing the work, the written grant should be revised, dated and authorized again.
statements.explanation: Changing the scope silently turns the earlier decision into a fiction; versioning keeps the record honest.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Minimizing the tool set is the right goal no matter what outcome is required.
statements.explanation: The aim is sufficient autonomy for the outcome, not minimum tools whatever the work.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Authorization to save an output file in a named folder is not authorization to modify other files.
statements.explanation: A grant names an operation and a target; staying inside both is what keeps the action in scope.

questions.source: The gate: choose the autonomy before you grant the capability
questions.stem: Before giving an AI system any tools, a team writes a short grant specification: the desired outcome, the capabilities required, the capabilities granted, the operations explicitly refused, the single authorized target, the condition that sends control back to a human, the evidence a reviewer will read, and a pass condition that can fail. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Writing this specification after the run is just as good, because it can be matched against the logs.
statements.explanation: A specification written afterward can be fitted to whatever happened; its value is that the decision is on record before the grant makes it by default.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A pass condition that cannot fail is not a useful test.
statements.explanation: Without a failing case the condition is a wish, because no outcome would ever contradict it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Naming a refused operation and an authorized target makes the grant checkable.
statements.explanation: A reviewer can then look for the refused operation or for activity outside the target.

statements.label: D
statements.text: When the granted capabilities are small, a condition that returns control to a human adds little and can be omitted.
statements.explanation: Even a small grant can be exceeded by a proposal, such as saving a file or touching a second document, and someone must decide what happens then.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A specification that grants the widest available interface because the user "wants help" names no operation that would ever be refused, so it is weak.
statements.explanation: A grant should be justified by what the task requires; availability and good intentions are not requirements.

questions.source: The gate: choose the autonomy before you grant the capability
questions.stem: Three ideas are often blurred under the word "autonomy": capability (what the system is able to do), control (who or what chooses the next step) and scrutiny (how hard the output must be checked). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Capability, control and scrutiny are separate dimensions, and a design decision is needed on each.
statements.explanation: Knowing one does not determine the others, so a recommendation should address all three.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Control concerns which tools are enabled for the system.
statements.explanation: Enabled tools are capability; control concerns whether a fixed program or the model chooses the next operation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A fixed program can write files, and a model-directed process can make many decisions without writing any file.
statements.explanation: Writing is a capability; who steers is control, and the two vary independently.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The scrutiny a result needs is determined mainly by which tools are enabled, not by the stakes of the work.
statements.explanation: Scrutiny depends on the work and its consequences; the same permissions can serve low-stakes and high-stakes tasks.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The recommendation "use an agent" is specific enough to settle the capability, control and scrutiny decisions.
statements.explanation: It is shorter than a real recommendation and says much less; each axis needs its own sentence.

questions.source: The gate: choose the autonomy before you grant the capability
questions.stem: A pipeline always runs the same three steps in the same order: one model call extracts fields from an invoice, a second validates them, and a final step inserts the record into a database. The code, not the model, decides the order and when to stop. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Under the common distinction between workflows and agents, this is a workflow.
statements.explanation: Workflows orchestrate models and tools through predefined code paths, which is the case here.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It must be an agent, because it writes to a database.
statements.explanation: Writing is a capability, not evidence of who directs the process.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A system in which the model decides at each step which tool to call next and when to stop is model-directed.
statements.explanation: That is the defining feature of an agent in the usual sense.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Whether a system is a workflow or an agent is settled by listing which tools it can call.
statements.explanation: The tool list shows capability; the distinction concerns who controls the sequence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A model-directed process is the more accurate choice for a task whose steps are known in advance.
statements.explanation: Added flexibility is not added accuracy; a fixed pipeline is often more predictable and easier to test.

questions.source: The gate: choose the autonomy before you grant the capability
questions.stem: Published guidance on building LLM applications recommends finding the simplest solution that works and adding complexity only when needed. Check each statement that is true about choosing between a single model call, a fixed workflow and an autonomous agent.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A single model call with good prompting and retrieval is often enough and should be tried first.
statements.explanation: Added structure costs latency, money and debuggability, so it should be earned by measured improvement.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Agents typically trade extra latency and cost for flexibility.
statements.explanation: Each additional model-chosen step adds a call and time.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Agents are the best fit for tasks whose steps are known in advance and can be hard-coded.
statements.explanation: Known steps are better served by a fixed workflow, which is more predictable and testable.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because errors can compound across steps, autonomous agents call for testing in a sandbox and for guardrails.
statements.explanation: Each unchecked step conditions the next, so mistakes can grow before anyone looks.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Open-ended problems where the number of steps cannot be predicted are where model-directed agents are most useful.
statements.explanation: When the path cannot be written in advance, flexibility is worth its cost.

questions.source: The gate: choose the autonomy before you grant the capability
questions.stem: A reviewer can carefully check 12 actions per hour and has 4 hours a day for review. An agent produces 30 actions per run and is run 5 times a day, so 150 actions per day. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The reviewer can carefully check at most 48 actions per day.
statements.explanation: 12 actions per hour times 4 hours is 48.

statements.label: B
statements.text: About 32% of the day's 150 actions can be carefully checked.
statements.explanation: 48 divided by 150 is 0.32.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Doubling the agent's output doubles the reviewer's capacity.
statements.explanation: Review capacity is set by the person's time and attention, which does not scale with generation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If daily output doubles to 300 actions, the checkable fraction stays at 32%.
statements.explanation: 48 divided by 300 is 16%, so the fraction halves.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Because generation scales with the machine and verification does not, a grant should account for what a person will actually be able to check.
statements.explanation: Granting more operations than can be reviewed adds output without adding assurance.

questions.source: Verify and reflect
questions.stem: An organization's agents perform thousands of actions per day, a stream large enough that sampling without replacement can be ignored. It audits a random sample of 20 of them and finds zero violations. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The sample shows that the true violation rate is exactly zero.
statements.explanation: A sample can only bound the rate; zero in 20 is consistent with a nonzero rate.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An approximate 95% upper bound on the violation rate after zero violations in 20 random draws is about 14%.
statements.explanation: Solving (1 - p)^20 = 0.05 gives p of about 0.139, close to the 3/n rule of thumb of 15%.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the true violation rate were 10%, the chance of seeing no violations in 20 random draws is about 12%.
statements.explanation: 0.9 raised to the 20th power is about 0.12.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Auditing 200 random actions with zero violations would bring the 95% upper bound to about 15%.
statements.explanation: The bound shrinks roughly in proportion to sample size; with 200 draws it is about 1.5%.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Auditing the 20 actions the agent labelled as its most representative is equivalent to a random sample.
statements.explanation: A sample the system chose is not random, so the bound does not apply.

questions.source: Events, not labels: what the record can show
questions.stem: An assistant is declared to have read and write capabilities. In one run its recorded events are: reason, read, reason. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The record is consistent with no write having occurred during this run.
statements.explanation: No write event appears in the list.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The declared write capability shows that a write happened.
statements.explanation: A capability describes what is available; an event record describes what is recorded as having happened.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The record shows the assistant lacked the write capability.
statements.explanation: It shows only that no write was recorded in this run, not that none was possible.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Whether the event record is complete is a separate question that the record itself cannot answer.
statements.explanation: A list can omit operations that were performed but not recorded.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A declared capability set is a record of what a particular run did.
statements.explanation: It describes what a surface can do, much as a population describes what a sample could contain.

questions.source: Events, not labels: what the record can show
questions.stem: A classifier assigns a label to a list of recorded events. If the list contains write it returns "agent"; otherwise if it contains read it returns "assistant"; otherwise it returns "chat". An unrecognized event name raises an error. Consider these lists. L1: [write, reason]. L2: [reason, read, reason, read]. L3: [] (empty). L4: [read, read, write, read]. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: L1 is labelled "agent".
statements.explanation: A write appears, which takes precedence over everything else.

statements.label: B
statements.text: L2 is labelled "assistant".
statements.explanation: It contains reads and no write; repeated reads do not change the label.

statements.label: C
statements.text: L3 is labelled "chat".
statements.explanation: With neither write nor read present, the default branch applies.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A classifier that looked only at the last event would label L1 differently from this rule.
statements.explanation: The last event of L1 is reason, which would give "chat" instead of "agent".

statements.label: E
statements.text: L4 is labelled "assistant", because its last event is a read.
statements.explanation: The rule checks for the presence of a write anywhere, so L4 is "agent".

questions.source: Events, not labels: what the record can show
questions.stem: A classifier based on which event types are present labels two runs "agent". Run P recorded [read, write], and the write saved a scratch file in a temporary directory. Run Q recorded [read, write], and the write overwrote the user's original document. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The label does not distinguish run P from run Q.
statements.explanation: Both contain a write, and the rule ignores targets.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Recording the target of each write would make the two runs distinguishable.
statements.explanation: The target is exactly what the label discards.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The label preserves what a reviewer needs, so the full trace can be discarded.
statements.explanation: The label discards order, repetition, targets, success and authority; the trace is the evidence.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A write event in the list indicates that the write succeeded.
statements.explanation: An event string records that an operation was named; success needs a result from the runtime or an observation of the state.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Whether run P also breaks the user's instructions depends on what was authorized, not on the label.
statements.explanation: If only a scratch file was allowed it may be fine; if no writes at all were allowed, it is not.

questions.source: Build It: your own classifier, then the second half of the gate
