questions.stem: A plan has two steps: "implement", which depends on "review", and "review", which depends on "implement". An ordering function raises a dependency-cycle error. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Resolving a cycle starts by asking what each step needs as input, not by deleting an arrow.
statements.explanation: The cycle may expose an unclear step definition, which deleting an edge would hide.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Deleting the edge from review to implement is the right fix without further thought.
statements.explanation: Removing an edge makes the error disappear without asking what each step actually needs.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Replacing the steps with plan_review, implement and result_review gives a valid linear order.
statements.explanation: Plan review precedes implementation, which precedes result review, so no cycle remains.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Plan review approves a proposed method, whereas result review evaluates what was actually produced.
statements.explanation: The first judges an intention, the second judges an outcome.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The cycle can indicate that one word is doing two jobs: approving a proposed method and evaluating actual output.
statements.explanation: Review before implementation and review after implementation have different inputs.

questions.source: Acyclic does not mean executable
questions.stem: In a plan, the step "review" is declared to come after "build", and build's described output is "the work is done". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Because review comes after build in the order, the reviewer has what it needs.
statements.explanation: Sequence does not guarantee the needed artifacts exist.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The better fix is a more precise handoff condition on the edge, not another arrow.
statements.explanation: Specifying the handoff content closes the gap, whereas arrows only order.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A reviewer can work from build's description "the work is done" alone.
statements.explanation: A reviewer needs concrete artifacts such as a diff, test results and acceptance criteria.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Adding more arrows between the same two steps would make the handoff clearer.
statements.explanation: Duplicate arrows carry no additional information.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The edge states order but does not define the handoff object.
statements.explanation: An arrow says one step follows another, not what is passed between them.

questions.source: Evidence belongs on the edges
questions.stem: A team wants handoff conditions that a stranger could apply, meaning someone who did not build the pipeline can read the condition, observe the system and decide whether it holds. Check each condition that is testable in that sense.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "All 14 tests named in the ticket pass in a continuous-integration run on the commit under review."
statements.explanation: It names the tests, the environment and the commit, so any observer reaches the same verdict.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "pytest exits with status 0 and `git diff --name-only` lists only paths under src/billing/."
statements.explanation: An exit status and a list of changed paths are observable and decidable by anyone.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "The summary is accurate."
statements.explanation: Accuracy has no stated criterion or reference to compare against.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "The assistant reports high confidence in its work."
statements.explanation: A model's self-reported confidence is a statement, not an observation of the system.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "The code has been reviewed and looks reasonable."
statements.explanation: "Reviewed" and "reasonable" are interpretive; different people would apply them differently.

questions.source: Evidence belongs on the edges
questions.stem: A coding agent finishes a task and writes, "I ran the tests and they pass." A team is deciding what counts as evidence for moving the work to the next step. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A good check fails differently from the thing it certifies.
statements.explanation: Independence of failure modes is what makes a second check informative.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The test runner's exit status and output are stronger evidence than the agent's description of them.
statements.explanation: The runner's record comes from executing the code, not from the model's account.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A model's explanation of why it chose a step is guaranteed to reflect the computation that produced the choice.
statements.explanation: Self-explanations are plausible stories, not verified traces of internal computation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A checker whose errors tend to correlate with the errors of the thing it checks adds less independent assurance.
statements.explanation: Shared blind spots mean the checker misses what the producer missed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Asking the same model to reread its own output and say it looks right is an independent check.
statements.explanation: A model checking itself repeats the same opinion and shares its blind spots.

questions.source: Evidence belongs on the edges
questions.stem: A plan defines a handoff from a test-run step to a review step. The targeted test fails when run. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The plan should define what happens when the evidence fails, not only what happens when it passes.
statements.explanation: A plan written only for success pressures every observation into forward motion.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Returning to implementation, or stopping pending diagnosis, is a reasonable route.
statements.explanation: A failed check should route to diagnosis or revision, not to approval.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Re-running the same command unchanged until it happens to pass, then recording the pass, is a sound policy.
statements.explanation: Selecting the passing run hides the failures and reports a result the code does not reliably produce.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The agent should proceed to review anyway because review is next in the order.
statements.explanation: Passing a failing result to review as if it were approval undermines the check.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If a source needed by a step is unavailable, the agent should substitute a plausible replacement.
statements.explanation: Inventing a stand-in input hides that the real evidence is missing.

questions.source: Evidence belongs on the edges
questions.stem: An agent works in a repository under version control. One step adds a new test file. Another step runs a shell command that deletes files in a directory outside the repository. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Both steps deserve identical scrutiny because both change state.
statements.explanation: Reversibility, cost of error and visibility of a trail all differ between the two steps.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The test-file step is reversible from the diff, so it needs evidence but not necessarily a human gate.
statements.explanation: Version control makes the change cheap to undo, which lowers the cost of being wrong.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Evidence conditions should be attached first to the edges that are cheapest to undo.
statements.explanation: State-changing edges that are hard to undo are where evidence matters most.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A clear sequence diagram makes an unsafe transition acceptable.
statements.explanation: A tidy diagram describes the order of steps; it does not make any step safe.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The deletion step cannot be reverted from the diff, so it needs hard human approval or should be outside the scope.
statements.explanation: A deletion outside version control is irreversible, so the cost of an error is high.

questions.source: Evidence belongs on the edges
questions.stem: Two teams propose AI pipelines for screening loan applications. Team 1 documents what each stage produces and the condition under which each handoff may occur. Team 2's document says only "the loan officer reviews." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Team 1's proposal can be reviewed on its substance.
statements.explanation: Stated handoffs give reviewers something specific to examine and dispute.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Reviews" is an interpretive word that would need to be replaced with a criterion.
statements.explanation: Words like "reviews" leave the actual check undefined.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Team 2's proposal cannot be assessed because nobody can say what the officer checks or what the pipeline does.
statements.explanation: Without a stated check, no one can tell what the review would do.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Team 1's documentation proves that the decisions inside its pipeline are good.
statements.explanation: A clear map can be reviewed, but its decisions may still be wrong.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Handoff documentation is unnecessary when the reviewer is experienced.
statements.explanation: Experience varies between reviewers, which is why a stated condition is needed.

questions.source: Computational Skepticism
questions.stem: Handoff conditions differ in who can apply them. Example 1: "the exit status of the test command is 0." Example 2: "the cited regulatory clause actually governs the proposed change." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Example 1 can be applied by any non-author who can read the output.
statements.explanation: It is a mechanical observation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Marking each condition with who can apply it shows which edges lack a competent reviewer.
statements.explanation: Naming the applicant exposes unstaffed or overloaded checks.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A condition that needs a qualified reviewer is worthless.
statements.explanation: Qualified-reviewer checks are essential for domain judgments; the point is to name who does them.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A condition that only its author can apply has not yet become a usable handoff condition.
statements.explanation: A condition others cannot apply gives the handoff no independence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Example 2 generally needs a qualified reviewer.
statements.explanation: Whether a clause governs a change is a domain judgment.

questions.source: Evidence belongs on the edges
questions.stem: A handoff from a test run to a review step requires: the exact commands run, their exit statuses, their output, and a hash or version description of the code that was tested. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Listing the exact commands lets the reviewer check that the checks match the proposal.
statements.explanation: Commands show whether the checks actually exercise the proposed behavior.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A bare statement that review comes after run gives order without correspondence between what ran and what is reviewed.
statements.explanation: The arrow orders steps but does not tie the evidence to the code under review.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The exit status and output come from the test runner, not from the model.
statements.explanation: Evidence should be produced by a component independent of whoever wrote the code.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A matching hash proves the code is correct.
statements.explanation: A hash shows which code was tested, not that the code is right.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Without identifying the code version, test results could describe an earlier state of the code.
statements.explanation: Evidence for an older version can be mistaken for evidence about the current diff.

questions.source: Stop conditions and refusal paths
questions.stem: A plan's stop field should define three exits: completion, halt and defer. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "The turn budget is exhausted with two scoped tests still failing" is a completion condition.
statements.explanation: An exhausted budget is a defer case; failing tests mean the task is not complete.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "The next command would write outside the permitted directory" is a halt condition.
statements.explanation: A boundary violation is a reason to stop before completing.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "All scoped tests pass and the named reviewer accepts the current diff" is a completion condition.
statements.explanation: It names observable outcomes and a named acceptor.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Reaching a time limit should produce an incomplete status and preserved partial artifacts, and name who decides whether to resume.
statements.explanation: A limit bounds effort without proving success, so the honest output is an incomplete status, not a fabricated finish.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Stop when it looks good" is an adequate completion exit.
statements.explanation: "Looks good" cannot be applied by someone else.

questions.source: Stop conditions and refusal paths
questions.stem: An agent run has a maximum of 30 turns and a separate finish action the agent can call. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A deadline makes it acceptable to skip verification without telling anyone.
statements.explanation: A reduced objective can be justified by a deadline when disclosed, but skipped verification cannot be silently accepted.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A turn limit and a finish action answer different questions: how much effort is allowed versus whether the task is complete.
statements.explanation: The limit bounds resources; the finish action reports a claim about the task.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Partial artifacts should be preserved, and it should be stated who decides whether to resume.
statements.explanation: A deferred run needs its partial work and a named decider so it can resume.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Reaching the limit means the task is done.
statements.explanation: Exhausting a budget is not evidence of completion.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Reaching the limit should yield an incomplete status, not a fabricated final result.
statements.explanation: A limit says nothing about success, so reporting success would be false.

questions.source: Stop conditions and refusal paths
questions.stem: A plan's stop field assigns an owner to each exit. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A person should decide whether a newly discovered risk changes the scope.
statements.explanation: Changing scope changes what is authorized, which needs accountable judgment.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A summary of evidence is not a decision with a name on it.
statements.explanation: A decision requires an accountable decider, which a summary lacks.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An automated test can own a halt that triggers on a failing assertion.
statements.explanation: A mechanical, objective trigger can be automated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If an exit has no owner, the agent should decide for itself.
statements.explanation: An unowned exit is a defect in the plan; letting the agent fill it silently moves authority to the agent.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The decision can be handed to the model because it summarizes evidence well.
statements.explanation: Skill at summarizing does not confer authority or accountability.

questions.source: Stop conditions and refusal paths
questions.stem: A team adds refusal paths to an agent's plan, where refusal means that the workflow preserves its state and reports what blocks the next transition. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A refusal report should say why the step stopped, what evidence was available and what decision would allow safe resumption.
statements.explanation: A useful stop tells a person what is blocked and what could unblock it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An unexplained halt is hard to tell from a crashed workflow.
statements.explanation: Without a reason, operators cannot distinguish a designed stop from a failure.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Refusal paths should cover missing authority, unavailable evidence, out-of-scope changes and failed checks.
statements.explanation: These are the situations in which continuing would be unsafe or unsupported.

statements.label: D
statements.text: When a source cannot support a claim, the agent should fill the field with plausible language to satisfy the checklist.
statements.explanation: Plausible filler satisfies the form while hiding that evidence is missing.

statements.label: E
statements.text: When a source cannot support a claim, shrinking the claim or marking it unresolved is acceptable.
statements.explanation: Narrowing the claim keeps the record honest about what is supported.

questions.source: Stop conditions and refusal paths
questions.stem: An agent runs the same failing test command three times, with no change to the code, the inputs or its hypothesis, and gets the same failure each time. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Activity counts as progress only when it changes the evidence or the decision state.
statements.explanation: An identical retry yields nothing new, so it is motion without progress.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the failure were random, rerunning would be expected to produce the same result every time.
statements.explanation: Random failures vary between runs, and the repeated identical failure points to a deterministic cause.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A better next step is to diagnose the cause, revise the plan or defer.
statements.explanation: Each of these changes what is known or decided.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A retry cap is a resource bound and is not evidence of success.
statements.explanation: A cap limits cost but proves nothing about correctness.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The number of reruns is a measure of progress.
statements.explanation: Repetition without new evidence is not progress.

questions.source: Stop conditions and refusal paths
questions.stem: An agent is blocked in two ways. In case 1 it lacks documentation that exists in an approved source it can search. In case 2 it lacks permission to change a production configuration. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Both cases should be handled by the same halt.
statements.explanation: One case is solved by looking, the other needs a person's decision, so they need different responses.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In case 2 proposing a smaller task that avoids the production change is an appropriate response.
statements.explanation: Narrowing the task is a legitimate way to continue without new authority.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In case 2 the agent can grant itself permission if it has a good reason.
statements.explanation: Permission can only be granted by whoever holds the authority, not by the party asking.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Missing information that can be obtained within scope differs from a decision that needs new authority.
statements.explanation: The distinction determines whether the agent may proceed or must stop.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In case 1 the agent can search the approved sources, since the information is obtainable within scope.
statements.explanation: Searching approved sources stays inside the authorized boundary.

questions.source: Stop conditions and refusal paths
questions.stem: A plan for reviewing a codebase produces several hundred items for human review without any prioritization. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: More review items always mean more assurance.
statements.explanation: Beyond reviewers' capacity, extra items reduce the chance each is examined.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A deadline can justify a reduced objective if the reduction is disclosed.
statements.explanation: Disclosed scope reduction is honest; the claim shrinks to match the work.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A deadline makes skipped verification acceptable without disclosure.
statements.explanation: Undisclosed skipped verification misleads anyone relying on the result.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The plan may be structurally complete and still practically unauditable.
statements.explanation: Human attention is a bounded resource, and an unprioritized flood defeats review.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The plan should state which items need human judgment.
statements.explanation: Prioritization directs scarce judgment to the items that need it.

questions.source: Review before action: a plan predicts, a result records
questions.stem: A team treats a plan as a set of predictions and the result as a record of what happened. Before running anything, they write down the expected observations and what a wrong outcome would look like. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A plan edited after the run to match the run has become a description of the result.
statements.explanation: Once the plan is rewritten to fit the outcome, it no longer predicts anything and the earlier review is lost.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The gap between the prediction and the record is where the team learns.
statements.explanation: A surprise shows which assumption was wrong.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Dating predictions before the run is analogous to preregistering a hypothesis.
statements.explanation: Stating expectations before seeing data is the logic of preregistration.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Predictions are unnecessary when the plan is detailed.
statements.explanation: Detail is not the same as a testable prediction.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The note describing a wrong outcome should be updated after the run to fit what happened.
statements.explanation: Revising the failure criterion after seeing the result removes the possibility of being wrong.

questions.source: Review before action: a plan predicts, a result records
questions.stem: A plan's objective is "restore the documented behavior of the date-parsing function for all supported formats." Its verification entry is "confirm that tests/test_dates.py exists." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: When a check is a proxy, the plan should name what the check can and cannot reject.
statements.explanation: Naming the proxy's limits keeps the claim honest.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A stronger entry would run the tests and compare outputs with expected values for each supported format.
statements.explanation: Running tests against expected outputs observes the claimed behavior.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The existence of the test file implies that the tests pass.
statements.explanation: A file can exist and contain failing, wrong or no tests.

statements.label: D
statements.text: There is no cross-field problem, because each field is individually nonempty.
statements.explanation: Contradiction between fields is a defect that nonemptiness cannot show.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The verification is a proxy that does not measure the outcome the objective names.
statements.explanation: A file existing says nothing about whether any format is parsed correctly.

questions.source: Review before action: a plan predicts, a result records
questions.stem: A plan's risks field reads "data loss; wrong output; cost overrun." No mitigation, owner or trigger is given for any of them. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Assigning ownership of a risk to a fictitious person is acceptable if the plan then looks complete.
statements.explanation: Ownership by a nonexistent person leaves the risk unowned while appearing owned.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A short list of risks, each tied to a mitigation, owner or trigger, can serve better than a long unconnected list.
statements.explanation: Usefulness comes from the link between a risk and what the plan does about it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Each risk should be stated as accepted, mitigated, or a trigger for deferral or halt.
statements.explanation: Each risk needs a stated consequence for the plan.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A risks list can be detailed and still be disconnected from what the plan does.
statements.explanation: Detail and relevance are independent.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Risks disconnected from the plan's actions give a reviewer little to challenge.
statements.explanation: A risk that changes nothing about the work is decoration.

questions.source: Review before action: a plan predicts, a result records
questions.stem: After a plan's risk analysis and verification were written, its objective is narrowed from "migrate all tables" to "migrate only the orders table." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The supporting fields should be left unchanged for consistency with the earlier review.
statements.explanation: Leaving stale fields in place creates a plan whose parts argue for different goals.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Narrowing an objective cannot affect verification.
statements.explanation: Verification must test the objective actually pursued.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Reopening a plan is a normal event when it carries a recorded reason.
statements.explanation: A recorded reason makes the revision part of the design history.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The versions should be preserved and the relevant review rerun.
statements.explanation: Keeping versions shows what changed, and rerunning review keeps supporting fields from going stale.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The earlier risk analysis and verification may no longer match the objective.
statements.explanation: Risks and checks written for a broader objective may be irrelevant or incomplete for the narrower one.

questions.source: Review before action: a plan predicts, a result records
questions.stem: Before approving a plan, a reviewer imagines, for each important field, a plan that satisfies the field's wording but fails its purpose. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A specific objective can still be wrong for the stakeholder.
statements.explanation: Specificity does not guarantee the objective serves the right person.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Writing one counterexample before approval and checking whether the plan rejects it is a way to test the plan.
statements.explanation: A counterexample turns a vague worry into a concrete test of the plan.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the plan rejects the counterexample, that proves the plan cannot fail.
statements.explanation: Rejecting identified counterexamples shows those failure modes were addressed, not that no others exist.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A verification step can be executable yet test only a proxy.
statements.explanation: An executable check may measure something other than the claim.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A stop condition can be observable and still trigger only after harm has occurred.
statements.explanation: Observability concerns detection, and detection can arrive too late.

questions.source: Review before action: a plan predicts, a result records
questions.stem: A reviewer asks an AI assistant for counterexamples to a proposed plan. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Rejected counterexamples should be kept with the reason for rejection, because a dismissal can reveal an assumption.
statements.explanation: The record of why a case was dismissed shows what the plan assumes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the plan survives the assistant's counterexamples, the plan cannot fail.
statements.explanation: Surviving a finite set of tests does not rule out untested failure modes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The assistant can generate many counterexamples quickly.
statements.explanation: Producing volume cheaply is a good use of a model.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The reviewer decides which counterexamples are plausible in this context.
statements.explanation: Plausibility depends on context that the plan alone does not contain.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Because the assistant has no stake in the outcome, it should decide which risks deserve load-bearing checks.
statements.explanation: Choosing where to put checks depends on stakes and accountability, which the assistant does not carry.

questions.source: Ship It: the reviewed plan
questions.stem: A reviewer ends a plan review with a written sign-off whose lines state what was checked, how it was checked, what was not checked, what is not claimed, and whether the reviewer signs or withholds. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The "not checked" line is where the sign-off is most informative about its limits.
statements.explanation: Stating what was not examined prevents readers from over-trusting the approval.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A fluent sign-off drafted by a model is as good as one written from the reviewer's own record.
statements.explanation: Fluency is not evidence of review; the statement should come from what the reviewer actually did.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Withholding a signature is an honest outcome when the evidence does not support signing.
statements.explanation: A refusal to sign, with reasons, reports the state of the evidence accurately.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A sign-off should claim the plan is safe beyond the situations that were examined.
statements.explanation: Claims beyond what was examined are unsupported.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A sign-off on a plan claims less than a sign-off on a result: it says the plan survived the described review, not that the work succeeded.
statements.explanation: A plan predicts action and has not yet been tested by running.

questions.source: The gate: a reviewed plan, before Claude implements
questions.stem: A team adopts a pre-implementation checklist. Item 1: the objective was chosen from at least three candidate formulations. Item 2: the structural check passes and a cross-field review found no contradictions. Item 3: an ordering exists and every state-changing edge has an evidence condition and a failure route. Item 4: the stop field has completion, halt and defer exits with owners. Item 5: one counterexample was written and the plan rejects it. Item 6: a named person approved the plan with a date. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Approval fixes the version being implemented, and a result that contradicts the plan reopens it.
statements.explanation: A reviewed version is what gets implemented, and contradicting evidence sends it back through review.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The approver in item 6 may be the model that drafted the plan.
statements.explanation: Approval is an accountable person's act; a model's sentence of approval records nothing.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Passing the structural check alone does not satisfy item 2.
statements.explanation: Item 2 requires both a structural pass and a semantic cross-field review.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Once approved, the plan is frozen.
statements.explanation: A plan is a versioned object that evidence may reopen.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If nobody has approved the plan, its status is pending and nothing consequential runs.
statements.explanation: Approval is the condition for acting, and its absence leaves the plan a draft.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against the plan
questions.stem: An assistant returns a plan with a persuasive explanation of why each step was chosen. A reviewer is deciding how to evaluate it. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The reviewer can ask the assistant to critique the reviewer's own plan, then verify each criticism against the plan and the code.
statements.explanation: Critique is useful input; verification keeps the reviewer in control.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The plan should be judged by what it commits to, not by how well it is argued.
statements.explanation: Commitments are what will be done and can be checked.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The reviewer should run structural checks on the returned plan.
statements.explanation: A mechanical check is cheap and catches omissions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A well-argued rationale lowers the need for independent checks of the plan's commitments.
statements.explanation: Persuasiveness is not correctness, so independent checks matter more when prose is fluent.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A criticism stated confidently by the assistant can be accepted without checking.
statements.explanation: Confidence is not evidence, and criticisms can be wrong.

questions.source: Build It: the baseline that lets you audit the plan
questions.stem: A developer writes tests for a function that orders plan steps by prerequisites and raises ValueError for a duplicate id, an unknown prerequisite and a cycle. When two steps are ready at once, the function returns them sorted by id. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A single test using a linear chain of steps is enough to exercise cycle detection.
statements.explanation: A chain has no cycle, so it exercises only the success path.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A test that asserts the exact order for a diamond-shaped graph is stable only because ties are broken deterministically.
statements.explanation: Independent ready steps could appear in either order unless a tie-break fixes it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A duplicate id and an unknown prerequisite deserve separate tests because they fail differently.
statements.explanation: Each defect has its own rejection message and remedy, so each needs its own test.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A step that lists itself as its own prerequisite is a useful boundary case for cycle detection.
statements.explanation: A self-edge is the smallest cycle and never becomes ready.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An empty list of steps is a useful boundary case, and the expected result is an empty list.
statements.explanation: With nothing to order, the loop never runs and an empty ordering is the natural result.

questions.source: Review before action: a plan predicts, a result records
questions.stem: A plan's steps include "read the customer table and compute churn rates." The inputs field lists only the source files of the analysis code, and the scope field excludes personal data. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A step needs information that is neither listed in inputs nor authorized by scope, so the plan is inconsistent.
statements.explanation: Cross-field review looks for exactly this kind of contradiction.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The plan should be revised and re-reviewed before the agent acts.
statements.explanation: Resolving the contradiction before action is cheap and keeps authority with the approver.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The mismatch is harmless because each field is nonempty.
statements.explanation: Nonemptiness does not show that the fields agree.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The agent should read the table anyway and record that it did so afterward.
statements.explanation: Acting first and documenting later turns the plan into a description of what already happened.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Every step should need only information that it is authorized to use.
statements.explanation: A step should not rely on data that the plan does not authorize.

questions.source: A tool description does not run a tool
questions.stem: An application advertises one tool to a model through a JSON definition: the name `convert_currency`, a short description, and an input schema declaring string properties `from` and `to` and a numeric property `amount`. The model replies with a structured block asking for `convert_currency` with three arguments. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Because the schema declares `amount` as a number, the application can skip its own argument checking.
statements.explanation: The schema guides generation but the model can still emit a wrong type, and the runtime must defend its own boundary.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The definition tells the model which request shapes the application is prepared to consider; it does not run any code.
statements.explanation: A schema is a description that guides the model's output, while execution happens only in application code.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The model might return `amount` as a string even though the schema says number, so server code should treat the schema as guidance and not as a guarantee.
statements.explanation: Generated arguments are not guaranteed to conform, so the receiving side validates them.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The application, not the model, decides what happens when a tool name is received.
statements.explanation: Mapping a requested name to behavior is application logic.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The model's reply is a proposal expressed as data; the application decides what the name means and runs its own implementation.
statements.explanation: The model emits a structured request and has no direct access to the application's functions.

questions.source: Dispatch belongs to the application
questions.stem: A developer implements dispatch for a tool-calling agent as `result = globals()[block["name"]](**block["input"])`, where `block` is a tool request produced by the model. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A model that proposes the name of any function defined in the module can trigger it, even if that function was never advertised as a tool.
statements.explanation: Name lookup in the global namespace has no closed set of permitted operations.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Wrapping the globals lookup in a try/except block makes the design safe.
statements.explanation: Error handling after the fact does not restrict which functions can be reached.

statements.label: C
statements.text: This design merges the description of an operation, the authority to run it, and its implementation into one step nobody reviewed.
statements.explanation: An explicit allowlist separates what is advertised from what is permitted and from how it runs.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because the model only sees the advertised tool list, it cannot propose any other name.
statements.explanation: Models can emit arbitrary names, by mistake or because untrusted text steered them, so the application must not assume the name is advertised.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Once names are restricted by an allowlist, validating the arguments of each call becomes unnecessary.
statements.explanation: An allowed operation can still be given harmful or malformed arguments, so arguments need their own rules.

questions.source: Dispatch belongs to the application
questions.stem: An agent has a `write_file(path, content)` tool that is supposed to write only inside `/srv/workspace`. The model proposes the path `/srv/workspace/../etc/cron.d/job`. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A symbolic link inside the root that points outside it could still defeat a check that only manipulates path strings.
statements.explanation: Resolving symlinks against the file system is needed to know where a write will actually land.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A purely lexical check that the path string starts with `/srv/workspace` would accept this path.
statements.explanation: The string does begin with the approved prefix even though the `..` segment moves it outside the directory.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A schema that declares `path` as a string would reject this value.
statements.explanation: The value is a string, so a type-level schema accepts it; the problem is semantic.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Resolving the path to its canonical absolute form before comparing it with the approved root would show that it escapes the root.
statements.explanation: Canonicalization collapses `..` segments, giving `/srv/etc/cron.d/job`, which is not under the root.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Adding "never write outside /srv/workspace" to the tool description enforces the restriction as reliably as a resolved-path check.
statements.explanation: A description steers the model but nothing in it constrains the code that performs the write.

questions.source: A tool description does not run a tool
questions.stem: A tool `send_report(recipient, dry_run=false)` emails a report unless `dry_run` is true. The model proposes `{"recipient": "ops@example.com", "dryrun": true}`, misspelling the key. The dispatcher silently ignores unknown keys, so a real email goes out. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The typo shows the tool's schema was invalid JSON Schema.
statements.explanation: The schema can be perfectly valid; the model simply produced a key the schema does not define.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Ignoring unknown keys is the safer choice because the call still succeeds.
statements.explanation: A call that succeeds with the wrong behavior is worse than one that fails visibly.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Declaring `additionalProperties: false` in the schema is sufficient even if the application never checks arguments against it.
statements.explanation: A schema only helps if something enforces it at the point of execution.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A default of `dry_run=false` is harmless because the model is expected to set the argument explicitly every time.
statements.explanation: Defaults are what happens when an argument is missing or misnamed, so they should be the safe choice.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Rejecting unknown keys would have surfaced the typo before any email was sent.
statements.explanation: Strict validation turns a misspelled parameter into a visible error instead of a silent default.

questions.source: A tool description does not run a tool
questions.stem: A Python tool guard is written as `if not all(isinstance(v, (int, float)) for v in args.values()): raise ValueError(...)`. The model proposes `{"a": true, "b": 2}`, which Python parses to `{"a": True, "b": 2}`, for an `add` tool. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The guard accepts this input and the addition returns 3.
statements.explanation: `True + 2` evaluates to 3 because `True` behaves as 1 in arithmetic.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Replacing the check with `isinstance(v, numbers.Number)` would reject `True`.
statements.explanation: `bool` is also registered as a `numbers.Number`, so this check still admits it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In Python `bool` is a subclass of `int`, so `isinstance(True, int)` evaluates to `True`.
statements.explanation: That inheritance is why a naive numeric guard admits booleans.

statements.label: D
statements.text: JSON `true` and the JSON number 1 are the same type, so accepting the value is correct.
statements.explanation: They are different JSON types and a sum of a flag and a number is semantically meaningless for an addition tool.

statements.label: E
statements.text: This guard would also reject `float('inf')`.
statements.explanation: Infinity is a float, so a type-only check accepts it; a separate finiteness check is needed.

questions.source: A tool description does not run a tool
questions.stem: A service parses tool arguments with Python's `json.loads`, which by default accepts the tokens `NaN` and `Infinity`. The model emits `{"a": NaN, "b": 1}` for an `add` tool. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Serializing the result with `json.dumps` emits a bare `NaN` token that strict JSON parsers reject, unless `allow_nan=False` is passed, in which case a ValueError is raised.
statements.explanation: Python's serializer produces non-standard output by default, so non-finite numbers should be refused before serialization.

statements.label: B
statements.text: `float('nan') == float('nan')` is `True`, so a NaN result can be detected by comparing it with another NaN.
statements.explanation: NaN compares unequal to everything including itself, so equality cannot be used to detect it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: `math.isfinite(float('nan'))` is `False`, so a finiteness check on inputs rejects the value.
statements.explanation: isfinite is false for NaN and both infinities.

statements.label: D
statements.text: `nan + 1` evaluates to `nan`, so a missing finiteness check lets the invalid value propagate into a reported sum.
statements.explanation: NaN is contagious through arithmetic and does not raise an error.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Python's json module parses `NaN` into `float('nan')` by default even though NaN is not valid in the JSON standard.
statements.explanation: The permissive default means non-standard numeric tokens can reach tool code.

questions.source: A tool description does not run a tool
questions.stem: An `add` tool checks that both inputs are finite floats. The model proposes `a = 1e308` and `b = 1e308`. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Both inputs are finite floats, so an input-only finiteness check passes.
statements.explanation: 1e308 is below the double-precision maximum of about 1.8e308.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Python raises OverflowError for `1e308 + 1e308`.
statements.explanation: Float addition quietly yields `inf`; OverflowError appears in other operations such as converting a huge int to float.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Verifying that both inputs are finite is enough to guarantee that the sum is finite.
statements.explanation: Two finite operands can add to a non-finite result, so the output needs its own check.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In IEEE 754 double-precision arithmetic the sum is `inf`.
statements.explanation: The exact sum exceeds the largest representable double and rounds to infinity.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Python's integer addition overflows at 2**63 like fixed-width integers in many languages.
statements.explanation: Python ints have arbitrary precision, so integer overflow of this kind does not occur.

questions.source: Conduct: what must be exact does not belong in the model
questions.stem: A team must put into a report the total of all line items above $10,000 across 200 invoices. Design X pastes all 200 invoices into a chat window and asks for the total. Design Y has a model extract fields from each invoice into structured records, and then ordinary code filters and sums them. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In Design X nothing outside the model's own output recomputes the number, so there is nothing to audit if it is wrong.
statements.explanation: A fluent total with no intermediate artifacts offers no seams for comparison.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In Design Y the model no longer touches the data, so extraction errors cannot occur.
statements.explanation: The model still performs the extraction, and its errors enter the pipeline there.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Design Y eliminates the possibility of error in the total.
statements.explanation: It makes the step inspectable, but extraction can still be wrong.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In Design Y the filter and the sum can be re-run, tested, and broken on purpose without involving the model.
statements.explanation: Deterministic code is inspectable and repeatable.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Design X produces intermediate records that can be compared with the source invoices.
statements.explanation: Intermediate structured records exist only in Design Y.

questions.source: Conduct: what must be exact does not belong in the model
questions.stem: A model performs a chain of 12 dependent arithmetic steps in free text. Assume it gets each step right with probability 0.98, independently of the other steps. Check each statement that is true. (0.98 raised to the 12th power is about 0.785.)

statements.label: A
statements.text: Running the same chain through deterministic code makes its output random from run to run.
statements.explanation: Deterministic code returns the same output for the same input, which is what makes errors findable by a test.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Raising per-step accuracy from 0.98 to 0.99 would push the all-correct probability above 0.9.
statements.explanation: 0.99**12 is about 0.886, still below 0.9.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the final answer is correct, every intermediate step must have been correct.
statements.explanation: Two errors can cancel, and a right final number does not certify the reasoning.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The probability that the final answer is right is about 0.98, because the chain is only as weak as one step.
statements.explanation: Errors compound across dependent steps, so the chain is less reliable than any single step.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The probability that all 12 steps are right is roughly 0.78.

questions.source: Conduct: what must be exact does not belong in the model
questions.stem: A function converts US dollars to euros using a rate table loaded from a CSV file last refreshed 14 months ago. Its unit tests check the arithmetic against hand-computed values and they all pass. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Comparing a sample of outputs against a current published rate would test for staleness, a failure the unit tests cannot see.
statements.explanation: A check from a different evidence source covers a failure the original route shares.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Because the code is deterministic, its outputs are correct.
statements.explanation: Determinism means repeatability, not correctness.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Replacing the code with a language model's recollection of the exchange rate removes the staleness problem.
statements.explanation: A model's recalled rate is not tied to today's rate either, and nothing would audit it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Passing arithmetic tests show that the rates in the table are current.
statements.explanation: The tests check the multiplication, not the freshness of the source data.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Because the rate data is old, the function will return a different value on each run.
statements.explanation: Stale data does not make deterministic code vary; it returns the same outdated value every time.

questions.source: Conduct: what must be exact does not belong in the model
questions.stem: Two agent designs are being compared. Design A offers one tool, `read_file`, restricted to a project directory. Design B offers `run_shell(command)` with no restrictions. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Every operation placed in the dispatcher is authority the application has granted to whatever the model produces.
statements.explanation: Capability is a grant of authority, not merely a feature.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Design A is easier to audit because it can do very little.
statements.explanation: A narrow allowlist limits the set of behaviors a reviewer must reason about.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The set of tools exposed does not change how much harm a mistaken model output can cause.
statements.explanation: Tool scope bounds the effects of any mistaken or manipulated output.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Design B's risk is adequately controlled by telling the model in the tool description to run only harmless commands.
statements.explanation: Instructions to the model are not a control on what the shell will execute.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In Design A, a malicious instruction hidden in a file the agent reads can make the agent write new files through its tools.
statements.explanation: With only a read tool available, tool calls cannot write files.

questions.source: Dispatch belongs to the application
questions.stem: A dispatcher raises `ValueError("b must be a finite number")` when the model proposes `b = "abc"`. The code surrounding the dispatcher catches that `ValueError` and returns a tool-result block, tied to the request's identifier, that has the message and an error flag. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Converting a bounded, anticipated validation failure into an error result avoids crashing the whole conversation.
statements.explanation: Expected failures can be handled as part of the protocol.

statements.label: B
statements.text: On its next turn the model can see that the request failed and why, and may propose a corrected request.
statements.explanation: An error result is useful evidence for repair.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Returning the error result guarantees that the model's next proposal will be valid.
statements.explanation: The model may repeat the mistake or introduce another one.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The application may now report to the user that the tool ran successfully, since a result block was produced.
statements.explanation: A result block with an error flag records a rejected request, not a successful execution.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Returning an error result means the arguments were validated and the operation was executed.
statements.explanation: The error result means the opposite: validation failed and nothing was executed.

questions.source: Dispatch belongs to the application
questions.stem: A developer changes `except ValueError` to `except Exception` in the code that builds tool results, so any exception becomes a model-visible error result containing the exception's message. A defect in the tool's own code now raises `KeyError` for some inputs. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A KeyError raised inside the tool's code is evidence that the model's arguments were wrong.
statements.explanation: It indicates a defect in the tool's own logic or data.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The KeyError now reaches the model as a routine-looking tool error while the host continues in an unknown state.
statements.explanation: A programming defect is relabeled as ordinary tool feedback and the system keeps running.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The model may respond to the defect by retrying with different arguments, which cannot fix a bug in the tool.
statements.explanation: Presenting an internal bug as an argument problem misdirects the repair attempt.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Catching every exception is a form of verification because all failures become visible in the trace.
statements.explanation: Visibility of a mislabeled failure is not a check, and the defect is hidden in a routine message.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Expected validation failures and unexpected programming errors deserve different handling, for example returning the first to the model and logging and halting on the second.
statements.explanation: Different failure classes call for different responses.

questions.source: The controller is a message machine
questions.stem: An agent loop is capped at 6 model requests. After an error result, the model proposes the same invalid call four times in a row, and the loop keeps feeding back the same error. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Raising the cap is the right fix for repeated invalid calls.
statements.explanation: More turns spend more budget without addressing why the same call keeps failing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The cap guarantees the task makes progress.
statements.explanation: A model can burn the whole budget on repeated calls that move nothing forward.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The cap bounds the number of model requests and therefore the cost of the loop.
statements.explanation: A hard turn limit prevents unbounded continuation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: When the cap is reached, reporting the outcome as `finished` is acceptable because the loop did stop.
statements.explanation: Stopping because the budget ran out is a different exit from finishing the task and should be reported as such.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Detecting repeated identical failing calls and stopping early is an additional control beyond the cap.
statements.explanation: Repeat detection limits wasted work without waiting for the limit.

questions.source: Identifiers create correspondence, not truth
questions.stem: A single assistant response contains three tool requests with identifiers `t1`, `t2` and `t3`. The application executes them and sends results in the order `t3`, `t1`, `t2` inside one user message. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Results are matched to requests by identifier, so the order inside the message does not change which result belongs to which request.
statements.explanation: The identifier is the correspondence mechanism, not position.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Leaving out the result for `t2` leaves a request unanswered, and tool-calling APIs such as Claude's and OpenAI's reject a follow-up request that has a tool request without a matching result.
statements.explanation: Every tool request must be answered in the next user message.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If `t2` failed validation, the application should omit it rather than return an error result.
statements.explanation: A rejected request still needs a result, flagged as an error, to close the exchange.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Running the three calls concurrently is always safe, even if `t2` reads a file that `t1` writes.
statements.explanation: Calls with dependencies or side effects on shared state must be ordered.

statements.label: E
statements.text: All three results belong in the same user message that follows the assistant message.
statements.explanation: Results for one assistant turn are returned together.

questions.source: Identifiers create correspondence, not truth
questions.stem: A dispatcher has a bug that maps the tool name `add` to subtraction. The model requests `add` with operands 17 and 25 under identifier `call-1`, and the application returns a result block with identifier `call-1` and content `-8`. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The result is correctly associated with the request that produced it.
statements.explanation: The identifier on the result repeats the request's identifier.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The matching identifier shows that the content `-8` is correct.
statements.explanation: The identifier says which request the result answers, not whether it is right.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Identifier correspondence establishes ownership of a result, and says nothing about the content.
statements.explanation: It works like a luggage tag: it identifies the suitcase without inspecting what is inside.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A unit test of the dispatcher with known operands and an expected sum would expose the defect.
statements.explanation: A test against an independently known value fails differently from the buggy mapping.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An independent hand calculation of 17 + 25 would reveal the defect.
statements.explanation: A separate derivation does not pass through the faulty mapping.

questions.source: Identifiers create correspondence, not truth
questions.stem: An assistant response contains two tool requests, `add(1, 2)` and `add(10, 20)`, and both blocks carry the identifier `x`. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A check that rejects duplicates within one response shows that identifiers are unique across the whole conversation.
statements.explanation: A per-batch check says nothing about identifiers used in earlier turns.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Silently discarding the second block is a safe way to resolve the ambiguity.
statements.explanation: That drops a request the model expected to be answered and hides an integrity problem.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the application returns two results labeled `x`, nobody can tell which result belongs to which request.
statements.explanation: Identity is the only link between request and result.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Returning results in order of arrival and assuming positions match is equivalent to correspondence by identifier.
statements.explanation: Positional matching is exactly the ambiguity identifiers exist to remove.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An accurate description of the guard is "duplicate identifiers within one processed batch are rejected".
statements.explanation: A check should be described with the scope it actually has.

questions.source: The controller is a message machine
questions.stem: An application using the Anthropic Messages API receives an assistant response with `stop_reason` set to `tool_use` and one tool request block. It must build the next request to the model. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The assistant's content, including the tool request block, should be appended to the history unchanged.
statements.explanation: The model needs to see its own request next to the result.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The application may drop the assistant's tool request block and send only the result, because the model will remember it.
statements.explanation: The model has no memory outside the supplied history, and the API expects each result to follow its request.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The result block refers to the request through the request's identifier.
statements.explanation: The identifier is the link between a result and its request.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The tool result is sent in a user-role message.
statements.explanation: Results are returned to the model as the user side of the conversation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In the user message, tool result blocks should come before any additional text blocks.
statements.explanation: Documented message-format rules put results first.

questions.source: The controller is a message machine
questions.stem: A controller handles responses from the Anthropic Messages API according to their `stop_reason` field. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: `end_turn` indicates the model finished its turn naturally and is not waiting on a tool.
statements.explanation: It is the normal completion signal.

statements.label: B
statements.text: `tool_use` indicates the model is waiting for the application to execute one or more requested tools.
statements.explanation: The controller must run the tools and continue.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Any stop reason other than `tool_use` can be treated as successful completion.
statements.explanation: Truncation and other stops are not completion, and treating them as success erases the reason execution ended.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A tool request in a response that stopped for `max_tokens` may have incomplete arguments and should not be executed as is.
statements.explanation: Truncation can cut the argument JSON off mid-structure.

statements.label: E
statements.text: `max_tokens` indicates the response was cut off at the output limit and may be incomplete.
statements.explanation: A truncated response needs an explicit policy, such as retrying with a larger limit.

questions.source: The controller is a message machine
questions.stem: A controller receives a response whose `stop_reason` is `tool_use`, but the content contains no tool request blocks. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Because the API produced the response, its fields can be assumed mutually consistent and no check is needed.
statements.explanation: Defensive handling of contradictory protocol signals is part of a bounded controller.

statements.label: B
statements.text: This is an inconsistent state, so raising an error or escalating is more appropriate than treating the run as finished.
statements.explanation: The signal and the content contradict each other.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The recommended handling is to retry the same request indefinitely until a consistent response arrives.
statements.explanation: Unbounded retries are the failure that turn limits exist to prevent.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The application can send an empty tool result to continue the loop.
statements.explanation: There is no request to answer, and fabricating a result would corrupt the history.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The anomaly can be ignored because the text blocks are the answer.
statements.explanation: The stop reason says the model was waiting for a tool, so those texts may be incomplete.

questions.source: The controller is a message machine
questions.stem: A controller returns the status `"verified"` whenever a response has `stop_reason == "end_turn"`. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The model saying "I have verified the result" in its reply is sufficient to justify the name.
statements.explanation: Self-report by the producing route is not a check from outside it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Naming the state `finished` or `completed` would describe the mechanism more accurately.
statements.explanation: An exit should be named for the evidence behind it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Downstream code that reads `verified` will reasonably infer that the answer was checked.
statements.explanation: People and programs read the name, not the mechanism.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The word `verified` should be reserved for a claim whose claim-specific check passed against evidence from outside the producing route.
statements.explanation: That is what makes the word informative.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The status name asserts more than the controller actually checked.
statements.explanation: The controller only observed a completion signal.

questions.source: The controller is a message machine
questions.stem: A team tests its tool-calling controller by injecting a function in place of the API client. The function returns scripted response dictionaries, including one that stops with `max_tokens`. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Injecting the callable makes the controller deterministic and testable offline.
statements.explanation: Known inputs give reproducible outputs without network access or cost.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Passing these tests shows that a live model will choose the right tool and operands.
statements.explanation: The model is not involved in a scripted test.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Exercising the truncated-stop path requires provoking a real truncation from a live model.
statements.explanation: A scripted response can emit a truncated stop on demand without a live model.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The scripted responses show how the controller behaves on those inputs and say nothing about how often a live model would produce them.
statements.explanation: The test isolates the control logic, not model behavior.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A report of these results may present the scripted responses as model output.
statements.explanation: Presenting a script as model output misrepresents the evidence.

questions.source: Ship It: the matrix, the trace, and the sign-off
questions.stem: A team's tool-loop test suite has six passing tests: a successful call, an unknown tool name, a boolean argument, preservation of the request identifier, an error result for a rejected call, and a truncated stop. Check each statement about what the suite supports.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The dispatcher is safe against hostile inputs.
statements.explanation: No test sends hostile inputs, so the suite is silent on that.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Concurrent calls are handled safely.
statements.explanation: None of the tests runs calls concurrently.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A regression that removed a duplicate-identifier guard would likely be caught by this suite.
statements.explanation: None of the six tests sends duplicate identifiers.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Identifiers are unique across a whole conversation.
statements.explanation: No test exercises identifiers across turns.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The six tested behaviors work for the inputs the tests use.
statements.explanation: A passing test supports exactly the behavior it exercises.

questions.source: 42 in the trace, 99 in the claim
questions.stem: A trace records the following. (1) The model requested `add(17, 25)` under identifier `k1`. (2) A result for `k1` with content `42` was returned. (3) A hand calculation gives 42. (4) The loop ended on `end_turn` and reported `finished`. (5) The final assistant message says "The answer is 99." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Item 4 supports the claim that the final answer is correct.
statements.explanation: Completion of the loop says nothing about the content of the last message.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Items 2 and 3 together support the claim that the tool's output for these operands is 42.
statements.explanation: An independent derivation agrees with the returned value.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Item 5 contradicts the evidence in items 2 and 3, so the final claim should not be reported as verified.
statements.explanation: The claim disagrees with both the tool output and the independent calculation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Whether 17 and 25 were the intended operands can only be settled by comparing the request with the user's task.
statements.explanation: The trace records what was requested, not what was meant.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Items 1 and 2 support the claim that the result belongs to the request `k1`.
statements.explanation: The identifiers correspond.

questions.source: 42 in the trace, 99 in the claim
questions.stem: After a tool returned 42, an assistant's final message says "The total is 99." A team wants the application to catch this kind of error. Check each statement that is a valid way to make the claim checkable.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Parse the number out of the final message and compare it with the value the tool returned.
statements.explanation: A programmatic comparison against tool evidence can reject a mismatch.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Have code insert the number into the report from the tool result, and let the model write only the surrounding explanation.
statements.explanation: Removing the model from the exact value eliminates narration drift for that value.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Ask the same model in the same conversation whether 99 is correct and accept a yes.
statements.explanation: The same route reviewing its own output is likely to repeat its error.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Add "double-check your arithmetic" to the system prompt and treat the reply as verified.
statements.explanation: An instruction to the producer is not a check that can say no.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A human should review every claim in every deployment regardless of stakes, as the only valid design.
statements.explanation: Verification depth should scale with consequence; a human on every claim is neither required nor always practical.

questions.source: Building a reusable tool evidence matrix
questions.stem: A verification step compares an agent's claim with a recomputed value and the two disagree. The controller then prompts the model, "Which number looks better?" and ships whichever the model picks. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The model's pick is independent evidence about which number is right.
statements.explanation: It shares the failure modes of the process that produced the first claim.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The check is working correctly because it surfaced a disagreement.
statements.explanation: A check that produces no action is theater; the disagreement must change what the system does.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Writing down what happens on disagreement before the check runs is part of designing the check.
statements.explanation: Deciding afterwards invites rationalizing the result.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A stop, retry or escalation policy decided before the run is what makes disagreement operational.
statements.explanation: A defined response gives the check consequences.

statements.label: E
statements.text: This turns the checker's evidence into another prompt instead of acting on it.
statements.explanation: The disagreement is delegated back to the system that produced the error.

questions.source: When the report is accurate and the reader is still misled
questions.stem: A file-writing tool returns "ok: wrote 1,284 bytes to /home/u/report.md". The agent then tells the user, "I saved your report." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A user may take "saved" to mean the file will still exist tomorrow, unchanged by other processes, which the result does not establish.
statements.explanation: Another process can modify or remove the file after the write.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The tool result is evidence that bytes were written to that path when the call ran.
statements.explanation: That is the narrow thing a write result establishes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A user may take "saved" to include that the content satisfies what they asked for, which the result does not establish.
statements.explanation: A write result says nothing about content quality or fit.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A user may take "saved" to include that the change is committed or backed up, which the result does not establish.
statements.explanation: Version control and remote copies are separate states.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Reading the file back and comparing it with the intended content would also establish that a remote repository holds the change.
statements.explanation: A local read-back says nothing about remote state.

questions.source: When the report is accurate and the reader is still misled
questions.stem: A `delete(path)` tool returns success after removing a file from the working directory of a project under version control. The agent reports "I deleted the customer export." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Copies may remain in backups, synced folders or on remote servers.
statements.explanation: Other copies are outside what the tool touched.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the call succeeded, describing the action as "permanently erased" is accurate.
statements.explanation: The evidence supports removal from one location only.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The file may still exist in earlier commits of the repository.
statements.explanation: Deleting from the working tree does not rewrite history.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A successful tool result establishes that the data no longer exists anywhere.
statements.explanation: The tool only reports on its own operation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A more accurate report states the scope, for example "removed from the working directory; still present in history".
statements.explanation: Naming scope prevents the reader from inferring a stronger outcome.

questions.source: When the report is accurate and the reader is still misled
questions.stem: A hypothetical screening model flags a scan and names two image regions as the main drivers of its prediction. A radiologist confirms that both regions are really present in the image and agrees with the flag. Unknown to anyone, the model had learned to rely on a scanner artifact that correlated with disease in its training data. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The explanation can be accurate about what influenced the model and still lead to a wrong decision.
statements.explanation: An accurate account of the mechanism does not show the mechanism is sound.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The radiologist's check that the regions are present does not test whether relying on those regions is clinically valid.
statements.explanation: The check addressed a different question from the one that mattered.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Asking what the reader will take the words to mean helps expose the gap between what was shown and what was concluded.
statements.explanation: Reports should be judged by the inference the audience draws.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An accurate account of what drove a prediction answers a different question from whether the decision is safe to act on.
statements.explanation: Feature attribution describes the model's mechanism, not the validity of its reliance.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Because the explanation was accurate, the reader's inference that the model reasons like a clinician is justified.
statements.explanation: The explanation said nothing about shortcut learning, so that inference is unsupported.

questions.source: Verification surfaces for real tools
questions.stem: An agent runs `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE status = 'open'` against a read replica and reports, "There are 1,204 open orders." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reporting the query text, time and data source alongside the count lets a reviewer test the claim.
statements.explanation: Parameters and timestamps make the evidence reproducible.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A successful query means the number is the current count of open orders.
statements.explanation: Success of execution does not establish freshness.

statements.label: C
