questions.stem: Two groups each have three analysts estimate a quantity. Group 1 is shown an AI-written synthesis of the evidence before forming any view. Group 2 writes down and dates their own estimates first, then is shown the synthesis. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Group 1 is more likely to anchor on the synthesis.
statements.explanation: Seeing a polished conclusion first pulls estimates toward it, an anchoring effect.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Collecting independent initial judgments first preserves variety in the views before a synthesis can compress it.
statements.explanation: Independent first judgments are the raw material for real disagreement, as in Delphi-style methods.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Showing the synthesis first improves the independence of the judgments.
statements.explanation: Prior exposure to a shared synthesis correlates the judgments rather than separating them.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Merging the three views into one smooth paragraph preserves dissent just as well as listing each view with its reasoning.
statements.explanation: A merged paragraph tends to average away minority views and their reasons.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A dated record of each initial judgment is unnecessary, because everyone remembers what they thought before reading.
statements.explanation: Memory of one's earlier view is reshaped by later exposure, and a dated record is the only proof of the sequence.

questions.source: Irreducibly Human
questions.stem: A three-person team decides which vendor to choose. Each person holds some facts that the other two do not, and all three hold some facts in common. Researchers describe a shared-information bias in group discussion. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In such a task, the best option can be identifiable only if the facts each person holds privately are pooled.
statements.explanation: This is the structure of a hidden-profile task, where the decisive evidence is spread across members.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Group discussion reliably surfaces each member's unique information.
statements.explanation: Groups tend to dwell on commonly held information and under-share what only one person knows.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A synthesis written only from the notes everyone saw contains the facts held privately by someone who did not write them down.
statements.explanation: A synthesis cannot include what no one put in the record.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If every fact behind the final decision was in the shared notes, one can conclude nobody had private information.
statements.explanation: It could also mean the private facts were lost or flattened before the decision, so the inference is not valid.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Telling the group to concentrate on points everyone already agrees on increases pooling of private facts.
statements.explanation: Emphasizing common ground deepens the bias; pooling needs prompts to bring out unshared facts.

questions.source: Integration is not sequencing
questions.stem: A shared record "due_day" is at version 3 with value "Friday". A researcher has found an updated official schedule saying "Monday" but has not yet written it to the store. An explainer worker read version 3 earlier and is now producing student instructions that say Friday. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: No version conflict has occurred at this point.
statements.explanation: Only one proposal exists, so no two writes have clashed on a version.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The store's expected-version check would flag the explainer's work as stale.
statements.explanation: The explainer has not attempted a write, so the version check never runs; the problem is new evidence, not a competing write.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A dependency map recording which outputs were built from which record versions shows what to pause.
statements.explanation: Version numbers order records, while a dependency map links decisions to the versions they rest on.

statements.label: D
statements.text: After version 4 ("Monday") is committed, instructions already produced from version 3 remain wrong until they are regenerated.
statements.explanation: A correction to the key does not reach artifacts already generated and circulated.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Committing the correction automatically fixes every downstream copy of the old value.
statements.explanation: Downstream artifacts are separate copies; they change only when regenerated or recalled.

questions.source: Integration is not sequencing
questions.stem: An incident process for a shared record uses these states: active, challenged, paused, reviewed, superseded, resumed. New official evidence has just contradicted the current value. Check each statement that is true about a sensible handling.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The assumption moves to challenged when contradicting evidence arrives, before anyone has judged it.
statements.explanation: Marking a claim challenged records that doubt exists without pretending it is resolved.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Downstream tasks whose correctness depends on the value move to paused.
statements.explanation: Work resting on the challenged value should stop until the question is settled.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A named person with authority reviews the evidence and its scope before a new value replaces the old one.
statements.explanation: Interpreting evidence and its scope is a judgment that needs an owner.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the evidence applies, the old record is marked superseded, a new version is committed with provenance, and affected work is regenerated before resuming.
statements.explanation: Supersession keeps the history, and regeneration repairs outputs built on the old value.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A single success or failure status is just as informative as these states.
statements.explanation: Two statuses cannot express paused work, pending review or superseded records.

questions.source: Integration is not sequencing
questions.stem: Reviewer R commits version 4 of the "due_day" record, replacing Friday with Monday and adding the qualification "for section B only". Worker Z, which read version 3, then submits "Monday" with expected=3 and is rejected as stale. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Automatically retrying Z's write at version 4 is unsafe, because the reviewed value carries a qualification Z's proposal lacks.
statements.explanation: A retry would overwrite the reviewed, qualified value with a less precise one.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A version conflict is a merge algorithm that combines the two proposals correctly.
statements.explanation: A version check only reports staleness; it does not combine content.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Z should reread the record, compare what changed in meaning, and either withdraw or submit a new proposal for review.
statements.explanation: The stale premise must be re-evaluated against the new state, with a human or reviewer deciding.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Catching the exception and logging success is acceptable because the store stayed internally consistent.
statements.explanation: Logging success hides a lost proposal and a decision that was never made.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Retrying at the fresh version is safe whenever the retried value equals what Z originally proposed.
statements.explanation: Equal wording to the earlier proposal does not make it correct against the new record.

questions.source: Integration is not sequencing
questions.stem: Two workers both read an order's status as pending and each call charge_card for order 981 for 40 dollars. Both calls succeed at the payment provider. Afterwards the second worker's stale update to the shared memory is rejected. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Rejecting the stale memory update afterward does not undo the second charge.
statements.explanation: The memory write and the card charge are separate effects; one cannot reverse the other.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An idempotency key derived from the logical operation (for example, the order and the charge purpose) would let the provider recognize the repeat.
statements.explanation: A stable key identifies the logical operation, so retries and duplicates collapse to one.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The memory store's version check protects external effects.
statements.explanation: The version check guards a record; it has no authority over calls to outside systems.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Generating a fresh random key for every attempt gives the same protection as a stable key.
statements.explanation: A new key per attempt makes each duplicate look like a distinct request.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A provider that deduplicates on key would still charge twice when both requests carry the same key.
statements.explanation: Deduplication on a shared key is precisely what prevents the second charge.

questions.source: Integration is not sequencing
questions.stem: An incident team stores full prompts and tool results from agent runs so that failures can be reconstructed. Some of the stored text contains customer information. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Retention helps replay but can hold private data, so the team should define what is stored, for how long, who can read it, and how deletion works.
statements.explanation: The competing needs of auditability and privacy are resolved by explicit retention and access policy.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Replacing every value with [REDACTED] always keeps the trace useful for explaining decisions.
statements.explanation: If every value is masked, the trace may no longer show which input led to which action.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Redaction should preserve enough structure that a reviewer can still see why a decision occurred.
statements.explanation: Targeted masking (for example consistent pseudonyms) can protect people while keeping relationships visible.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Keeping all traces indefinitely is the safest policy because evidence is never lost.
statements.explanation: Indefinite retention increases exposure and may violate retention limits.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The trace store needs access rules as carefully as the memory store does.
statements.explanation: A trace containing prompts and tool results can reveal as much as the store itself.

questions.source: Ship It: the premortem and the sign-off
questions.stem: A user asks for their data to be deleted. An engineer removes the key from the in-memory dictionary that backs the agent's memory and reports "deleted." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Deleted from this dictionary" is a claim the engineer's check can support, and "deleted everywhere" is not.
statements.explanation: The engineer observed one location; the wider claim needs evidence about the other locations.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Because the dictionary entry is gone, no copy can exist in prompt logs, backups, or summaries derived from the record.
statements.explanation: Logs, backups, replicas and transcripts are separate stores holding their own copies.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Summaries of the record written into other records are removed automatically when the original is deleted.
statements.explanation: Derived records are independent data and need their own deletion.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A thorough deletion test examines each place a copy could live and reports any place it did not inspect.
statements.explanation: Naming unchecked locations keeps the claim from exceeding the evidence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A successful delete call proves the data is gone from backups.
statements.explanation: A return code from one system says nothing about other systems.

questions.source: Integration is not sequencing
questions.stem: An incident log shows that a worker read a record "sometime before version 4 was committed" but did not save which version it received. Someone asks a language model to write the incident timeline from the log fragments. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The timeline should say that the version the worker read is unknown.
statements.explanation: Missing evidence should be marked as missing rather than reconstructed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Filling in version 3 is acceptable because it is the most likely value.
statements.explanation: A guess presented as a log entry becomes false evidence for later decisions.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A language model will usually write a coherent account even from fragments that do not fit together.
statements.explanation: Fluent narration is a strength of language models and can hide gaps or contradictions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A replay should record which output depended on which version and who had authority to interpret the new evidence.
statements.explanation: Dependencies and decision authority are what make the replay useful for assigning corrections.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A replay that reads as a coherent story is therefore complete.
statements.explanation: Coherence is not completeness; a smooth story can still be built over unrecorded events.

questions.source: Design the record and the triggers before the prompt
questions.stem: An application stores the record {"due_day": "Monday"} and later needs to place it in a prompt for a worker that writes public instructions. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The value should be rendered as a quoted claim with its provenance inside a data section, not in the system instruction channel.
statements.explanation: Presenting the value as quoted data with source keeps it from being read as an instruction.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Putting stored values in the system prompt is safe because the store is internal.
statements.explanation: Anything an untrusted writer can store could then carry instruction authority.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Keeping data apart from instructions lets the application apply different levels of trust to each.
statements.explanation: Separate channels allow the data to be validated and the instructions to be controlled.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because memory is shared, every worker should see every record.
statements.explanation: Sharing a store does not remove the need-to-know and sensitivity rules for each read.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A worker producing public text should receive only fields that are public, current and accepted.
statements.explanation: Reads should follow the purpose of the task, which limits exposure and error.

questions.source: Design the record and the triggers before the prompt
questions.stem: A design has research workers put candidate facts into a proposal queue. A reviewer checks the meaning of each proposal and either approves it or rejects it with a recorded reason. A coordinator then commits approved proposals to the store with the expected version. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The queue separates proposed facts from accepted facts.
statements.explanation: Workers cannot write directly into the accepted record.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The commit with an expected version ensures that the approved change still applies to the current record.
statements.explanation: If the record changed after the review began, the stale commit fails instead of overwriting.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A rejection with a recorded reason leaves an audit trail of the decision.
statements.explanation: Recording the reason lets later readers understand why a change did not occur.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The queue discards older proposals when newer ones arrive, so only the last proposal is kept.
statements.explanation: Discarding older proposals would erase disagreement and evidence that a reviewer may need.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Having a reviewer step guarantees correct values even if the reviewer never sees the evidence.
statements.explanation: Review adds protection only when the reviewer actually examines evidence.

questions.source: Design the record and the triggers before the prompt
questions.stem: A team's tests for a memory store check four things: (1) a missing key returns version 0, (2) the first write returns version 1, (3) a write with a stale expected version raises, and (4) a write with a blank source raises. All four pass. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A store whose read returns the stored list itself, with no copy, would also pass all four tests.
statements.explanation: None of the four tests mutates a returned value, so aliasing goes undetected.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A store that does the version comparison outside any lock would also pass all four tests, which run one call at a time.
statements.explanation: Sequential tests cannot interleave, so a race stays hidden.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A coordinator that silently retries every rejected write at the fresh version would go undetected by all four tests, because the tests exercise the store alone.
statements.explanation: The tests call the store directly, so none of them exercises what a coordinator does after a rejection.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Passing all four tests establishes that the store is safe under concurrent use.
statements.explanation: Four sequential tests say nothing about threads or processes.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If a required property cannot be tested, the honest record says it was not checked.
statements.explanation: Listing untested properties stops the sign-off from claiming more than the evidence supports.

questions.source: Ship It: the premortem and the sign-off
questions.stem: A team writes a risk plan for a multi-agent system with a shared memory, and lists a control for each failure. Check each statement that is true about matching controls to failures.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An expected-version check at commit time is a control for stale reads.
statements.explanation: The check rejects a commit built on a version that is no longer current.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An idempotency key at the point where an external action is issued is a control for duplicate actions.
statements.explanation: A stable key lets the receiving system recognize and collapse repeats of the same logical action.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Quarantining suspicious records is a control for duplicate actions.
statements.explanation: Quarantine keeps suspect text out of prompts, which addresses injection, not repeated side effects.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Field-level minimization combined with access rules is a control for privacy exposure from retained data.
statements.explanation: Storing less and limiting who can read it reduces exposure.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An access log alone proves that requested deletions were carried out.
statements.explanation: A log shows who accessed data, which says nothing about whether copies still exist.

questions.source: Ship It: the premortem and the sign-off
questions.stem: Two proposed entries for a risk plan about shared memory are compared. Entry X says "Monitor for stale memory." Entry Y says "On a stale-version exception for a record used by an active task, pause dependent actions, preserve both proposals, notify the decision owner, and resume only after a reviewed version is committed." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Entry Y names a trigger, a response, an owner and a recovery condition, so it can be implemented and tested.
statements.explanation: Each element gives a testable condition and an observable outcome.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Entry X can be tested by simulating a stale write and observing what happens.
statements.explanation: "Monitor" names no trigger, action or success condition, so there is nothing definite to simulate or observe.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Recording residual risk beside each control is unnecessary, because a control removes the risk it targets.
statements.explanation: Every control has its own failure modes, such as a quarantine nobody reviews.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Detecting a failure and recovering from it are the same test.
statements.explanation: A system can detect a problem and still fail to restore a safe state; recovery needs its own test.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Entry X is the better entry because its wording covers more cases.
statements.explanation: Breadth without specified behavior is not operational.

questions.source: Ship It: the premortem and the sign-off
questions.stem: A workflow lets reviewers look at a stale-write conflict, but the implementation always commits the newest proposal after the review step. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The workflow amounts to last-writer-wins with a review-shaped step in front of it.
statements.explanation: If the outcome never depends on the reviewer's decision, the review changes nothing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A test should include the case where the reviewer rejects the change and records a reason.
statements.explanation: The rejection path is the one that proves the reviewer's decision is respected.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Showing that the conflict was detected is enough to show that recovery works.
statements.explanation: Detection and recovery are separate; recovery needs a test that the system returns to a safe state.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It is acceptable for the paused task to resume without rereading the record, as long as the task finishes.
statements.explanation: Resuming on the stale value defeats the purpose of pausing.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the accept path passes its tests, the reject path is bound to pass too.
statements.explanation: Accept and reject are separate code paths and can fail independently.

questions.source: Ship It: the premortem and the sign-off
questions.stem: An engineer asks an AI assistant to draft the closing statement of a risk review. The statement is meant to record what was checked, how, what was not checked, and what is not being claimed. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A sound statement lists what was checked and how, what was not checked, and what is not being claimed.
statements.explanation: Scope statements let a reader judge how far to rely on the work.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An AI-drafted statement tends to omit the not-checked line, because the assistant has no record of what the engineer did not do.
statements.explanation: The assistant knows only what it was given, and omissions are invisible to it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A statement that claims more than the record supports repeats the original failure: a fresh, attributed claim nobody checked.
statements.explanation: Overclaiming produces exactly the unverified-but-official-looking record the review is meant to prevent.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the evidence does not support signing, withholding the sign-off is a legitimate result.
statements.explanation: A review that cannot be supported should not be signed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Fluent wording in the statement is evidence that the checks were actually performed.
statements.explanation: Fluency is cheap for a language model and says nothing about what was done.

questions.source: Computational Skepticism
questions.stem: A worker writes a note into a shared channel. In a later run, the same worker reads the channel, finds the note and treats it as outside evidence. Language-model agents can mistake their own earlier messages in a shared channel for the output of a second agent. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A claim that rests only on the worker's own earlier note counts as zero independent confirmations.
statements.explanation: Reading one's own output back adds no new information.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Tagging each record with its writer and run lets a reviewer find evidence that the worker wrote itself.
statements.explanation: Writer and run identifiers make self-citation detectable.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Two runs of the same worker agreeing is independent evidence.
statements.explanation: Runs of one worker share its model, prompts and tendencies, so their agreement is correlated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because the note sits in a shared store, it is outside evidence.
statements.explanation: Where text is stored does not establish who produced it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Listing which workers may write and read which keys helps check interaction patterns, not only individual agents.
statements.explanation: Many multi-agent failures arise from the pattern of reads and writes among workers.

questions.source: Conducting AI
questions.stem: A project's analyses of three data streams all point to the same site, which feels like confirmation. A fourth analysis, about labor costs, is recorded in the project file but nothing in the decision depends on it. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Three analyses agreeing may reflect shared assumptions or shared inputs rather than independent confirmation.
statements.explanation: Convergence is persuasive only to the extent that the routes are independent.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A recorded finding that changed nothing is either rightly irrelevant, and one can say why, or a missed reason to reopen an earlier decision.
statements.explanation: Unused evidence should either be explained away on its merits or acted on.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Checking that each section of the project is internally sound is enough to catch contradictions between sections.
statements.explanation: Each section can be sound while two sections contradict each other.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Weaknesses are often found at the joints between sections rather than inside them.
statements.explanation: Interfaces are where assumptions meet and checks are often skipped.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If no idle evidence is found, the reviewer should create a reopening event to complete the exercise.
statements.explanation: Manufacturing an event adds a fabricated record.

questions.source: Two workers, one key
questions.stem: A test runs three calls in sequence on a version-checked store. Call 1 writes "blue" at expected 0 and is accepted. Call 2 writes "red" at expected 1 and is accepted. Call 3 writes "blue" at expected 1 and is rejected. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The sequence shows the store's version behavior deterministically.
statements.explanation: Sequential calls give a repeatable trace of accept and reject decisions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The sequence shows how the store behaves under many simultaneous writers.
statements.explanation: Simultaneity is exactly what a sequential run excludes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Call 3's rejection is correct concurrency behavior whether "red" or "blue" is the true value.
statements.explanation: The rejection depends only on the version mismatch and not on the content.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because the rejected call carried the better-sourced value, the store has shown it can tell which value is wrong.
statements.explanation: The store never evaluated sources, so it cannot know which value is better supported.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Running this sequence once is enough to describe the store as robust.
statements.explanation: One happy-path sequence leaves many cases untested, including contention and restarts.

questions.source: Anthropics
questions.stem: A team builds a long-running agent whose conversation will exceed its context window. They consider several techniques that are widely described in guidance on context engineering for agents. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Compaction summarizes a conversation that is nearing the context limit and continues with the summary in place of the full history.
statements.explanation: This is the standard definition of compaction.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Structured note-taking writes notes to storage outside the context window so the agent can pull them back in later.
statements.explanation: External notes persist beyond the window and can be retrieved when needed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A sub-agent can explore with its own context and return a condensed result to the lead agent.
statements.explanation: Delegating exploration keeps the lead's context focused on the condensed result.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A larger context window means every token in it is used with equal reliability.
statements.explanation: Long contexts can dilute attention, so quality can degrade as the window fills.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Keeping lightweight references and loading the data only when it is needed (just-in-time retrieval) can conserve limited context.
statements.explanation: Preloading everything consumes limited context and can bury what matters, so loading on demand is often preferred.

questions.source: Anthropics
questions.stem: An orchestrator agent uses 30,000 tokens. It spawns five sub-agents that run in parallel and use 40,000 tokens each. A single agent doing the same task alone would use 90,000 tokens. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The multi-agent run uses 230,000 tokens in total.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Running the sub-agents in parallel can shorten wall-clock time without reducing total token use.
statements.explanation: Parallelism changes how the work is scheduled, not how much of it is done.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In this scenario the multi-agent run is cheaper in tokens than the single agent.
statements.explanation: 230,000 tokens is more than 90,000.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Tasks whose steps depend heavily on each other are generally worse candidates for parallel sub-agents than broad, independent searches.
statements.explanation: Interdependent steps need shared state and sequencing, which parallel workers lack.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The orchestrator can skip checking sub-agent outputs because they come from the same model.
statements.explanation: Same-model outputs share the same failure modes and still need checking, especially at handoffs.

questions.source: Memory is stored state, not recollection
questions.stem: A designer describes an agent's memory using common terms. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The contents of the model's context window act as its working, or short-term, memory for a task.
statements.explanation: Only what is in the window is directly available to the model within a call.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An external store the agent queries lets it carry information across sessions without keeping everything in the prompt.
statements.explanation: Retrieval lets a store hold more than fits in any one prompt.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Episodic memory means general facts that are independent of any particular event.
statements.explanation: That describes semantic memory; episodic memory records specific past events or interactions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Procedural memory covers stored how-to knowledge, such as instructions or learned routines.
statements.explanation: Procedural memory is knowledge of how to do things.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Writing a note to an external store is equivalent to fine-tuning the model on that note.
statements.explanation: Fine-tuning changes model weights, while an external write changes only data.

questions.source: Memory is stored state, not recollection
questions.stem: An agent ranks stored memories by a weighted sum of three scores, each between 0 and 1: recency, importance and relevance to the current task. Memory M1 has recency 0.9, importance 0.2, relevance 0.5. Memory M2 has recency 0.3, importance 0.9, relevance 0.8. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: With equal weights of 1 on all three scores, M2 outranks M1.
statements.explanation: M2 totals 0.3 + 0.9 + 0.8 = 2.0, which is above M1's 1.6.

statements.label: B
statements.text: With equal weights, M1's total score is 1.6.

statements.label: C
statements.text: With weights recency 5, importance 1 and relevance 1, M1 outranks M2.

statements.label: D
statements.text: With weights recency 1, importance 1 and relevance 3, M1 outranks M2.
statements.explanation: M1 totals 0.9 + 0.2 + 1.5 = 2.6 against M2's 0.3 + 0.9 + 2.4 = 3.6, so M2 still leads.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A high retrieval score guarantees that the retrieved memory is correct.
statements.explanation: Scores rank likely usefulness and say nothing about whether the stored content is true.

questions.source: Check: what each guard establishes
questions.stem: An agent keeps a rolling summary of its history. After every step it replaces the earlier summary and raw records with a new, shorter summary of everything so far. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Details dropped from one summary cannot be recovered from later summaries.
statements.explanation: Each new summary is built from the previous one, so lost information stays lost.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An error introduced in an early summary can persist through every later summary built from it.
statements.explanation: Later summaries inherit and often restate earlier mistakes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Discarding the raw records after each summary keeps the system easier to audit.
statements.explanation: Without raw records nobody can check the summary against what actually happened.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A summary is always at least as accurate as the material it summarizes.
statements.explanation: Summarization can omit conditions, introduce errors or overgeneralize.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Compaction of history into a summary is lossless.
statements.explanation: Compression necessarily discards information.

questions.source: Revision boundaries and optimistic concurrency
questions.stem: When two workers submit conflicting values for the same record, a system must choose a resolution policy. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Last-writer-wins can silently discard a correct earlier value.
statements.explanation: The later write replaces the earlier one regardless of merit.

statements.label: B
statements.text: First-writer-wins does not test which value is true either.
statements.explanation: Order of arrival is unrelated to truth.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Compare-and-set with an expected version surfaces the conflict to the caller instead of resolving it silently.
statements.explanation: The stale writer gets an error and must decide what to do next.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A merge rule that automatically combines concurrent edits guarantees that the merged value is true.
statements.explanation: A merge rule can produce a coherent-looking value that neither source supports.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A policy that always keeps the value with the latest timestamp judges which value is correct.
statements.explanation: Recency selects the newest claim, and a newer claim can be a newer mistake.

questions.source: Design the record and the triggers before the prompt
questions.stem: A team debates whether a shared record should be updated in place or kept as a chain of versions in which each new version points to the one it supersedes. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Keeping earlier versions with a pointer to what each supersedes supports audit.
statements.explanation: The chain lets a reviewer follow how a value changed and which version each decision used.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Overwriting in place loses the ability to reconstruct what a worker read at a given time.
statements.explanation: Once the old value is gone, a replay cannot show what a worker saw.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Superseded versions should be deleted immediately to avoid confusing readers.
statements.explanation: Deleting history removes what an incident review needs; readers can be shown only the current version by default.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A record that supersedes version 3 proves that version 3 was wrong.
statements.explanation: Supersession records a decision to replace, not that the earlier value was false; the earlier value may have been correct for its time.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Retaining history can conflict with privacy requirements, so the retention rules need to be decided deliberately.
statements.explanation: Retention serves audit, while privacy and legal limits can require deletion or minimization.

questions.source: Design the record and the triggers before the prompt
questions.stem: A team adds a field "verification" with values such as "unverified" and "human-reviewed" to each stored record. In the first version of the code, any worker can set this field to any value when it writes. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A worker setting its own record to "human-reviewed" is self-attestation, not verification.
statements.explanation: The field would record the writer's own claim about itself.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Letting any worker set the field is fine as long as the value is one of the recognized strings.
statements.explanation: Valid-looking strings do not show that a reviewer did the work; permission to set the field should be restricted and the setter recorded.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Adding more fields to a record automatically increases how much it can be trusted.
statements.explanation: More fields add detail, but trust depends on whether anything checks them.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Adding a field removes the need for validation rules about how it is set.
statements.explanation: Every field raises questions about who may set it and what empty values mean.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If code and policy do not enforce what the field means, it gives only the appearance of rigor.
statements.explanation: A label with no enforcement is decoration.

questions.source: Computational Skepticism
questions.stem: A team of agents shares a store. The team writes down which workers may write which keys and which may read which keys. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Such a matrix lets a reviewer check whether any worker's supporting evidence was written by that same worker.
statements.explanation: The matrix identifies who could have produced each key's content.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Giving every worker write access to every key is safest because it keeps the system flexible.
statements.explanation: Broad write access widens the set of workers that can introduce errors or malicious text.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Least-privilege write access limits the damage a compromised or faulty worker can do.
statements.explanation: A worker that cannot write a key cannot corrupt it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Restricting reads is unnecessary once writes are restricted.
statements.explanation: Reads control what sensitive or low-trust data a worker can see and act on.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The matrix makes record-level provenance unnecessary.
statements.explanation: A matrix describes permissions, while provenance records what actually happened to a particular claim.

questions.source: Ship It: the premortem and the sign-off
questions.stem: A shared store holds 200 notes, 10 of which are wrong. A reviewer checks 20 notes chosen uniformly at random without replacement. The probability that the sample contains none of the wrong notes is about 0.34, so the probability of seeing at least one is about 0.66. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The reviewer has about a 66 percent chance of seeing at least one wrong note.
statements.explanation: One minus 0.34 is about 0.66.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A clean sample of 20 proves the store has no wrong notes.
statements.explanation: A clean sample is compatible with a store that contains wrong notes, as the 34 percent shows.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The chance of missing all 10 wrong notes is about 34 percent.
statements.explanation: The probability of drawing none of the 10 wrong notes is about 0.34.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Checking 40 notes instead of 20 lowers the chance of missing every wrong note.
statements.explanation: A larger sample leaves fewer places to hide; with 40 notes the miss chance falls to about 10 percent.

statements.label: E
statements.text: After a clean sample, a sign-off can say "no wrong notes" without qualification.
statements.explanation: The accurate statement is limited to the sample and its size.

questions.source: Multiple workers: Claude coordinates, humans deliberate
questions.stem: A writer agent produces a wrong note 5 percent of the time. One reviewer catches 80 percent of wrong notes. Two reviewers who miss errors independently each catch 70 percent of wrong notes. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: With the single 80 percent reviewer, about 1 percent of all notes are both wrong and pass review.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Two independent 70 percent reviewers together miss about 9 percent of wrong notes.
statements.explanation: Independent misses multiply: 0.3 x 0.3 = 0.09.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If two 70 percent reviewers always miss exactly the same notes, together they still miss 30 percent of wrong notes.
statements.explanation: Perfectly correlated misses add no coverage beyond one reviewer.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Adding a second reviewer built from the same model and prompt as the first lowers the miss rate to 9 percent.
statements.explanation: The same model and prompt tend to share blind spots, so misses are correlated and the improvement is far less than the independent case.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A reviewer who is shown the writer's conclusion first catches errors at the same rate as a blind reviewer.
statements.explanation: Seeing the conclusion first can anchor the reviewer on it and lower the catch rate.

questions.source: Verify and reflect
questions.stem: A test log shows three observations: a write raised "Stale memory version"; another write returned version 5; and a read afterward returned the value "red". Check each statement that is supported by those observations alone.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The first write was rejected.
statements.explanation: An observed exception means the store refused the write.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The second write was committed.
statements.explanation: A returned version number means the write was committed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The second write's value was verified.
statements.explanation: Verification needs a criterion and evidence that the log does not contain.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Red" is what is true in the world.
statements.explanation: The store holds what it was given; nothing here tests the world.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The rejection resolved the disagreement between the two workers.
statements.explanation: Refusing one write leaves the underlying disagreement about which value is right unresolved.

questions.source: Revision boundaries and optimistic concurrency
questions.stem: A store uses a single key "room" to hold the reservation state for both room 505A and room 505B. Workers updating different rooms use the same version counter. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A worker updating 505A can be rejected because a worker updated 505B, even though the updates are unrelated.
statements.explanation: One counter for both rooms makes unrelated updates look like conflicts.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Splitting into one key per room means any decision that depends on both rooms is covered by a single version.
statements.explanation: After splitting, there are two counters and neither covers a decision that spans them.

statements.label: C
statements.text: After splitting, a decision based on both rooms needs its own dependency tracking to detect that one input changed.
statements.explanation: Cross-key decisions need recorded input versions or a single covering version.

statements.label: D
statements.text: How many things one version covers is irrelevant to which conflicts the store can see.
statements.explanation: The scope of a version determines which conflicts are visible.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Placing all application data under one key is always the safest design.
statements.explanation: One giant key creates many false conflicts and serializes unrelated work.

questions.source: Multiple workers: Claude coordinates, humans deliberate
questions.stem: A reviewer agent is given a budget of one pass over its inputs and an instruction that any item it cannot judge goes to a named person. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A budget cap limits the cost of a worker that loops or gets stuck.
statements.explanation: A bound on steps or tokens caps the damage from loops and drift.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Deciding who receives uncertain items is a design decision made before the worker runs.
statements.explanation: An escalation route chosen in advance keeps uncertainty from being resolved by guessing.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Retrying indefinitely until the worker succeeds is a safe default.
statements.explanation: Unbounded retries burn resources and can repeat the same error without learning anything new.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Removing budgets and escalation paths makes accountability simpler.
statements.explanation: Unbounded workers make it harder to say who decided what.

statements.label: E
statements.text: When the budget runs out, the worker should return its best guess marked as verified.
statements.explanation: Marking a guess as verified would misreport its status.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against your gate
questions.stem: A developer asks an assistant to write a deliberately faulty version of a store, for example one that returns a reference to the stored list or one that retries a rejected write at the fresh version, and then runs the existing tests against it. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If a faulty version passes all the tests, the tests are too weak for that fault.
statements.explanation: A surviving fault shows an untested behavior.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If a faulty version fails a test, that test is shown to detect that type of fault.
statements.explanation: A failing test confirms that it is sensitive to that behavior.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Tests that pass on the correct implementation prove that no fault exists.
statements.explanation: Passing tests only show the behaviors that were tested.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Seeding plausible faults to see whether tests catch them is a form of mutation testing.
statements.explanation: Introducing mutants and checking whether tests kill them is the definition of mutation testing.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Only the assistant that wrote the implementation should write the tests for it.
statements.explanation: Tests written by the same source share its assumptions and blind spots; independent authorship is better.

questions.source: Opening section: predict before reading
questions.stem: Before running a piece of code, a learner writes down and dates predictions about what it will do, then runs it and records the results. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Writing predictions before running guards against hindsight bias.
statements.explanation: Once the result is known, people tend to feel they had predicted it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Editing the predictions after seeing results preserves their value as a check on one's mental model.
statements.explanation: Editing after the fact erases the very gap the exercise is meant to expose.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A mismatch between prediction and result is evidence about the learner's model and worth keeping.
statements.explanation: Surprises show where the mental model was wrong.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The predictions do not need dates, because the order of events is obvious from the results.
statements.explanation: A dated record is what shows the prediction came before the result.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Only predictions that turn out correct should be kept in the record.
statements.explanation: Keeping only successes hides what was learned from errors.

questions.source: A gate is not a button
questions.stem: An autonomous coding agent pauses and shows a human reviewer a dialog that says only "The agent wants to run a command. Allow?" with Allow and Deny buttons. A security engineer proposes redesigning the request so that a yes from the reviewer actually means something. Check each statement that is true about the redesign.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The request should state what operation will occur and against which resolved target, since consequences cannot be judged without both.
statements.explanation: An approval is only as informative as the action and object it names; "a command" names neither.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The request should say why the action serves the user's task, not merely that the agent is able to perform it.
statements.explanation: Capability does not establish intent; the purpose is what lets a reviewer notice an action that does not fit the task.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Showing the agent's self-reported confidence score is a sufficient substitute for describing the action, since high confidence means the action is safe.
statements.explanation: Confidence is not a description of what will happen, and a model's self-assessment is not evidence about the world.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The request should say how the action could be undone, including when it cannot be undone.
statements.explanation: Recoverability changes how much scrutiny an action deserves, and an honest "not reversible" is a key input.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A long free-text paragraph written by the agent removes the need for any structured fields, because a reviewer can read it to find what matters.
statements.explanation: Unstructured prose lets omissions hide; named fields make a missing effect or rollback visible.

questions.source: A gate is not a button
questions.stem: An agent proposes "overwrite config.yaml in the project". The workspace contains ./config.yaml and ./deploy/config.yaml. ./config.yaml is a symbolic link to /etc/shared/config.yaml, a file other teams depend on. A reviewer approves after seeing only the display name "config.yaml". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The approval does not establish which file will be modified, because the display name does not identify one object.
statements.explanation: Two files share the name, and the consequential difference between them is hidden by the label.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An experienced reviewer who knows the repository layout makes resolved paths unnecessary, since they can infer what each name refers to.
statements.explanation: Even experts cannot see a link target that the interface does not show, and layouts change.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Whatever file the agent ends up opening is covered by an approval that named "config.yaml", because the name was what the reviewer saw.
statements.explanation: An approval covers the object the reviewer understood; a name that fits several objects does not bind to any one of them.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Showing the resolved real path would let the reviewer see that a shared file outside the project is affected.
statements.explanation: Resolved identities (path, account, environment) expose consequences that friendly names conceal.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Writing to a path that is a symbolic link modifies only the link itself and never the file it points to.
statements.explanation: Opening a symlink for writing follows it and modifies the target file on POSIX systems.

questions.source: A gate is not a button
questions.stem: An agent asks for approval to send a customer-facing announcement email to 4,000 recipients. The rollback field in its request reads "undo the send". The email platform has no recall feature, and recipients' mail clients may already have downloaded the message. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Irreversible external effects are the effects that most need to be visible to the reviewer.
statements.explanation: Once the message is out, only the pre-action decision can prevent harm.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A rollback field filled with any plausible-sounding text serves its purpose, because reviewers seldom rely on it when deciding whether to approve.
statements.explanation: A plausible but false rollback plan is worse than an admitted gap, since it lowers the scrutiny the action needs.

statements.label: C
statements.text: When rollback is impossible, the request should make the impact and alternatives more prominent, not less.
statements.explanation: Absent recovery, the reviewer's decision is the last control, so the information it depends on should be unavoidable.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Assessing a rollback plan includes checking its assumptions: that a prior copy exists, is accessible, and that dependent effects have not occurred.
statements.explanation: "Restore from backup" is only valid if the backup exists, can be read, and restores the relevant state.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The rollback claim is unreliable; an honest request would say the send cannot be undone and offer a partial remedy such as a correction message.
statements.explanation: Reassurance that does not match what the system can do misleads the reviewer on the point that matters most.

questions.source: A gate is not a button
questions.stem: An approval workflow rejects any proposal in which one of six required text fields is empty. An agent submits a proposal where all six are filled: action "do task", target "files", reason "needed", effects "none", evidence "looks good", rollback "revert". The validator accepts it. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The validator checks presence only, so acceptance says nothing about whether the descriptions are adequate.
statements.explanation: A non-empty string can be uninformative or wrong; structural validity is a different property from substantive adequacy.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Acceptance by the validator means the proposal is safe to approve, since every required field has been checked.
statements.explanation: The validator has no view of meaning, so safety is not something its output can claim.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A rule that rejects phrases such as "n/a" and "looks good" removes the need for human judgment about adequacy.
statements.explanation: A blocklist catches some filler but cannot tell fluent, specific-sounding text that is wrong from text that is right.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Adding a minimum character length per field fully solves the problem, because longer text must contain more information.
statements.explanation: Padding with filler satisfies a length rule without adding information.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A reviewer should treat "evidence: looks good" as an unsupported claim, because it points to no artifact that can be checked.
statements.explanation: Evidence is a pointer to a result someone can inspect, not an assertion that things are fine.

questions.source: A gate is not a button
questions.stem: A coding agent asks to delete the build cache directory. Its stated reason is "I have write permission to that directory." Check each statement that is true about this request.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A good reason is one the reviewer can verify, for example by pointing to the failing build the deletion is meant to fix.
statements.explanation: Verifiability is what separates a reason from a rationalization.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Having permission describes capability, not purpose, so it does not justify the action.
statements.explanation: Permissions are usually broader than intent; "I am allowed" does not say "this is wanted".

statements.label: C
statements.text: The reason field is redundant whenever the action and target are shown, because purpose can always be inferred.
statements.explanation: Identical actions can serve opposite purposes, and an inferred purpose is a guess.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A reason that merely restates the action ("delete the cache") is as informative as one linking the deletion to the user's goal.
statements.explanation: Only a goal-linked reason lets the reviewer judge whether the action fits the task.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Reasons matter only for after-the-fact audit and do not help a reviewer decide now.
statements.explanation: A reason that does not match the task is a signal the reviewer can use before approving.

questions.source: Evaluation comes before authorization
questions.stem: A pipeline runs a unit test suite, a policy checker that flags edits outside approved directories, and an LLM-based rubric grader on an agent's proposed change. All three report green, and the dashboard shows them above an Approve button. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A passing test suite can evaluate selected behavior, but cannot establish that a destructive change is worth making.
statements.explanation: Tests check specified properties; whether the trade-off is acceptable is a judgment about consequences.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A green score from the model grader is itself the decision, because the grader was given a rubric by the team that owns the process.
statements.explanation: A grader's score is evidence with its own failure modes, not an authorization.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Each instrument produces evidence about a bounded set of properties; none of them decides whether the change should be made.
statements.explanation: Evaluation tells you what happened or could happen against criteria; permitting the action is a separate act.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Evaluation asks how well the proposal meets stated criteria; authorization asks whether a responsible person or policy permits it.
statements.explanation: These two questions are often merged on one screen, which is where gates become unreliable.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A policy checker can flag an unapproved directory but cannot judge whether an exception would serve the people affected.
statements.explanation: Rule compliance and the value of an exception are different questions.

questions.source: Evaluation comes before authorization
questions.stem: A team evaluating an agent's new tool-use behavior first watches the agent attempt ten tasks. They then write the evaluation cases around what it did and, where its output was reasonable, adjust the expected answers to match. After the edits all ten cases pass, and the team reports "10/10". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Deciding what would count as evidence against the system before looking at its outputs keeps an evaluation able to fail.
statements.explanation: Setting criteria in advance prevents the evidence from selecting its own standard.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Running each of the ten tasks several more times fixes the problem, because averaging removes any bias in the cases.
statements.explanation: Repeats measure noise, not the bias introduced by choosing criteria after seeing outputs.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The adjustment is harmless as long as the ten final cases are legitimate tasks that the agent could plausibly be asked to do.
statements.explanation: Legitimate tasks can still be a biased sample if their expected answers were fitted to one system's behavior.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The cases were shaped to fit the observed behavior, so the pass count records accommodation rather than a test that could fail.
statements.explanation: A test whose expected result was changed to match the output could not have embarrassed the system.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Because expected answers were adjusted only where the output was reasonable, 10/10 is a conservative estimate of quality.
statements.explanation: Adjusting toward the observed output biases results upward, not downward.

questions.source: Evaluation comes before authorization
questions.stem: An agent is asked to close inactive accounts. Its tool trace shows a single call, UPDATE accounts SET status='closed' WHERE last_login < '2025-01-01', which returned success with "42 rows affected". The agent's final message says "I closed all 99 matching accounts." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Where the fluent final message and the trace disagree, the message should be preferred because it is a summary of the whole task.
statements.explanation: Fluency is not accuracy; the message is the least verified of the three artifacts.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The final message contradicts the trace, which reports 42 rows, so the claim of 99 is unsupported by the available evidence.
statements.explanation: When narration and tool output disagree, the narration has no independent standing.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A trace showing that a command ran is not the same as an observation that the intended end state exists.
statements.explanation: Execution evidence and outcome evidence answer different questions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The trace remains useful as a record of what was attempted, but it must be kept distinct from observations of actual outcomes.
statements.explanation: Both records matter for diagnosis; they should not be merged into a single "success" flag.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A separate post-action query counting accounts in the closed state would be stronger evidence than the trace or the narration.
statements.explanation: An independent observation of the world can contradict the agent's account.

questions.source: Evaluation comes before authorization
questions.stem: A team reports that a file-writing agent "passed 20 of 20 evaluation cases." All 20 cases write ordinary text files into a newly created empty directory. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The result says little about symbolic links, permission errors, concurrent changes, or ".." in paths, because no case exercised them.
statements.explanation: A pass count is only informative about the situations the cases actually cover.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Exclusions matter only if the agent has previously failed in those situations; otherwise they can be ignored.
statements.explanation: Absence of past failures is not evidence about conditions that were never tried.

statements.label: C
statements.text: 20 of 20 shows the agent handles any file operation it will meet in production, since the cases passed without a single failure.
statements.explanation: Production inputs include conditions that none of the 20 cases represent.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The report is more interpretable if it states only the pass count, since listing excluded situations distracts readers.
statements.explanation: Without the covered and excluded situations, a reader cannot tell what the pass count means.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Adding 20 more ordinary writes would substantially improve coverage of the risky boundaries, because the sample size would double.
statements.explanation: More of the same does not probe different failure modes.

questions.source: Evaluation comes before authorization
questions.stem: An evaluation set for an agent that decides whether to carry out requested file operations has 20 cases where the correct behavior is to proceed. An agent that always proceeds is scored on it. The team then adds 5 cases where the correct behavior is to refuse, and scores the same always-proceed agent again. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Adding refusal cases is wrong unless their share of the set matches their frequency in production.
statements.explanation: A set meant to expose boundary behavior may deliberately oversample rare, high-consequence cases.

statements.label: B
statements.text: On the expanded 25-case set, the always-proceed agent scores 80% (20 of 25) because it gets only the original cases right.
statements.explanation: It fails exactly the 5 refusal cases.

statements.label: C
statements.text: On the original 20 cases, the always-proceed agent scores 100%, because every correct answer is to proceed.
statements.explanation: Every case rewards proceeding, so an indiscriminate agent looks perfect.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A set without refusal cases would still reveal an indiscriminate agent, because such agents fail ordinary tasks too.
statements.explanation: Ordinary tasks reward proceeding, so indiscriminate agents pass them.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A set with no should-refuse cases cannot distinguish a careful agent from a reckless one.
statements.explanation: The distinguishing behavior, declining when it should, is never exercised.

questions.source: Evaluation comes before authorization
questions.stem: After redesigning an approval screen so that details sit behind a "show more" link, a team reports: median time to approval fell from 90 seconds to 25, reviewer satisfaction rose, and task success stayed at 94%. The share of executed actions later judged invalid rose from 1% to 4%. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A useful evaluation reports a portfolio that includes error and deferral rates, not one celebratory rate.
statements.explanation: Errors and deferrals are the evidence a single success rate discards.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Faster approvals can reflect reflexive clicking rather than a more efficient review.
statements.explanation: Less time per decision can mean less attention per decision.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Unchanged task success shows the redesign is safe, because the agent completes the same share of tasks as before.
statements.explanation: Task success does not capture invalid actions that happen to leave the task output intact.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The metrics pull in different directions, so a single headline number such as time to approval would mislead.
statements.explanation: Speed, satisfaction, success and error rates measure different things and can move oppositely.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The invalid-action share quadrupled, from 1% to 4%, which is consistent with reviewers catching fewer problems.
statements.explanation: 4/1 = 4; the direction fits a less informed review, though it does not by itself prove the cause.

questions.source: Evaluation comes before authorization
questions.stem: To score free-text rollback plans, a team uses two LLM graders. Both use the same rubric prompt, which rewards "specific, step-by-step recovery instructions". The two graders agree on 96% of items. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: 96% agreement between the graders shows that their scores are accurate, since independent judges rarely agree by chance.
statements.explanation: Agreement measures consistency between graders, not correctness against ground truth.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Model graders should replace deterministic checks whenever the output is free text, because they can judge meaning.
statements.explanation: Deterministic checks, where they exist, are cheaper and more reliable and should be combined with model grading.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A fluent step-by-step plan that omits an irreversible side effect would be scored poorly under this rubric, since omissions are penalized.
statements.explanation: The rubric rewards the appearance of specific detail, which fluent text can supply without being correct.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Calibration against human-labeled examples becomes unnecessary once the two graders agree with each other this closely.
statements.explanation: Only comparison with trusted labels reveals systematic error.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Agreement between graders that share a prompt and similar biases does not make them independent verifiers.
statements.explanation: Shared assumptions or blind spots can make two judges wrong in the same direction.

questions.source: Evaluation comes before authorization
questions.stem: A team's approval-gate prototype passes all 6 of 6 evaluation cases. A manager proposes reporting that the approval gate is "100% reliable". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: With so few cases, the best report is a single pass rate with no further detail, because details add noise.
statements.explanation: Listing the cases and exclusions is more informative than a percentage of a tiny set.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Six passing cases show that the six covered properties are sufficient to establish that the approval gate is correct overall.
statements.explanation: Passing a set of tests shows only that those statements hold, not that they are the right or complete statements.

statements.label: C
statements.text: With six independent random cases and zero failures, the 95% upper bound on the true failure rate is still about 39% (1 - 0.05^(1/6)).
statements.explanation: A small clean sample is compatible with a high underlying error rate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Six passes support reporting a reliability percentage, as long as each case was run carefully and the results were recorded.
statements.explanation: Care does not turn a handful of cases into a population estimate.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the six cases were hand-picked to cover distinct failure modes, they still support a population-level percentage.
statements.explanation: Hand-picked cases are not a random sample and do not estimate a rate.

questions.source: Evaluation comes before authorization
questions.stem: An agent succeeds on a given task independently with probability 0.7 on each attempt. A team evaluates it with three independent trials per task. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For an action that is harmful when it fails, "at least one success in k trials" is the better headline measure.
statements.explanation: Harmful failures call for the stricter all-trials view; best-of-k hides inconsistency.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Because a model is nondeterministic, a single trial per task is enough to characterize it.
statements.explanation: One trial cannot show the variation between runs that the measures above quantify.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The probability of at least one success in three trials is 0.973, which is 1 minus 0.3 cubed.
statements.explanation: Complement of three consecutive failures: 1 - 0.027.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "At least one success" and "all trials succeed" are the same measure whenever the trials are independent.
statements.explanation: They differ sharply here, 0.973 versus 0.343.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The probability of succeeding on all three trials is about 0.343, which is 0.7 cubed.
statements.explanation: Independent successes multiply.

questions.source: Evaluation comes before authorization
questions.stem: Before running an evaluation, a team writes down the expected outcome for each case. After the run, case 7's actual result differs from its expected outcome. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If the expectation or requirement is changed, no record of the change is needed once the final version of the test passes.
statements.explanation: Without a record, the evaluation looks as if it was always satisfied and the reason for the change is lost.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Locking expectations in advance is pointless because they will need revision after the first run anyway.
statements.explanation: The commitment is what makes a later change visible and accountable.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Failing cases should be removed from the set as unrepresentative, so that the set reflects normal operation.
statements.explanation: Removing failures guarantees a passing set and destroys the evidence.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The expected outcome should be silently edited to match the result so that the final report is clean and consistent.
statements.explanation: A clean-looking report built on edited expectations conceals what was learned.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The discrepancy could come from the implementation, the test expectation, or the original requirement, and each should be investigated.
statements.explanation: Any of the three could be wrong, and blaming the implementation by default skips real diagnoses.

questions.source: Canonical content and its fingerprint
questions.stem: Two services build the same approval request as Python dictionaries. One inserts the keys in the order action, target, reason; the other inserts them in the order reason, target, action. Each computes SHA-256 over json.dumps(request).encode(), with no sort_keys option, and the services compare digests. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Python dictionaries keep insertion order and json.dumps emits keys in that order, so the services produce different bytes and digests.
statements.explanation: The hash is computed over bytes, and the bytes differ.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The digests would match anyway, because SHA-256 hashes the meaning of the data rather than the particular bytes used to write it.
statements.explanation: A hash function sees only bytes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Passing sort_keys=True makes the serialization independent of insertion order for JSON-compatible data.
statements.explanation: Sorting gives one canonical key order.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A mismatch caused by key order would reject an unchanged proposal, which is a false rejection that fails closed.
statements.explanation: Wasted re-approvals are a usability cost, not a security hole.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A JSON object is defined by its key order, so the two requests really are different proposals that need separate decisions.
statements.explanation: JSON objects are unordered collections; order is a representation detail.

questions.source: Canonical content and its fingerprint
questions.stem: A Python service and a JavaScript service both hash what they believe is the same JSON approval payload and get different digests. The payload contains the number 1.0, the string "é", and a nested object whose keys are listed in a different order in each service. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: SHA-256 behaves differently across programming languages, so identical bytes can give different digests on different platforms.
statements.explanation: SHA-256 is a standard function; identical bytes always give identical digests.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If both services sort their keys, no other source of disagreement remains, because key order is the only variable in JSON.
statements.explanation: Number formats and Unicode normalization still differ.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Number formatting can differ between serializers (1.0 versus 1), which changes the bytes that are hashed.
statements.explanation: Python's json.dumps writes 1.0 where other encoders write 1.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Reliable cross-language hashing needs a written canonicalization specification, such as RFC 8785, instead of each language's defaults.
statements.explanation: A shared specification pins down key order, number format and escaping.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The character é can be one code point or e plus a combining accent, giving different UTF-8 bytes unless the text is normalized.
statements.explanation: Unicode has multiple equivalent encodings of the same visible text.

questions.source: Canonical content and its fingerprint
questions.stem: A developer says: "We log only the SHA-256 digest of each approval request, so the requests are protected, and the log proves who approved." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Different requests will frequently produce the same SHA-256 digest, so a matching digest is unreliable as evidence of identical content.
statements.explanation: Accidental collisions for SHA-256 are negligible in practice.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A plain digest says nothing about who produced a record, because anyone can compute it.
statements.explanation: No secret is involved in computing a SHA-256 digest.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Attributing a decision to a person needs more than the hash, such as a digital signature or an authenticated session.
statements.explanation: Identity needs a credential that only the signer controls.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Anyone who can guess the request text can compute its digest and compare, so hashing predictable content does not hide it.
statements.explanation: Hashing is not encryption; low-entropy inputs can be confirmed by brute force.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A SHA-256 digest of the request acts as the approver's digital signature, because only the approver's system could produce it.
