statements.explanation: A signature requires a private key bound to an identity; a hash has none.

questions.source: Canonical content and its fingerprint
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about using SHA-256 to fingerprint a serialized approval request.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The digest can be decrypted with the right key to recover the original request, as with symmetric encryption.
statements.explanation: Hashing is one-way and has no key or decryption step.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Changing one character of the input changes the digest unpredictably and completely, with no resemblance to the old value.
statements.explanation: This is the avalanche property of cryptographic hashes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Two requests that mean the same thing always have equal digests, however they were serialized.
statements.explanation: The digest depends on bytes, so different serializations of the same meaning differ.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The digest gets longer as the request gets longer, so large proposals have larger fingerprints.
statements.explanation: The output length is fixed at 256 bits regardless of input size.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The digest is 256 bits long, conventionally written as 64 hexadecimal characters, whatever the input size.
statements.explanation: 256 bits at 4 bits per hex digit gives 64 characters.

questions.source: Canonical content and its fingerprint
questions.stem: A Python validator rejects an approval proposal when `not proposal.get(field)` is true for any of its six required fields. Consider proposals that are otherwise complete. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A required field whose value is the string "0" is accepted, because the string is non-empty.
statements.explanation: Any non-empty string is truthy, including "0".

statements.label: B
statements.text: A proposal with an extra, unrequired key is rejected because the validator checks the whole dictionary.
statements.explanation: The check iterates over the required names only; extra keys do not affect it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A required field containing only spaces, such as "   ", is accepted, because the string is not empty.
statements.explanation: A whitespace-only string is non-empty and therefore truthy.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A required field whose value is an empty list is rejected, because an empty list is falsey in Python.
statements.explanation: An empty list is falsey in Python, so `not []` is true.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A required field whose value is None is rejected, because None is falsey in Python.
statements.explanation: `proposal.get(field)` returns None, which is falsey.

questions.source: Canonical content and its fingerprint
questions.stem: A gate computes its fingerprint over the entire proposal dictionary, but validation requires only six named fields. After a decision is recorded against a proposal, an agent adds a seventh key, "environment": "production", and resubmits it with the old decision. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Validation of the six required fields would reject the extra key, since it is not on the list of allowed fields.
statements.explanation: Validation only checks presence of the required names.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the fingerprint covered only the six named fields, adding the seventh key would leave the approval valid, a weakness.
statements.explanation: A consequential field would then be able to change without invalidating the approval.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Because the extra key is part of the serialized proposal, the fingerprint changes and the old decision no longer matches.
statements.explanation: The digest covers every serialized byte.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It is safe for a fingerprint to ignore unknown fields, because only declared fields can influence execution.
statements.explanation: Executors may act on any field they receive, declared or not.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Hashing as many extra attributes as possible has no downside, because more coverage always means more safety.
statements.explanation: Volatile attributes such as timestamps or request IDs cause spurious invalidations and re-approvals.

questions.source: The approval predicate
questions.stem: An approval check returns true only when: the decision is a dictionary; decision.get("approved") is True (identity comparison); the approver is a string that is not blank after strip(); and the recorded fingerprint equals the fingerprint freshly computed from the proposal. Check each statement that is true about how it treats these decision records, where the recorded fingerprint matches the current proposal unless stated otherwise.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A record with approved=True whose fingerprint came from an earlier version of the proposal is rejected.
statements.explanation: The recorded digest differs from the fresh digest of the current proposal.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A record with approved=True and approver "   " is accepted, because the approver string is not empty.
statements.explanation: After strip() the approver is empty, so the nonblank condition fails.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A record with approved=1 is accepted, because 1 equals True in Python comparisons.
statements.explanation: `1 is True` is false in Python; only the Boolean object passes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A record with approved="yes" is accepted, because the string "yes" is truthy in Python.
statements.explanation: The identity comparison with True rejects the string "yes".

statements.label: E
statements.text: A record with approved=True, a nonblank approver "dana" and a matching fingerprint is accepted.
statements.explanation: All four conditions hold.

questions.source: The approval predicate
questions.stem: A system computes a proposal's fingerprint when the proposal is displayed to the reviewer and stores it in the decision. At execution time, the executor checks that the decision's stored fingerprint is well formed, but never recomputes it from the proposal it is about to run. Between review and execution a different component changes the target field. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The fingerprint should be recomputed from the exact proposal about to execute, at the point where the effect happens.
statements.explanation: Binding is enforced only if the comparison uses fresh content at the effect boundary.

statements.label: B
statements.text: This is a time-of-check to time-of-use gap, in which the verified state differs from the state used.
statements.explanation: The state verified at review time can differ from the state used at execution time.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The check compares the decision with itself, so it passes whatever proposal the executor actually runs.
statements.explanation: Nothing ties the stored value to the content at the moment of use.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Computing the fingerprint at review time is enough, because the reviewer's screen shows what will run.
statements.explanation: The screen shows what was displayed, not what the executor receives later.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Making the proposal read-only in the user interface closes the gap even if the executor receives a different object.
statements.explanation: Interface-level immutability does not constrain what a separate component passes to the executor.

questions.source: The approval predicate
questions.stem: A decision record contains {"approved": true, "approver": "reviewer-1", "fingerprint": <digest matching the current proposal>}. The system's predicate checks exactly these three fields and returns true. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Nothing in the record shows that the reviewer opened, read, or understood the proposal.
statements.explanation: A digest records which bytes the record refers to, not whether anyone looked at them.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The record was written against exactly this proposal content, as the matching digest shows.
statements.explanation: The matching digest binds the decision to the serialized proposal.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The predicate also enforces expiry and single use, since a decision record normally includes those limits.
statements.explanation: Those properties need explicit fields and checks that this predicate does not have.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The true result shows that a person with authority gave informed consent to this specific action.
statements.explanation: The predicate checks the shape and content binding of a record, not the circumstances of its creation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The approver string shows that an authenticated human logged in and reviewed the proposal.
statements.explanation: A name field in a record can be typed by anyone or generated by a program.

questions.source: The approval predicate
questions.stem: An approval can be bound to three different things: the exact content of the proposal; the scope and time of its validity (environment, deadline, number of uses); and the person who decided, with their authority. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Content binding alone is sufficient for an irreversible action that is executed once.
statements.explanation: Content binding does not establish who decided, with what authority, or that the decision is still current.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Content binding automatically gives the decision an expiry, because a digest changes over time.
statements.explanation: A digest has no time dimension.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Verifying that the fingerprint matches also supplies person binding, because the digest is tied to the approver.
statements.explanation: A digest identifies content, not who produced the record.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An approval for a "deploy" action reused two weeks later in a different environment lacks scope-and-time binding.
statements.explanation: Nothing limited when, where, or how often the decision applies.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A decision filed under a name that anyone could type lacks person binding, because no identity was verified.
statements.explanation: There is no authenticated identity or authority behind the name.

questions.source: Scope, expiry, revocation, and replay
questions.stem: A single-use approval is enforced like this: step 1 reads the decision's "used" flag; if it is false, the action runs; step 2 afterwards sets the flag to true. Two workers receive the same valid decision at nearly the same moment. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Checking and marking the decision as used must be one atomic step, such as a compare-and-set, transaction, or unique constraint.
statements.explanation: Atomicity removes the gap that two concurrent workers exploit.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Reading the flag twice with a short delay in between closes the gap, because the second read sees the other worker's update.
statements.explanation: A delay shortens, but does not eliminate, the window for a race.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Both workers can read used=false before either sets it, so the action may run twice.
statements.explanation: Check and update are separate steps with a gap between them.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A matching fingerprint alone limits nothing about how many times the same decision is presented.
statements.explanation: Content binding says what was approved, not how often it may be used.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Hashing the decision a second time before running prevents the duplicate, because the second hash would differ.
statements.explanation: A second hash does not change who sees the flag as false.

questions.source: Scope, expiry, revocation, and replay
questions.stem: A decision stores its expiry as "2026-03-01 17:00" with no time zone, and the checking code calls the system clock inside the predicate. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Expiry matters only for decisions that are never used, because once a decision has been used it can no longer be exercised.
statements.explanation: Expiry limits how long an unused decision can be exercised.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Passing the current time into the check as a parameter lets tests assert behavior just before and after the deadline without waiting.
statements.explanation: Injecting the clock makes boundary tests deterministic.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Storing the expiry as an unambiguous instant, such as UTC, and stating whether the deadline itself is valid avoids boundary disputes.
statements.explanation: A comparison policy needs both a time basis and a rule for equality.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The deadline is ambiguous, because servers in different zones can interpret the same local time as different instants.
statements.explanation: A zone-less timestamp does not identify a single moment.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A predicate that takes the time as an argument cannot be used in production, because callers could then supply any time.
statements.explanation: The production caller supplies its trusted clock reading as the argument.

questions.source: Scope, expiry, revocation, and replay
questions.stem: At 09:00 a reviewer approves exporting a dataset, with the approval valid for 24 hours. At 11:00 the dataset is reclassified as restricted. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An approval obtained after its premises have expired is acceptable as long as the fingerprint matches.
statements.explanation: A matching fingerprint says the content is unchanged, not that the premises still hold.

statements.label: B
statements.text: New evidence or changed premises can make an approval stale before its stated deadline passes.
statements.explanation: Expiry is not just a timer; the basis for the decision may have disappeared.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Revocation withdraws a still-unexpired decision, and the execution-time check should consult revocation state.
statements.explanation: A withdrawal that is never checked at the effect boundary has no effect.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Including the data classification in the bound proposal would make a changed classification force re-review.
statements.explanation: Binding a relevant attribute turns its change into a content mismatch.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The approval remains fully valid until 09:00 the next day, because validity is purely a matter of time.
statements.explanation: Reclassification changes what the reviewer would have approved.

questions.source: Scope, expiry, revocation, and replay
questions.stem: A team adds revocation to its approval system. Check each statement that is true about a sound design.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The design should specify what happens to work that has already started when a revocation arrives.
statements.explanation: Without a rule, in-flight actions are handled inconsistently.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Revoking a decision means deleting its record, which keeps the log clean and avoids confusion about its status.
statements.explanation: The audit trail should show that a decision existed and was withdrawn.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The execution-time check must consult revocation state at the effect boundary, not only at review time.
statements.explanation: A revocation that is not checked where the action happens is advisory only.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A revocation record should say who revoked, under what authority, and which decision or proposal it affects.
statements.explanation: Withdrawals are consequential decisions and need accountability of their own.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The original decision should be preserved in the audit trail and marked as withdrawn, not erased.
statements.explanation: History remains inspectable after revocation.

questions.source: Scope, expiry, revocation, and replay
questions.stem: A reviewer approves "ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN plan text" against the staging database. The identical SQL text is later submitted against the production database with the old decision attached. The proposal fields contain only the SQL text. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The environment is operational detail that does not belong in an approval request, which should describe only the action.
statements.explanation: The environment is one of the most important facts for judging the effect of an action.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The fingerprint matches because the text is identical, so a content-only gate accepts it although the environment was never part of the proposal.
statements.explanation: Binding is only as semantic as what the proposal includes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Matching SQL text means the risk is identical, so the approval should transfer to the production database.
statements.explanation: Running on production data has consequences staging does not.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Include the identities whose change should force reconsideration and no others; over-binding causes spurious re-approvals.
statements.explanation: Choosing which identities matter is a judgment about consequence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Identifiers such as the resolved target, account, environment, repository revision, and data classification are candidates for binding.
statements.explanation: These attributes determine the actual consequences.

questions.source: Scope, expiry, revocation, and replay
questions.stem: A single-use approval authorizes one database migration. The executor claims the decision and starts the migration, but the process crashes halfway. An operator proposes simply retrying using the same decision. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Because the fingerprint still matches, the system has nothing else to check before the retry.
statements.explanation: Use constraints, expiry, revocation, and current state still matter.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Recording "claimed or in progress" separately from "completed" lets the team make a deliberate decision about retrying.
statements.explanation: A single used flag cannot distinguish a crash from success.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The crash proves the original approval was invalid, because a valid approval would have allowed completion.
statements.explanation: A failure during execution says nothing about whether the approval was valid.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A decision authorizes one bounded attempt, and a partially applied state may differ from the state the reviewer assessed.
statements.explanation: The reviewer judged effects and rollback from the starting state, not from a half-finished one.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Retrying with the same decision is always appropriate, because the approved content has not changed.
statements.explanation: Unchanged content does not guarantee the premises, effects, or rollback assumptions still hold.

questions.source: Scope, expiry, revocation, and replay
questions.stem: An agent's request proposes to rotate production API credentials, and the rollback field reads "restore the old keys". The old keys will be revoked by the provider as part of the rotation, and services that cached them will fail until redeployed. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Dependent effects, such as services that fail while using cached keys, belong in the effects field.
statements.explanation: Downstream impact is part of what the reviewer is approving.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The rollback claim assumes that the old keys remain valid after rotation, which is false in this situation.
statements.explanation: A rollback plan is only valid if its prerequisites survive the action.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A reviewer-facing request should state that full rollback is not possible and describe the recovery path, such as issuing new keys.
statements.explanation: Admitting a gap is more useful than inventing reassurance.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because the operation is scripted, a successful exit code establishes that the rollback works.
statements.explanation: Exit codes report that a command ran, not that its recovery assumptions hold.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A rollback field is satisfied by any statement that sounds reasonable to the person filling it in.
statements.explanation: The field is only useful if it is true and testable.

questions.source: Scope, expiry, revocation, and replay
questions.stem: Four edits are made to an approved proposal before it executes: (1) its keys are re-ordered; (2) whitespace in the serialized JSON is changed; (3) the target path changes from "/srv/app/report.md" to "/srv/other/report.md"; (4) the environment attribute changes from "staging" to "production". The approval gate fingerprints a canonical serialization of the full proposal. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Edits (1) and (2) are representation changes, so a good canonical form keeps the fingerprint unchanged and no new approval is needed.
statements.explanation: Forcing re-approval over formatting wastes reviewer attention.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Edit (3) changes the object acted on, so the fingerprint changes and the old decision no longer applies.
statements.explanation: A different target is a different proposal.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Edit (4) changes the environment, so the fingerprint changes and a new decision is needed.
statements.explanation: The environment is part of what was approved.

statements.label: D
statements.text: All four edits should keep the old approval valid, because the action name is unchanged and the action name is what was approved.
statements.explanation: The action name is only one part of what the reviewer judged.

statements.label: E
statements.text: All four edits should invalidate the approval, because any byte change must be treated as a new proposal.
statements.explanation: Normalizing representation noise is the purpose of canonicalization.

questions.source: The approval predicate
questions.stem: An approval flow is attacked in three ways: (i) an attacker steals a reviewer's login and approves a proposal; (ii) a junior contractor with no authority over the data approves a data release; (iii) an overworked reviewer clicks Approve on a proposal without opening its evidence. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Case (ii) is a failure of authority, addressed by a registry mapping actions or data to roles that may approve them.
statements.explanation: Being able to click is different from having the right to decide.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Case (iii) is a failure of comprehension and attention, which interface design, workload limits and review practice affect more than cryptography does.
statements.explanation: No hash can show that a human read the material.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the approver field is non-empty, all three cases are excluded, because a name implies a verified person.
statements.explanation: A non-empty name field is easy to fill falsely and says nothing about authority or attention.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A content fingerprint on the decision prevents all three cases, because it ties the decision to the approver's login.
statements.explanation: The fingerprint only ties the decision to content.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Case (i) is a failure of authenticated identity, addressed by controls such as strong authentication and signed decisions.
statements.explanation: The record would look right but the wrong person created it.

questions.source: Write the approval predicate before anything is approved
questions.stem: A team's six unit tests for an approval check all pass: (1) a valid decision is accepted; (2) re-ordering the proposal's keys does not change the fingerprint; (3) changing the target field causes rejection; (4) a decision with no approver is rejected; (5) a decision with approved=False is rejected; (6) the fingerprint is 64 hexadecimal characters. Three alternative implementations also pass all six tests. X fingerprints only the six named proposal fields. Y tests `if decision.get("approved")` instead of requiring the Boolean True. Z checks that a decision is unused and marks it used in two separate steps. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Mutants that pass the suite show carelessness by the implementers rather than weakness in the tests.
statements.explanation: A mutant that survives is by definition a behavior the tests failed to specify.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A test that adds an extra field to an approved proposal and expects rejection would catch X; a test using approved="no" would catch Y.
statements.explanation: Each test targets the specific weakness the mutant introduces.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The suite is too weak, because X, Y and Z are wrong in ways none of the six tests detect.
statements.explanation: Passing tests show that the tested statements hold, not that the implementation is right.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Catching Z requires a test that interleaves two consumers of the same decision, because the flaw is a race.
statements.explanation: Single-threaded tests cannot expose a gap between check and update.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Passing all six tests demonstrates that the original implementation is correct, since each test covers a distinct requirement.
statements.explanation: Six tests cannot establish that six statements are the right or complete statements.

questions.source: Write the approval predicate before anything is approved
questions.stem: Before running the tests on a new approval gate, an engineer writes and dates one sentence describing what the output would look like if the approval gate approved something it should not. Check each statement that is true about this practice.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If the prediction turns out wrong, it should be rewritten to match what happened so the record is consistent.
statements.explanation: The recorded miss is information about the engineer's understanding.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A prediction written after seeing the output is as informative as one written before it, since both describe the same result.
statements.explanation: After the fact, a prediction can only describe what was seen, so it cannot turn out wrong.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The sentence is unnecessary when the tests are automated, since the test results already say what failed.
statements.explanation: The sentence defines what a failure would mean; automation only runs checks.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Writing the failure criterion beforehand lets the check surprise the engineer instead of confirming whatever appears.
statements.explanation: A prediction made first is falsifiable.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Predictions should be kept vague so that they cannot turn out wrong and embarrass the engineer later.
statements.explanation: A vague prediction cannot fail, which defeats its purpose.

questions.source: Write the approval predicate before anything is approved
questions.stem: A team writes the specification of an approval gate before any code exists. Check each item that belongs in that specification.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Rules for how long, where and how often a decision may be used, and how it is withdrawn.
statements.explanation: These govern where, how long, and whether a decision can be used.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A statement that the approver's trust in the AI system is high enough to skip review of low-effort cases.
statements.explanation: Trust in the proposer is not a gate condition and undermines the approval gate's purpose.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A named decision owner, expressed as a role that can be asked, not "the team".
statements.explanation: Accountability needs someone specific.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An evaluation set that includes cases designed to make the proposal fail, not only to pass.
statements.explanation: A set that cannot embarrass the proposal does not evaluate it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The approval predicate: the exact conditions under which a decision authorizes one attempt.
statements.explanation: The predicate is the core contract the code and tests must satisfy.

questions.source: Write the approval predicate before anything is approved
questions.stem: A developer asks an AI coding assistant to write both an approval check and its unit tests from a one-sentence description. All the tests pass, and the developer reports the approval gate as verified. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Tests written by the same model that wrote the implementation can share its blind spots, so passing them is weak evidence.
statements.explanation: The same misunderstanding can appear in both the code and the tests.

statements.label: B
statements.text: AI-written tests are invalid by nature and should be discarded, whatever they check and however they were reviewed.
statements.explanation: Generated tests can be useful; the issue is their independence, not their origin.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Asking the assistant for a deliberately wrong version that still passes the tests is a cheap way to find gaps in the tests.
statements.explanation: A surviving wrong version proves the tests do not constrain that behavior.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Acceptance criteria written by the accountable person before implementation give an independent standard to test against.
statements.explanation: Independence is what makes a check informative.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Once the tests pass, reading the implementation is unnecessary, because the tests encode every requirement.
statements.explanation: Passing tests do not reveal behaviors they do not cover.

questions.source: Use It: conduct Claude Code against your gate
questions.stem: An AI assistant returns an implementation that adds decision IDs, deadlines, revocation and single-use consumption to an approval check. A reviewer inspects the diff for places where consequential decisions are hidden. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If the assistant's own explanation describes the logic correctly, reading the diff is optional, since the explanation was produced from the code.
statements.explanation: An explanation is another output of the system under review, not independent evidence.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Only variable names and comments need review, because the behavior of the code is described there.
statements.explanation: Names and comments are claims; behavior is in the logic.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Where the current time is read matters, because it decides whether expiry can be tested and whether callers can influence it.
statements.explanation: A hidden clock read makes boundaries hard to test and can be a manipulation point.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Where a used decision is recorded matters, including whether checking and recording happen as a single atomic step.
statements.explanation: A separate check and record leaves a race.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The reviewer should confirm that earlier strictness was not weakened, for example that approved must still be exactly True.
statements.explanation: Feature additions often relax earlier checks.

questions.source: The approval interface is part of the control
questions.stem: A team designs the screen on which a human reviews an agent's proposed action. Check each statement that is true about a sound design.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Approve should be pre-selected to speed up the common case, because most proposals end up approved.
statements.explanation: A default selection biases the decision toward yes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The action and the target should appear first, before secondary details such as evidence and rollback.
statements.explanation: The reviewer's first need is to see what will happen to what.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Differences from a previously reviewed version should be highlighted, for example "target changed from A to B; prior approval invalid".
statements.explanation: Reviewers notice changes more reliably when they are surfaced.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Showing a friendly summary while the fingerprint covers hidden fields is acceptable, since the hash protects the content.
statements.explanation: A decision binds to bytes the reviewer never meaningfully inspected.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Collapsing irreversible effects behind an expandable panel is fine as long as the information remains available.
statements.explanation: The most consequential facts should be unavoidable, not optional.

questions.source: The approval interface is part of the control
questions.stem: A review dialog shows a large green "Continue" button beside a small gray "refuse" link, and a message "Approve within 60 seconds or the job fails!" generated by the agent that submitted the request. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The countdown message is a legitimate priority signal because the agent knows its own work best.
statements.explanation: A proposer's urgency claims serve the proposer and are not independent evidence of urgency.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Requiring a written reason for refusing but not for approving is neutral, since both are recorded decisions.
statements.explanation: Extra effort to refuse biases the decision toward approval.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Offering a "defer" option in addition to approve and refuse adds noise and should be removed.
statements.explanation: Deferral is a real outcome when evidence is insufficient or authority is unclear.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The visual weighting of the green button over the gray link nudges the reviewer toward approval.
statements.explanation: Unequal prominence is a standard dark pattern that undermines genuine choice.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The design is fine as long as the refuse option exists somewhere on the screen.
statements.explanation: Availability in principle differs from availability in practice.

questions.source: The approval interface is part of the control
questions.stem: A proposal's evidence field is the URL of a test report on a shared drive. The fingerprint covers the proposal text, including the URL. After the reviewer approves, someone overwrites the report at the same URL with a different result. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Binding only the proposal text leaves a substitution path, because the evidence can change while the fingerprint stays the same.
statements.explanation: The URL is stable; the content behind it is not.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A decision should bind to the representation the reviewer saw together with any immutable artifacts it references.
statements.explanation: Otherwise the reviewer approved something different from what executes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Since the fingerprint still matches, the evidence is unchanged and the approval remains informed.
statements.explanation: A fingerprint of the URL string says nothing about the document behind it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The URL being in the proposal means the evidence is automatically trustworthy, since the reviewer could open it.
statements.explanation: A reference is not the content, and its target may change.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Referencing the evidence by an immutable identifier, such as a content hash or version ID, binds the decision to what the reviewer saw.
statements.explanation: Immutable references keep the evidence from changing silently.

questions.source: The approval interface is part of the control
questions.stem: At execution time, an executor recomputes a proposal's fingerprint and finds that it differs from the one in the stored approval decision. Check each statement that is true about appropriate responses.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Block the action, show the reviewer which fields changed, and return the proposal to review.
statements.explanation: A changed proposal is a new object that needs a new decision.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Overwrite the stored fingerprint with the new value so the next check passes.
statements.explanation: That would manufacture an approval for content nobody reviewed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Ask the model whether the old approval probably still applies, and proceed if it agrees.
statements.explanation: The proposer's model has an interest in proceeding and is not an authority.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Treat the old decision as authority for the new proposal when the action name is unchanged, since the reviewer chose that action.
statements.explanation: The reviewer decided on content that has since changed, so the decision cannot cover it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Proceed if the agent classifies the difference as minor, since it understands its own change best.
statements.explanation: The party seeking approval should not decide what counts as minor.

questions.source: The approval interface is part of the control
questions.stem: A reviewer is assigned a proposal to export a dataset containing customer data. The reviewer understands the proposal fully but has no authority over that data. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The reviewer should approve to avoid blocking the project and flag any concerns afterwards, since approvals can be undone.
statements.explanation: Approval given to avoid friction converts the approval gate into a ritual.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Deferring with documented unresolved gaps is a successful outcome for the approval gate, not a failure.
statements.explanation: The approval gate worked: it prevented an unsupported yes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Refusal and deferral should be recorded as outcomes of the process, not treated as errors in it.
statements.explanation: Treating them as failures pressures people to approve.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A gate should provide a path to escalate to someone with authority, so the reviewer need not impersonate an approver.
statements.explanation: Authority and understanding are different properties.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A reviewer's full understanding of a proposal does not by itself confer authority to approve it.
statements.explanation: Authority comes from role and ownership, not from comprehension.

questions.source: Human attention is a finite gate resource
questions.stem: Autonomous agents submit 5 proposals per hour for human review. One reviewer can carefully review 2 proposals per hour. Nothing is dropped, and no proposal is approved without review. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Showing the reviewer less detail so that 5 can be reviewed per hour solves the capacity problem.
statements.explanation: It changes the quality of review, not the capacity for careful review.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Doubling the reviewer's speed to 4 per hour would stop the backlog from growing, since the review rate would nearly match arrivals.
statements.explanation: 5 arrivals minus 4 reviews still adds 1 per hour.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Three reviewers at 2 per hour each would match the arrival rate of 5 per hour.
statements.explanation: 3 x 2 = 6, which is at least 5.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The backlog grows by 3 proposals per hour, since 5 arrive and only 2 can be carefully reviewed.
statements.explanation: Arrival minus service rate.

statements.label: E
statements.text: After 4 hours, 12 proposals are waiting, because 20 have arrived and 8 have been reviewed.

questions.source: Human attention is a finite gate resource
questions.stem: Five proposals are pending. A is a reversible local formatting change. B sends material to an external recipient. C changes a production target. D duplicates B's effect. E depends on C being approved first. One reviewer has capacity to review two carefully in this period. Check each statement that is true about a sound queue policy.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A should be auto-approved to clear the queue, since it is reversible and affects only local files.
statements.explanation: Only a separately authorized low-risk policy can approve A without review.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The priority should follow the urgency labels the proposing agents attach to their own work.
statements.explanation: Self-assigned urgency is unvalidated and serves the proposer.

statements.label: C
statements.text: B and C should be prioritized, because their effects are external or high-impact.
statements.explanation: Review effort should follow consequence.

statements.label: D
statements.text: D should be detected as a likely duplicate of B and held rather than reviewed separately.
statements.explanation: Approving a duplicate wastes review capacity and may double the effect.

statements.label: E
statements.text: E can be reviewed independently of C, because each proposal is separate.
statements.explanation: E depends on C, so deciding it first is premature.

questions.source: Human attention is a finite gate resource
questions.stem: Proposals now arrive faster than reviewers can examine them, and the backlog is growing. Check each statement that is true about responses consistent with good oversight practice.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Narrow what the agents are allowed to attempt so fewer proposals need review.
statements.explanation: Reducing scope reduces the volume that requires human judgment.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Add qualified reviewers so that careful review capacity rises with the volume of proposals.
statements.explanation: Capacity is raised without lowering the quality of each review.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Trim the information shown to reviewers so that they can click through proposals faster.
statements.explanation: Less information per decision degrades judgment rather than raising capacity.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Treat a proposal as approved if no reviewer has responded within a fixed period, to keep work moving.
statements.explanation: Silence is the absence of a decision.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Pause intake of new proposals until the backlog is back under control.
statements.explanation: Limiting inflow preserves review quality.

questions.source: Human attention is a finite gate resource
questions.stem: A pipeline lets an action proceed when any one of these is true: no reviewer has responded within 30 minutes; the agent reports confidence above 0.95; or an automated evaluation score is at least 90%. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A self-reported confidence of 0.95 can serve as authorization because the model is well calibrated.
statements.explanation: Calibration is unestablished here, and confidence is not an authorization in any case.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A timeout is the absence of a decision, not consent, however long the reviewer has been silent.
statements.explanation: Failing to answer does not constitute permission.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A pre-authorized, narrowly defined standing policy for a low-risk class differs from treating silence as consent.
statements.explanation: The policy is a deliberate, accountable decision made in advance.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A 90% evaluation score authorizes the action, because it shows the change meets the team's quality bar.
statements.explanation: A score is evidence about performance on a set of cases, not a decision by someone with authority.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Auto-proceeding on timeout is acceptable for destructive actions if reviewers were notified.
statements.explanation: Notification is not consent, and irreversibility raises the need for an explicit decision.

questions.source: Human attention is a finite gate resource
questions.stem: A team finds that its reviewers approve 99.6% of proposals with a median review time of 8 seconds, and a dashboard ranks reviewers by throughput. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Ranking reviewers by throughput will improve the quality of oversight by rewarding efficient reviewers.
statements.explanation: Rewarding speed trains the approval gate toward ceremony.

statements.label: B
statements.text: More prompts always mean more oversight, because each prompt is another chance to catch a problem.
statements.explanation: Past the available attention, additional prompts produce habituation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Refusal and deferral rates should be tracked alongside approval rates, not only approvals.
statements.explanation: A gate that never says no or later is not demonstrating oversight.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A 99.6% approval rate proves that the agent is reliable and that the proposals were good.
statements.explanation: The rate describes decisions, not whether the decisions were informed or the proposals correct.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A near-universal approval rate may reflect habituation, so the team should check whether reviewers have real options, evidence and support to say no.
statements.explanation: High agreement can be a symptom of rubber-stamping.

questions.source: Human attention is a finite gate resource
questions.stem: Reviewers keep receiving nearly identical, low-consequence proposals, such as formatting changes in documentation inside a sandbox repository. The team considers replacing individual approvals for this class with a standing policy. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The policy should be accompanied by monitoring and a defined way to revoke it if problems appear.
statements.explanation: A standing authorization needs a way to detect problems and withdraw it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The exclusions should be tested, meaning cases just outside the class must still be routed to a reviewer.
statements.explanation: The edge of the policy is where errors occur.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The agent can set the policy's scope, because it knows which of its proposals are routine.
statements.explanation: Scope is a governance decision owned by accountable people, not the proposer.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The policy should extend automatically to adjacent classes as they come to look similar.
statements.explanation: Extending scope without review is how standing policies drift.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The class should be defined precisely, so it is clear which proposals fall inside it.
statements.explanation: Vague boundaries let consequential changes slip in.

questions.source: Human attention is a finite gate resource
questions.stem: A team wants to improve the quality of human review in its approval process. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Once an action is approved, its outcome is operations' concern and not part of gate design.
statements.explanation: The approval gate's design should respond to what happens after approval.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Inspect approvals that were later reversed to learn what the reviewer lacked at the time.
statements.explanation: Reversals are informative failures of the approval gate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An unexpected outcome that turned out harmless needs no change to the evaluation set.
statements.explanation: Unexpected behavior of any kind is a reason to update the next evaluation set.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Average time per decision is a reliable measure of the quality of review, since careful review takes longer.
statements.explanation: Time can fall because reviewers click reflexively.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Compare effects predicted in proposals with outcomes actually observed after the actions ran.
statements.explanation: Prediction errors show where review or evidence was inadequate.

questions.source: Human attention is a finite gate resource
questions.stem: A team adopts agents that produce 10 times as many proposals per day, going from 20 to 200, while the reviewers can still carefully review 20 per day. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: At most 10% of the proposals can receive careful review, since 20 of the 200 fit within capacity.
statements.explanation: 20 divided by 200 is 0.10.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The other 90% can be checked to the same standard by skimming them quickly, since most are routine.
statements.explanation: Skimming is a different, weaker review.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the unreviewed proposals proceed anyway, the extra output is effectively unverified.
statements.explanation: Generation scaled up but verification did not.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Review capacity should be treated as a design constraint that is measured or declared, not left implicit.
statements.explanation: Throughput limits determine which controls are actually feasible.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Speeding up generation also speeds up verification, because the same model can be asked to review the proposals.
statements.explanation: A model checking its own family's output does not supply the independent human judgment that authorization requires.

questions.source: Human attention is a finite gate resource
questions.stem: A marketing manager is asked to approve an agent's proposed database migration. The proposal is well written and every claim sounds reasonable. The migration contains a subtle locking problem that will cause an outage. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Adding the agent's explanation of why the migration is safe makes it verifiable by a non-expert.
statements.explanation: The explanation is another claim the reviewer cannot check.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The proposal should be routed to a reviewer who has the expertise to audit it, or to a specialist.
statements.explanation: Matching reviewer to proposal is part of gate design.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Fluent, confident text is a reliable signal that a proposal is correct, because errors usually look awkward.
statements.explanation: Fluency is independent of correctness.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Judging whether a claim is credible depends on the reviewer's own domain knowledge, so errors outside it tend to pass.
statements.explanation: A reviewer cannot detect problems that they lack the background to recognize.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A careful reading by any experienced manager will catch database-specific errors, whatever their own specialty.
statements.explanation: General experience does not substitute for domain expertise.

questions.source: The approval interface is part of the control
questions.stem: An approval screen shows only the first 30 characters of any target, followed by an ellipsis. An agent proposes writing to /srv/app/exports/archive/2026/../../../private/keys.txt, which the operating system resolves to /srv/app/private/keys.txt. The screen displays "/srv/app/exports/archive/2026/…". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Truncation is harmless because the full path is included in the fingerprint, so any change would be detected.
statements.explanation: A hash over text the reviewer never saw does not make the reviewer informed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Resolving the path to its canonical form before display would show the true target.
statements.explanation: Normalization collapses ".." segments and reveals where the write will land.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Lookalike Unicode characters, such as a Cyrillic letter for a Latin one, are another way a displayed name can differ from the real identifier.
statements.explanation: Visually identical strings can be different byte sequences.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Training reviewers to expand every path manually fixes the design problem, since the information remains available to them.
statements.explanation: Relying on vigilance to compensate for hidden information moves the burden to the person least able to carry it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The reviewer cannot see the part of the path that determines the final location, so the approval would not be informed.
statements.explanation: The truncated text suggests an archive folder, while the real target is a private file.

questions.source: Canonical content and its fingerprint
questions.stem: A review interface parses the raw JSON text {"target":"report.md","target":"/etc/passwd"} using a parser that keeps the first value of a repeated key, and shows the reviewer "report.md". The backend that executes the action parses the same text with Python's json.loads. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Hashing the raw text guarantees that both parsers interpret it the same way, because the bytes being parsed are identical.
statements.explanation: A digest identifies bytes; it does not make parsers agree on their meaning.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The reviewer and the executor can see different targets even though both read the same text.
statements.explanation: Different parsers resolve duplicate keys differently, creating a parsing differential.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Python's json.loads keeps the last value of a repeated key, so the backend would use "/etc/passwd".
statements.explanation: By default, later duplicates overwrite earlier ones in Python's decoder.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The JSON standard requires every parser to keep the last value, so the backend's behavior is the only correct one.
statements.explanation: The standard leaves behavior for duplicate names unspecified and says names should be unique.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Rejecting documents that contain duplicate keys at ingestion removes this ambiguity.
statements.explanation: A strict parser makes one interpretation the only one.

questions.source: Attestation: what the signer states, and the right to withhold
questions.stem: An engineer is drafting a written sign-off for an evaluated approval gate. Check each item that belongs in a useful sign-off.

statements.label: A
statements.text: What was tested, with the specific checks, the criteria and the results obtained.
statements.explanation: The reader needs to know what evidence exists.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Who cleared which gate, naming a person or role per decision who can be asked about it.
statements.explanation: Answerability requires someone specific.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Verbs worded at the strength of the evidence, so "passed a stated test" is distinguished from "believe safe".
statements.explanation: Overstated verbs create false assurance.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A closing statement that the system is safe for production use, so readers know the final conclusion.
statements.explanation: A sign-off states what was established; a blanket safety claim exceeds the evidence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: What was not tested, including conditions not probed and known failure modes not reached.
statements.explanation: A list of only what passed reads as a clean bill of health and hides where harm may lie.

questions.source: Attestation: what the signer states, and the right to withhold
questions.stem: An engineer gives an AI assistant no test logs or notes and asks it to write the sign-off statement for the validation work she just finished. The assistant returns a fluent, well-structured paragraph that names a reviewer and states that a full review took place. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The fluent structure suggests the assistant checked the validation work before writing the paragraph.
statements.explanation: Structure is not verification.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The remaining risk is only stylistic, such as tone and formatting of the paragraph.
statements.explanation: The risk is that the statement is empty of substantive claims.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Naming a reviewer in the statement makes it trustworthy, because a named person can be held to account.
statements.explanation: A name in a generated paragraph is not evidence that the person reviewed anything.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The paragraph has the form of a sign-off but nothing behind it, unless the assistant was given the actual record.
statements.explanation: A language model cannot know what was tested or skipped unless told.

statements.label: E
statements.text: She can sign it if the content sounds plausible and matches what she remembers doing.
statements.explanation: Plausibility is not the standard; a signature asserts facts she can support.

questions.source: Attestation: what the signer states, and the right to withhold
questions.stem: A company requires a sign-off from the test lead before each release. In two years the lead has signed every release, and the process has no recorded way to decline or defer. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Withholding a sign-off is a process failure that the process should work to minimize.
statements.explanation: Treating non-approval as failure pressures people to manufacture certainty.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Having a signature on the release proves that a full review took place before it shipped.
statements.explanation: A signature shows that someone put their name on a statement.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The signer's authority to withhold or defer is essential for a sign-off to mean anything.
statements.explanation: Real assurance requires a real possibility of refusal.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because a person signed, accountability for every gap rests wholly on that person, with no organizational owner needed.
statements.explanation: Governance should name organizational owners and escalation paths rather than placing all consequence on the signer.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the only permitted outcome is "signed", the process is a rubber stamp that hides missing review behind a name.
statements.explanation: A signature that cannot be withheld carries no information.

questions.source: Attestation: what the signer states, and the right to withhold
questions.stem: The engineer who built a validation gate sits down to write its sign-off and finds that she wants to write "no known issues." Check each statement that is true about practices that counter ownership bias.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For each untested item, say whether it was skipped because it was out of scope or because time ran out.
statements.explanation: The reason affects how much weight the omission deserves.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The builder is best placed to sign, since she knows the system best, so independent review adds little.
statements.explanation: Knowing a system well is compatible with, and can increase, bias in assessing it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Require a minimum number of entries, such as three, in the "not tested" section.
statements.explanation: A forced list pushes against the pull toward a clean bill.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Ask whether any untested condition is the region where harm would most likely occur.
statements.explanation: Omissions matter most where consequences are largest.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If she cannot think of any untested conditions, the approval gate is fully verified and the sign-off can say so.
statements.explanation: Being unable to list gaps usually means she has not looked hard enough.

questions.source: Attestation: what the signer states, and the right to withhold
questions.stem: An organization introduces named sign-offs for high-risk automated actions. A year later it reviews the effects. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Named sign-offs have no effect on release speed, because the signature is a quick formality.
statements.explanation: Documenting limits and naming signers takes effort and can delay release.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Such a regime supports legible answerability: after a failure one can find who signed and what they did and did not warrant.
statements.explanation: Written, attributable claims make accountability possible.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An anonymous sign-off provides the same answerability as a named one, as the statement still exists.
statements.explanation: Without a name, nobody can be asked about the claim.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The cost includes speed and deniability, because someone must be willing to be named and "what did we not test?" arrives as friction.
statements.explanation: Accountability trades convenience for clarity.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A digital signature on the sign-off proves that the signer read and understood the evidence.
statements.explanation: A signature can strengthen identity evidence without proving comprehension.

questions.source: Where the approval step sits in the build so far
questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about the order of events in a sound approval workflow for an agent's proposed action.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Scoped evaluation, and the recording of what it does not cover, happens before the proposal is frozen and fingerprinted.
statements.explanation: The reviewer needs evidence and exclusions in front of them when deciding.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The fingerprint, expiry, revocation, and use constraints are rechecked at execution, just before the effect.
statements.explanation: Conditions can change between decision and use.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The actual outcome is observed after execution and stored as a separate record linked to the decision.
statements.explanation: Approval permits an attempt; the result must be checked independently.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If a proposal changes after approval, only the executor's check needs to be rerun, because the evaluation remains valid.
statements.explanation: The evidence was about the previous proposal and must be re-evaluated for the new one.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The fingerprint should be computed after the reviewer clicks Approve, from the form's current state, so that last-second edits are captured.
statements.explanation: The fingerprint must be fixed before review so the reviewer approves exactly what is later checked.

questions.source: Where the approval step sits in the build so far
questions.stem: An approved action runs, its fingerprint check passes at execution, and a post-action check shows that the file contains the wrong content. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The proposal fingerprint, the effect evidence and the post-action check should be separate linked records.
statements.explanation: Merging them hides which of the three failed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Approval permits a bounded attempt; it does not guarantee that the intended result occurs.
statements.explanation: Authorization is about permission, not outcome.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The decision record should be amended to say that the outcome was correct, so the record is consistent.
statements.explanation: The outcome contradicts that claim and records should not be edited to match hopes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because the fingerprint matched at execution, the outcome must have been correct, since the right proposal was run.
statements.explanation: A match shows the executed proposal equals the approved one, not that execution had the intended effect.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The post-action check replaces the need for any pre-action evaluation, since it measures the real result.
statements.explanation: The checks serve different times and purposes.

questions.source: A gate is not a button
questions.stem: A developer sets an agent's permissions to allow any command that matches the pattern "npm run *" without prompting. A repository the agent works in defines an npm script named "cleanup" that runs rm -rf ~/projects. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Pattern-level approval binds to the form of the command, not what the script does, so the destructive script runs unprompted.
statements.explanation: The pattern cannot see the script's contents.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Because the developer wrote the rule, every package.json the agent encounters can be treated as trusted.
statements.explanation: Repositories can contain scripts written by others, including untrusted ones.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Permission rules make sandboxing and other controls unnecessary, since the rules already limit what runs.
statements.explanation: Layered controls cover cases a single permission rule misses.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Pattern approval is equivalent to approving each command's contents individually, because the pattern covers only known scripts.
statements.explanation: Approving a prefix approves every possible continuation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Narrower allow rules, such as specific script names, together with deny rules for destructive commands reduce exposure.
statements.explanation: Smaller grants and explicit denials limit blast radius.

questions.source: The driver's seat
questions.stem: A team lists tasks in an approval workflow and decides which should be done by an AI assistant and which should remain with a person. Check each statement that is true about an appropriate split.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Running every checker and grouping the resulting traces for the reviewer is suitable for the assistant.
statements.explanation: Mechanical collection of evidence is what automation does well.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Deciding to approve, refuse, defer or escalate, within the person's authority, stays with a person.
statements.explanation: Authority and accountability attach to a person.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Deciding which identities, beyond the named fields, should force a new decision if they change is suitable for the assistant.
statements.explanation: That is a judgment about consequence that belongs with the accountable person.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Drafting the structured proposal and flagging the fields it could not fill is suitable for the assistant.
statements.explanation: This is preparation work that saves time and exposes gaps.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The cases that can embarrass the proposal should be chosen after seeing the assistant's results.
statements.explanation: Cases chosen after the fact record accommodation.

questions.source: Ship It: a gate design that survives a skeptical reader
questions.stem: An engineer is told that a prototype approval check has been built: it fingerprints the proposal and verifies that an approved flag and a nonblank approver string are present. Check each statement that is true about what must still be added before relying on it in production.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Expiry, revocation and single-use consumption, enforced where the action happens.
statements.explanation: The prototype has no time or use limits.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Audit logging with access control, retention rules and an incident-response path.
statements.explanation: Production use requires accountability and handling for failures.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Authenticated identity for the approver, because a name string can be typed by anyone.
statements.explanation: Identity must come from a credential only the approver controls.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Nothing further is needed because SHA-256 is a secure hash and the content binding is therefore strong.
statements.explanation: The hash secures content identity only; it does not address identity, authority, time, or use.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A registry or policy stating who has authority to approve which actions.
statements.explanation: Authority is a separate property from identity.

questions.source: Evaluation comes before authorization
questions.stem: A team measures four things about an approval workflow: (1) whether the agent completed its tasks; (2) whether its actions complied with the organization's policy; (3) how much time and effort reviewers spent; and (4) whether a person with authority approved each consequential action. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: These are four separate questions, and a high value on one says little about the others.
statements.explanation: Each captures a distinct property.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A high task-success rate implies that the actions complied with policy.
statements.explanation: An agent can complete tasks by violating policy.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Policy compliance by automated check amounts to human authorization.
statements.explanation: A checker can flag violations but cannot give consent on anyone's behalf.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Low reviewer burden shows that decisions were well informed, since reviewers had less to read.
statements.explanation: Burden can fall because information was hidden or reviewers click reflexively.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Reporting only task success is adequate because the other three follow from it.
statements.explanation: None of the others is implied by task success.

questions.source: Ship It: a gate design that survives a skeptical reader
questions.stem: A student's approval-gate project tests its code with a hard-coded decision record whose approver field reads "simulated-reviewer". The code binds the decision to a fingerprint of the proposal and the tests pass. Check each statement that is true about what the project may honestly claim.

statements.label: A
statements.text: It may claim that approval is authenticated, since the approver field is nonblank.
statements.explanation: A literal string is not an authenticated identity.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It may claim that the code binds a decision record to exact proposal content under a simulated approver, and nothing about any person's review.
statements.explanation: A hard-coded test record shows that the mechanism works; it is not a decision by anyone.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It may claim that the proposal is safe, since the content-binding tests pass.
statements.explanation: Binding says nothing about the proposal's safety.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It may claim that the proposal was reviewed and approved, since a decision record exists and the tests pass.
statements.explanation: A generated record is not a review.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It may present the simulated record as evidence of stakeholder agreement, if it is labeled with a reviewer's role.
statements.explanation: Inventing stakeholder agreement misrepresents the record, whatever the label.

questions.source: Scope, expiry, revocation, and replay
questions.stem: An executor must check a stored approval decision before running an action, but the approval service it calls is unavailable and the request times out. Check each statement that is true about how the executor should behave.

statements.label: A
statements.text: It should proceed, since the outage is not the agent's fault.
statements.explanation: An unverifiable check is not a pass.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It should refuse to run the action and keep it queued until a decision can be verified.
statements.explanation: An authorization check that cannot be completed must fail closed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It should fall back to checking only that an approval record exists, without verifying its fingerprint.
statements.explanation: A weaker check defeats the binding the approval gate relies on.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It should use the most recent approval for a similar action as a stand-in.
statements.explanation: A different action's approval does not authorize this one.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It should ask the agent to confirm that approval was previously granted and proceed on its answer.
statements.explanation: The party seeking approval cannot vouch for it.

questions.source: Where the approval step sits in the build so far
questions.stem: A deployment tool shows a reviewer a "plan" of the changes it will make. At apply time, the tool re-runs its planning step against the live environment and applies whatever it computes then. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Saving the reviewed plan as an artifact and applying exactly that artifact ties the execution to what was approved.
statements.explanation: The artifact is the object of the decision.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Binding approval to a fingerprint of the saved plan lets the apply step detect any modification of it.
statements.explanation: A digest over the plan content detects changes after review.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Re-planning at apply time is safe, because the same tool computes both plans.
statements.explanation: The same tool can compute different results from different inputs.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The reviewer approved one computed plan, but the change applied is a different, freshly computed one that nobody reviewed.
statements.explanation: Approval and execution are not tied to the same artifact.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the live state has drifted since the plan was made, the saved plan should be rejected and a new plan reviewed instead of silently adapted.
statements.explanation: A plan computed against a different state is a different proposal.

questions.source: Evaluation comes before authorization
questions.stem: Of 250 agent proposals, reviewers approved 180, refused 40 and deferred 30. Of the 180 approved proposals, 9 were later reversed because the outcome was wrong. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The reversal rate among approved proposals is 20% (9 of 45).
statements.explanation: There is no group of 45 here; the denominator is the 180 approved proposals.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The deferral rate is 12% (30 of 250).

statements.label: C
statements.text: The refusal rate is 16% (40 of 250).

statements.label: D
statements.text: Among approved proposals, the reversal rate is 5% (9 of 180).

statements.label: E
statements.text: The approval rate is 72% (180 of 250).

questions.source: Evaluation comes before authorization
questions.stem: An automated risk screen flags 30 of 250 proposals as risky. Of the 30 flagged, 24 are truly risky; across all 250 proposals, 40 are truly risky. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The screen's recall is 60% (24 of 40 truly risky proposals were flagged).
statements.explanation: Recall is true positives divided by actual positives.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The screen's recall is 80%, because 24 of the 30 flagged were truly risky.
statements.explanation: That figure is precision; recall uses all truly risky proposals as the denominator.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The screen missed 6 risky proposals.
statements.explanation: Six is the number of false alarms (30 - 24); the number missed is 40 - 24 = 16.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because precision is high, unflagged proposals can skip human review.
statements.explanation: Sixteen risky proposals went unflagged, so the unflagged group still contains risk.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The screen's precision is 80% (24 of 30 flagged are truly risky).
statements.explanation: Precision is true positives divided by flagged items.

questions.source: Scope, expiry, revocation, and replay
questions.stem: An agent's request to rotate a production credential lists the rollback as "restore the previous credential from the secrets vault". Before the request goes to a reviewer, the team wants to evaluate that rollback claim. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If rehearsal shows only partial recovery is possible, the request should say so.
statements.explanation: An honest partial rollback beats an unsupported complete one.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The check should confirm that the previous credential is still stored and not purged or rotated away at the provider.
statements.explanation: The plan depends on an artifact that may no longer exist.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A well-written rollback description is sufficient evidence that rollback will work.
statements.explanation: Fluent text can describe a procedure that fails when attempted.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The evaluation should look for effects that restoring does not undo, such as requests rejected during the gap.
statements.explanation: Restoration to a prior state is not the same as undoing consequences.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The restore procedure can be rehearsed in a sandbox to see whether it works end to end.
statements.explanation: A rehearsal tests the claim instead of trusting it.

questions.source: Opening: a complete register is not a responsible team
questions.stem: A team keeps an AI-use register for an LLM workflow. Every required field is filled: owner is "project team", incident contact is "project owner", evaluation is "citation audit". A script that checks only that each field is non-empty reports the record as ready for human review. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Because the owner is a group, it is unclear who can pause the workflow when it causes harm.
statements.explanation: Pause authority attaches to a person or a defined role-holder, not to a collective label.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A green completeness check is sufficient evidence that the workflow complies with applicable regulation.
