statements.explanation: Compliance is a legal and institutional determination; a format check cannot make it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A record can be structurally complete while no individual has accepted responsibility for the workflow.
statements.explanation: Filling a field with a group or role label satisfies a presence check without assigning any person the work.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Presence checks still have value because they make omissions visible.
statements.explanation: A required field left blank is an unambiguous gap; surfacing it costs nothing and prevents silent omissions.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A non-empty check on the owner field verifies that the named owner has agreed to the role.
statements.explanation: A script can see that text exists; it cannot see whether anyone accepted anything.

questions.source: Opening: what Claude can and cannot do in a governance register
questions.stem: A manager asks an LLM assistant to draft a risk register for a new customer-support automation. In seconds it returns an owner, an alerting threshold, a retention period and a paragraph on risks, all fluent and plausible. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Because the assistant produced the register, it remains answerable for the workflow after the conversation ends.
statements.explanation: The assistant holds no ongoing duty or channel; responsibility stays with the people and organization that deploy the system.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The assistant has no first-hand knowledge of the people the automation will affect.
statements.explanation: It only sees what was put in the conversation, so its picture of affected people is inferred, not observed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A fluent, internally consistent draft is evidence that its proposed threshold is one the organization can actually act on.
statements.explanation: Fluency says nothing about whether staffing, tooling and authority exist to respond when the threshold trips.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Writing a person's name into the owner field makes that person the accountable owner.
statements.explanation: Accountability exists only when the person accepts the role; the draft cannot create that acceptance.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The assistant can produce a useful first draft quickly.
statements.explanation: Drafting structured text from a description is something language models do well.

questions.source: Teardown of the validator: what a status means
questions.stem: A governance validator returns one of three statuses: "incomplete" (fields missing), "review-required" (an issue was flagged for a person) and "ready-for-human-review" (no issues found). A record gets "ready-for-human-review". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The status "review-required" routes the decision to a person instead of resolving it automatically.
statements.explanation: When the machine cannot decide, the conservative design hands the question to a human.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A human has already reviewed the record.
statements.explanation: The status says the record is ready to be reviewed, not that review happened.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The record cleared the validator's structural checks.
statements.explanation: That is exactly what the status reports and nothing more.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Everyone whose data is processed has consented.
statements.explanation: Consent is given by individuals; no field-presence check can establish it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The workflow has been approved.
statements.explanation: Approval is an act by an authorized person on a specific proposal; a script's output is not that act.

questions.source: Who decided? Five choices that exist before the form does
questions.stem: A department head lists Dana as the "owner" of an LLM triage workflow in a spreadsheet and never tells her. Dana has no authority to disable the workflow and no time allocated to monitor it. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An owner is accountable only for the initial launch; after that the workflow belongs to whoever operates it day to day.
statements.explanation: Drift, new data and new uses appear after deployment, and someone must still answer for the workflow as it runs.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An owner who cannot stop the workflow holds a label rather than control.
statements.explanation: Accountability without authority to pause or change the system cannot be exercised when it matters.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Being the person who wrote the original code makes someone the owner of the workflow as a continuing system.
statements.explanation: Authorship of the initial code says nothing about ongoing monitoring, change decisions or incident response.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Assigning owner, approver and incident contact all to one person is the best way to avoid gaps.
statements.explanation: It removes independent review and creates a single point of failure; it often just completes the form.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Listing Dana's name does not by itself create accountability.
statements.explanation: Responsibility has to be accepted by the person; being named in a cell is not acceptance.

questions.source: Who decided? Five choices that exist before the form does
questions.stem: A team needs five governance decisions for a new LLM workflow: who owns it, which signal triggers a response, how long data is kept, who was consulted, and how an affected person reaches a human. They ask an assistant to fill in a template first and plan to "review it afterwards". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A decision no one has accepted should be recorded as unresolved, with the workflow constrained until someone accepts it.
statements.explanation: Constraints such as draft-only output, synthetic data or no external writes keep exposure bounded while authority is missing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The team should leave thresholds and owners to emerge from the template because the form structure forces good decisions.
statements.explanation: Structure prompts questions; it does not supply the power or evidence to answer them.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A fluent draft is neutral and does not influence how reviewers decide.
statements.explanation: Reviewers tend to adjust a supplied draft rather than generate their own answer, so a draft shapes the outcome.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An unresolved owner is acceptable if the workflow launches at full scope, since ownership can be settled later.
statements.explanation: Launching at full scope with no accountable person means harm could occur with nobody authorized to respond.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A form filled before the decisions are made records the shape of a decision rather than a decision.
statements.explanation: The fields can be populated with plausible text regardless of whether anyone has actually decided anything.

questions.source: Owners, thresholds, and bounded responses
questions.stem: A team is rewriting vague monitoring promises into thresholds. A threshold is useful for governance when a stranger, reading only the record, could tell whether it fired. Check each statement that would qualify as such a threshold.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Any single confirmed disclosure of personal data triggers an immediate stop and an incident review."
statements.explanation: A confirmed-event trigger is observable and has a defined response.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Quality will be monitored regularly."
statements.explanation: It names no signal, measurement or trigger, so nobody could tell whether it fired.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "If a weekly random sample of 100 outputs contains more than 2 unsupported claims, publication pauses and the content owner investigates."
statements.explanation: It specifies a signal, a measurement procedure, a numeric trigger, a response and a responsible role.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "The team will remain responsive to concerns raised by users."
statements.explanation: It states an attitude, not a condition and a response.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "We will intervene when risk becomes unacceptable."
statements.explanation: "Unacceptable" is undefined and there is no observable condition to check.

questions.source: Owners, thresholds, and bounded responses
questions.stem: A team monitors an LLM drafting tool that produced 20,000 outputs last month. Its dashboard shows a 99.5% pass rate on an automated quality check. Review of the 100 failing outputs found that 2 of them exposed customers' personal data. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reducing the failure rate from 0.5% to 0.4% guarantees fewer personal-data disclosures.
statements.explanation: The aggregate can fall while the rare severe category stays the same or grows.

statements.label: B
statements.text: 100 outputs failed the check.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The pass rate already accounts for severity, so the two disclosures need no separate handling.
statements.explanation: A pass rate counts failures; it does not weight them by harm.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A 99.5% aggregate pass rate can coexist with severe incidents.
statements.explanation: Averages weight every failure equally, so rare high-severity events disappear into the denominator.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Severe harm classes should be handled only by trend thresholds, since a single event is statistically meaningless.
statements.explanation: One severe event can be unacceptable on its own, which is why stop rules respond to the first occurrence.

questions.source: Owners, thresholds, and bounded responses
questions.stem: An incident owner has been named for an LLM-powered publishing pipeline. Managers have told the team that delays will count against its quarterly goals and that shipping on time is rewarded. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If incentives punish delay, a nominal pause authority is unlikely to be used.
statements.explanation: People respond to what is rewarded; unused authority is governance on paper only.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The owner needs explicit authority to pause the pipeline for the role to have effect.
statements.explanation: A nominal owner who must ask permission to stop cannot respond at the speed harm requires.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A written policy that says the owner may pause the pipeline is enough regardless of incentives.
statements.explanation: Policy that conflicts with how performance is judged is routinely ignored in practice.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The cost of a pause should fall on the individual who triggers it, so that they weigh the decision carefully.
statements.explanation: Making the individual absorb the cost discourages use of that power; the organization should absorb it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: How staff are evaluated is an HR matter that a governance record need not address.
statements.explanation: How people are rewarded determines whether controls are used, so it is part of whether governance works.

questions.source: Worked incident rehearsal
questions.stem: The designated incident contact for an LLM service is on leave. An alert about a possible data exposure has gone unacknowledged for six hours; the declared acknowledgment window is two hours. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Waiting for the primary contact to return is acceptable if the exposure may be ongoing.
statements.explanation: Continued exposure means harm accrues while the response waits.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The AI agent running the service can close the gap by nominating itself as the responsible party.
statements.explanation: An agent is not an accountable person or organization; self-nomination assigns nothing.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The system halting its own work while the alert is open is a reasonable safe default, as long as a person remains responsible for the outcome.
statements.explanation: Stopping is low-risk and reversible; responsibility still has to sit with an authorized human.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A documented backup with delegated pause authority should receive the alert and act.
statements.explanation: A backup path exists precisely so that response does not depend on one person's availability.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If no backup exists, the team can treat the gap as acceptable because the contact will eventually return.
statements.explanation: A missing escalation path is a defect to fix; harm can accrue while waiting for one person.

questions.source: Tear down the validator
questions.stem:
A validator checks the retention period with this function:

```python
def valid_days(d):
    return isinstance(d, int) and d >= 0
```

Check each statement that is true about its behavior in Python.

statements.label: A
statements.text: valid_days(30.0) returns True.
statements.explanation: 30.0 is a float, not an int instance, so the isinstance test fails.

statements.label: B
statements.text: valid_days(0) returns False.
statements.explanation: Zero is an int and is not negative, so the function returns True.

statements.label: C
statements.text: bool is not a subclass of int in Python.
statements.explanation: bool derives from int, which is why True behaves as 1 in arithmetic.

statements.label: D
statements.text: valid_days(True) returns True.
statements.explanation: bool is a subclass of int in Python, so isinstance(True, int) is True and True >= 0.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Replacing isinstance(d, int) with type(d) is int would make valid_days(True) return False.
statements.explanation: type(True) is bool, which is not int, so an exact type test rejects Booleans.

questions.source: Tear down the validator
questions.stem: A validator decides which required fields are missing with `missing = [f for f in FIELDS if not record.get(f)]`. A record supplies every field, including `retention_days: 0` as a deliberate design intent of no retention after processing, and `data_classes: []`. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: This check distinguishes a legitimate zero from an absent value.
statements.explanation: Falsiness treats both the same; a test such as `value is None` or a key-presence test is needed to separate them.

statements.label: B
statements.text: retention_days is reported as missing.
statements.explanation: 0 is falsy in Python, so `not 0` is True and the intended value is treated as absent.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A key that is absent from the record is not reported as missing, because get returns None and None is ignored.
statements.explanation: record.get returns None for an absent key and `not None` is True, so the field is reported.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A field containing only the string " " (a single space) is reported as missing.
statements.explanation: A non-empty string is truthy even when it contains only whitespace.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The empty data_classes list is reported as missing.
statements.explanation: An empty list is falsy, which here happens to be the desired behavior.

questions.source: Tear down the validator
questions.stem: A validator receives `data_classes` and runs `set(classes) - {"public", "synthetic", "internal"}`; any leftover element adds the issue "sensitive or unknown data review". It has no type check. A caller passes the bare string `"public"` instead of the list `["public"]`. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The validator reports no issues because "public" is an allowed label.
statements.explanation: The allowed-label comparison never sees the whole string; it sees p, u, b, l, i, c separately.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An explicit check that the value is a list of strings would reject the bare string with a clear error.
statements.explanation: Failing fast on the wrong shape is clearer than a misleading downstream review flag.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A string and a list of labels are interchangeable inputs for this comparison.
statements.explanation: Both are iterable, but they iterate different things, so results differ in meaning.

statements.label: D
statements.text: With the same case-sensitive allowlist, the input `["Public"]` would also be flagged.
statements.explanation: "Public" is not equal to "public", so the exact comparison leaves one unmatched element.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The validator flags the record for review.
statements.explanation: Iterating a string yields single characters, none of which equals an allowed label, so the set difference is non-empty.

questions.source: Tear down the validator
questions.stem: A team debates two designs for checking data labels. Design 1 keeps a denylist of known sensitive labels (for example "medical", "financial") and raises a flag on a match. Design 2 keeps an allowlist of approved labels and sends anything else to human review. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A flag from Design 2 proves the data is sensitive.
statements.explanation: It only shows that this label was not recognized; the data may be perfectly harmless.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Design 2 establishes that data labeled "internal" is safe to use in the proposed workflow.
statements.explanation: A label being on the allowlist says nothing about whether the specific use of that data is appropriate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Design 1 will miss a sensitive category that nobody thought to put on the list.
statements.explanation: A denylist only catches what it enumerates.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A case-sensitive allowlist will silently accept 'Public', which is a safety gap.
statements.explanation: An exact comparison fails for 'Public', so the value is routed to review rather than accepted.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Design 2 routes unknown labels to a person, which is the more conservative default.
statements.explanation: When the machine cannot classify, the safe fallback is to ask a human.

questions.source: Tear down the validator
questions.stem: A designer wants an automated check that rejects governance records whose owner, purpose or evaluation lines are "bad". One proposal is a list of banned phrases such as "everyone", "team", "looks fine". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If an LLM judge scores an owner line as adequate, the named person no longer needs to confirm the role.
statements.explanation: A model's score cannot substitute for the person accepting the role.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A narrow validator that claims only what it checks is more honest than one implying it assesses quality.
statements.explanation: Overstated validators encourage readers to trust status labels beyond what was tested.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A string-matching validator can reliably decide whether an evaluation line describes an adequate test.
statements.explanation: Adequacy depends on the system and the harm; strings cannot encode that.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Leaving the adequacy judgment to a human reviewer is a legitimate division of labor with the validator.
statements.explanation: The machine refuses what it can refuse exactly; people judge whether a line is true and sufficient.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A phrase blacklist is easy to evade with minor rewording.
statements.explanation: "The whole group" or "seems okay" passes while saying the same thing.

questions.source: Tear down the validator
questions.stem: A validator contains `if record.get("external_write"): issues.append("external action approval")`. Check each statement that is true about this check.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A record where external_write is False or absent adds no issue.
statements.explanation: A falsy value fails the condition.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It identifies which external system will be written to.
statements.explanation: The flag is a boolean-style value and carries no target information.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A record where external_write is the string "no" would still trigger the flag.
statements.explanation: Non-empty strings are truthy in Python regardless of their meaning.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It confirms that someone approved the external action.
statements.explanation: It only marks that approval is needed; it never looks for evidence of approval.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It flags a condition that must be handled by another control.
statements.explanation: The flag is a routing signal for an approval step, not the approval itself.

questions.source: Complete, reviewable, and still weak
questions.stem: A governance validator accepts any record whose fields are non-empty and well-formed. This record gets "ready-for-human-review": owner "everyone", purpose "help", data classes ["public"], retention_days 99999, approver "manager", evaluation "looks fine", incident contact "team". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A human reviewer must question what each line means.
statements.explanation: The vague lines can only be tested against the real world by a person.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Adding a policy maximum for retention to the validator would catch that value without needing human judgment.
statements.explanation: A numeric range is something a validator can enforce exactly.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A retention period of 99999 days (roughly 274 years) deserves scrutiny regardless of the validator's verdict.
statements.explanation: It is effectively unlimited retention, which defeats the purpose of stating a period.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The record is a counterexample to reading the status as evidence of adequate governance.
statements.explanation: A status that lets such a record through cannot certify quality.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The validator has a defect, because it should have rejected this record.
statements.explanation: Relative to its narrow contract (presence and shape) it behaved correctly.

questions.source: Build It, Use It, Ship It
questions.stem: A developer writes a test suite for a retention validator before asking an assistant to implement it. Two deliberately wrong implementations exist: V1 accepts any value for which isinstance(d, int) is true; V2 treats any falsy value as missing, so 0 is rejected as missing. The correct implementation accepts 0, rejects True, and rejects negative numbers. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A suite containing only the normal-success case and the empty-record case is enough to catch both wrong versions.
statements.explanation: Both wrong versions still pass those two cases.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A test that expects retention_days=0 to be accepted distinguishes the correct version from V2.
statements.explanation: V2 reports 0 as missing and would fail that test.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the suite passes on an implementation, that implementation is correct for all inputs.
statements.explanation: Tests demonstrate only the behavior they exercise.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Checking the suite against deliberately wrong implementations is unnecessary if the correct implementation passes.
statements.explanation: A suite can pass the correct version and still pass wrong ones; only trying wrong versions shows whether it can tell them apart.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A test that expects retention_days=True to be rejected distinguishes the correct version from V1.
statements.explanation: V1 accepts True because bool is a subclass of int.

questions.source: Build It, Use It, Ship It
questions.stem: A developer asks an LLM assistant to write both a validator and its tests, then runs the tests and sees all pass. Separately, a colleague wrote tests first from a written specification and then asked the assistant to write only the implementation. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Tests and implementation produced by the same model can share the same misreading of the specification.
statements.explanation: The model's error appears on both sides, so agreement between them is weak evidence.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the assistant cannot produce a wrong version that passes the tests, the suite is proven complete.
statements.explanation: Failure to find a counterexample is not proof that none exists.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A person who never writes a baseline version can audit the assistant's version just as well as one who did.
statements.explanation: Building a baseline first gives the person a concrete reference for spotting differences in behavior.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A passing result in the first setup is stronger evidence than in the second, because the tests were consistent with the code.
statements.explanation: Consistency between two products of one source is not independent confirmation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Tests written by a person before seeing the implementation capture that person's intent independently.
statements.explanation: They are not shaped by what the implementation happens to do.

questions.source: Complete, reviewable, and still weak
questions.stem: A reviewer is deciding how to word claims in a validation write-up so that each claim is no stronger than the evidence behind it. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A team that sends a labeled test report to the incident contact and observes an acknowledgment within the stated time has evidence the route works.
statements.explanation: The route was exercised, not merely listed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "The validator reported that all seven fields were present and well shaped" is a precise description of a script run that did exactly that.
statements.explanation: The verb matches what the script did: reported, not confirmed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Inspecting the stores you control supports claims about backups that a vendor operates.
statements.explanation: Evidence covers only what was actually examined; vendor-operated copies remain unexamined.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A passing test suite on the validator is permission to apply the workflow to cases the tests never exercised.
statements.explanation: Test coverage bounds the claim; untested cases remain unknown.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Reading a provider's documentation that says logs are deleted after 30 days supports "we verified deletion at the provider".
statements.explanation: Documentation is a claim by the provider; verifying requires inspecting the store or independent evidence.

questions.source: A register makes questions inspectable
questions.stem: A summarization assistant was approved for condensing public course notes. Six months later the same assistant is pointed at student-submitted essays. The register's purpose field reads "use AI". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A broad purpose statement is preferable because it permits future uses without re-review.
statements.explanation: A broad purpose excludes nothing, which is exactly why scope creep goes unnoticed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the model and prompt are unchanged, the risk profile is unchanged.
statements.explanation: Risk depends on the data, the people and the consequences, not only on the model.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Pointing the assistant at student essays is a use beyond the original scope that should trigger re-review.
statements.explanation: Different data, different people affected and different risks need a fresh decision.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A purpose field is only decoration because the validator cannot judge it.
statements.explanation: The field's value is in forcing the team to state a boundary that people can later check.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A purpose of "use AI" fails to bound what the system may be used for.
statements.explanation: It excludes nothing, so no later use can be identified as out of scope.

questions.source: Retention is a lifecycle
questions.stem: A register states "retention: 30 days" for user prompts. Prompts also appear in: an application log (deleted at 30 days), a nightly backup retained for 90 days, an exported weekly report e-mailed to managers, and a third-party model provider's service logs under the provider's own terms. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A prompt captured by the first nightly backup after it arrived could still exist in that backup about 90 days later.
statements.explanation: The backup's own 90-day retention sets its lifetime regardless of the 30-day application policy.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The policy is satisfied once the primary store deletes at 30 days.
statements.explanation: The policy is about the data, not only the primary store.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Deleting the prompt from the application log also removes summaries derived from it elsewhere.
statements.explanation: Derived artifacts live in their own stores and may still reveal source content.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The declared 30 days does not show that the backup, the exported report and the provider logs are deleted at 30 days.
statements.explanation: A retention number describes the policy for one store; other copies follow their own lifecycles.

statements.label: E
statements.text: To verify the policy, the team must list each copy and say how deletion is performed and checked.
statements.explanation: Without an inventory of copies, deletion cannot be tested.

questions.source: Retention is a lifecycle
questions.stem: A design document sets `retention_days = 0` for a workflow that handles customer messages. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Stating zero in the record is evidence that no copies exist.
statements.explanation: A stated value is a design intent; copies can exist whatever the record says.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Zero can mean different things: delete immediately after the task, do not persist application data, or keep only de-identified evidence.
statements.explanation: The number does not define which of those is intended, so the document needs to say.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A validator that treats falsy values as missing would incorrectly report this record as missing a field.
statements.explanation: 0 is falsy, so a presence check must test for absence, not falsiness.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Zero retention means a third-party model provider processes nothing, so the provider's terms are irrelevant.
statements.explanation: Processing by a provider still occurs and is governed by its own terms.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A validator should reject zero as invalid because data must always be kept for some period.
statements.explanation: Zero can be a legitimate design intent; rejecting it prevents expressing a minimal-retention design.

questions.source: Retention is a lifecycle
questions.stem: A team claims that a customer's personal data was removed from their LLM application. They deleted the row from the application database. The same customer's data also fed a vector index of embeddings, a nightly summary report, a log of hashed email addresses used for matching, and a backup. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Unverified stores, such as provider systems and backups, should be listed as open rather than assumed clean.
statements.explanation: Reporting unknowns avoids turning a desired policy into a claim about systems no one inspected.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Removed from this table" supports the claim "erased everywhere".
statements.explanation: The claim covers only the store inspected.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The team can test deletion by inserting a labeled test record, running the full lifecycle, and inspecting the stores it controls.
statements.explanation: An end-to-end test on marked data checks what actually happens rather than what the policy says.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A hash of an email address can still be personal data if it can be matched against a small known set.
statements.explanation: Hashing a guessable input is reversible by lookup; the hash can identify the person.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Deleting the row does not show that derived artifacts such as embeddings and summaries are gone.
statements.explanation: Derived data can retain or reveal source information.

questions.source: Retention is a lifecycle
questions.stem: A team is deciding how long to keep traces of an LLM agent's actions. Option 1 keeps full prompts and outputs forever. Option 2 keeps nothing. Option 3 keeps an operation ID, the policy decision taken, references to evidence stored elsewhere, an error category, and the responsible role, with sensitive payloads kept only when justified and protected. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Audit logs are exempt from retention limits because they are used for oversight.
statements.explanation: Audit records are still data with a lifecycle and a risk; they need their own retention decision.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Option 2 can make accountability and incident investigation impossible.
statements.explanation: With no record of what happened, causes cannot be established.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Option 1 improves the ability to investigate incidents but enlarges privacy exposure.
statements.explanation: More retained detail helps replay and raises the cost of any breach or misuse.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Full payloads should be stored by default because debugging value always outweighs privacy cost.
statements.explanation: Data minimization says to keep only what is needed and justified.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Option 3 is inferior to Option 1 in every respect because it removes investigative detail.
statements.explanation: Option 3 keeps the information needed to reconstruct decisions while cutting privacy exposure, so it is not worse in every respect.

questions.source: Who bears the error
questions.stem: Two agents each score 92% on the same 500-item evaluation set. Agent A reads public notes, writes a local draft, keeps inputs one day, and requires a person to publish. Agent B reads internal HR records, publishes directly to an external site, and keeps complete traces for a year. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Equal accuracy implies equal governance needs.
statements.explanation: Accuracy measures output correctness under selected tests, not consequences or reversibility.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Agent B has a larger action surface and longer exposure window than Agent A.
statements.explanation: Direct external publication and long retention of sensitive traces expand both.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Both agents made 40 errors on the evaluation set.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Ethical review can wait until after model selection because model score determines risk.
statements.explanation: Data, authority and retention choices shape harm before any score exists.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The architectural choices of Agent A (minimal data, human publication, short retention) reduce the harm surface independent of model accuracy.
statements.explanation: These choices limit how much damage an error can do.

questions.source: Who bears the error
questions.stem: Two document summarizers are tested on the same 300 policy questions. Each makes exactly 12 deadline errors, so both score 96%. Summarizer X errs by stating a deadline its sources do not support. Summarizer Y errs by omitting the deadline when sources conflict. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Y's omissions are harmless because users can always check the source.
statements.explanation: Omissions impose costs: delay, support requests and missed deadlines for people who do not check.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A single accuracy figure is sufficient to choose between them.
statements.explanation: It hides the type of error, which matters more than the count here.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The accuracy number does not say which kind of error to prefer.
statements.explanation: Choosing means weighing whose costs count, which is a value judgment.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Both kinds of error harm the same people, so the choice between them has no distributional effect.
statements.explanation: A wrong date harms those who rely on it; an omission harms those who must seek clarification, so the burdens differ.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Both have an identical overall accuracy figure.

questions.source: Who bears the error
questions.stem: A risk-scoring model is applied to two groups. Group 1 has a base rate of 50% positives and group 2 has 20%. For both groups the classifier has a true positive rate of 0.8 and a false positive rate of 0.2. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The positive predictive value (precision) for group 1 is 0.80.
statements.explanation: Of every 100 people, 40 true positives and 10 false positives are flagged, so 40 / 50 = 0.80.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The precision gap indicates a computation bug in the classifier.
statements.explanation: It follows arithmetically from equal error rates and unequal base rates.

statements.label: C
statements.text: With differing base rates, holding error rates equal across groups and also holding precision equal is generally impossible unless prediction is perfect.
statements.explanation: This is a known impossibility result for fairness criteria, which follows from Bayes' rule.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The two groups are flagged at the same rate.
statements.explanation: Group 1 is flagged at 0.50 and group 2 at 0.32 of the population.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The positive predictive value for group 2 is 0.50.
statements.explanation: Of every 100 people, 16 true positives and 16 false positives are flagged, so 16 / 32 = 0.50.

questions.source: Who bears the error
questions.stem: A team building a scoring tool for loan applications must pick a fairness criterion. Its data scientist says "the numbers will tell us which definition is correct". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Choosing among fairness definitions is a normative decision, not only a technical one.
statements.explanation: Each definition protects a different kind of equality and trades off against the others.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Two parties can both report accurate statistics and still disagree about which statistic should decide fairness.
statements.explanation: The disagreement is about values, not about arithmetic.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The definition should be whichever the default loss function happened to encode.
statements.explanation: An implicit default is a choice made by accident; the decision should rest with an accountable party.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The decision need not be recorded, since the chosen metric speaks for itself.
statements.explanation: A recorded rationale with alternatives and conditions for change is what makes the choice reviewable.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the tool does not rank or allocate opportunities among people, the team should add demographic columns to its evaluation to look rigorous.
statements.explanation: Metrics should be tied to a harm mechanism that exists; invented columns add the look of rigor without meaning.

questions.source: Who bears the error
questions.stem: A risk register for an LLM-based tool lists the risk "There may be bias or privacy concerns." Another entry reads: "A student relies on a summary that states the wrong submission deadline and misses the real one." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A register with 40 generic risks is more useful than one with three concrete harm scenarios.
statements.explanation: Concreteness, not count, makes a register actionable.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A concrete harm entry lets reviewers ask who bears the cost and who could have prevented it.
statements.explanation: Specificity connects a harm to people with different roles.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Generic risk language tells a team what to do.
statements.explanation: Without a person, mechanism or consequence it guides no specific action.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The second entry names an affected person, a mechanism and a consequence.
statements.explanation: Those elements allow someone to design a test and a mitigation for it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The first entry is a concrete harm description.
statements.explanation: It names no person, mechanism or consequence and could be pasted into any register.

questions.source: Who bears the error
questions.stem: A company uses an LLM to screen resumes. It reports 90% overall agreement with past hiring decisions on an evaluation set built from people who were hired. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Candidates wrongly rejected bear the cost of false negatives.
statements.explanation: They lose an opportunity and may never learn why.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Whether a rejected candidate can reach a human who can change the decision is a governance question that accuracy does not capture.
statements.explanation: Recourse is a property of the surrounding system, not the model score.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An overall agreement of 90% implies that errors are spread evenly across groups of applicants.
statements.explanation: Aggregate figures say nothing about distribution across subgroups.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An evaluation set drawn only from past hires under-represents people who were never hired.
statements.explanation: Selecting on the outcome hides how the model treats those excluded by earlier processes.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Recruiters bear part of the cost of false positives because they spend time reviewing weak candidates.
statements.explanation: Errors have costs for the staff who must correct them.

questions.source: Consultation and recourse are people's work
questions.stem: A team plans to consult people affected by a new AI workflow. It decides to ask one friendly colleague to speak for all stakeholders, and to ask only how to make the planned deployment more acceptable. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Consultation is meaningful only if the answers could change the purpose, boundaries, retention or the decision to automate.
statements.explanation: If nothing can change, the process is performance rather than input.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Participants should be enrolled by default, with an explanation of how their answers are used given only if they ask.
statements.explanation: Voluntary, informed participation is the basis for treating answers as input or consent.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The team should promise that every request will be adopted.
statements.explanation: Promising what cannot be delivered erodes trust; the team should explain how decisions and conflicts will be recorded.

statements.label: D
statements.text: One convenient person can stand in for every stakeholder group.
statements.explanation: Different groups have different stakes, and a single proxy hides the ones missing from the room.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Asking only how to make a predetermined deployment more acceptable is participation theater.
statements.explanation: The outcome was already fixed, so affected people's views cannot matter.

questions.source: Consultation and recourse are people's work
questions.stem: A team prepares for stakeholder conversations by asking an LLM to play an affected student and answer questions about a new AI workflow. The model replies agreeably. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The model's agreeable answers are statements by the student.
statements.explanation: The model generates plausible text; the student said nothing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The record should label simulated responses as simulation and state which real consultation is still pending.
statements.explanation: Honest labeling prevents later readers from mistaking rehearsal for evidence.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The model's reaction shows what real students in this program think.
statements.explanation: It reflects patterns in training data and the prompt, not the actual views of these people.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Invented agreement counts as consent.
statements.explanation: Consent is something a real person gives, knowingly.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Role-play can reveal unclear explanations and missing questions.
statements.explanation: A fluent responder will expose confusing wording and obvious gaps.

questions.source: Consultation and recourse are people's work
questions.stem: A researcher drafts interview questions for people who will be affected by an automated decision tool. Check each statement that is true about which questions invite honest disagreement.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Leading questions produce stronger consent because respondents agree more often.
statements.explanation: Agreement obtained by framing is not informed consent.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "What would make you withdraw your support?" invites disagreement.
statements.explanation: It surfaces conditions under which the respondent would object.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "What information should never enter this workflow?" invites disagreement.
statements.explanation: It asks for boundaries and lets the respondent veto parts of the design.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Does this helpful tool sound good?" mostly solicits reassurance.
statements.explanation: The wording presupposes the tool is helpful and invites agreement.

statements.label: E
statements.text: After interviews, actual statements should be kept separate from AI-generated summaries, with a summary returned to the participant for confirmation when appropriate.
statements.explanation: This prevents a model's paraphrase from replacing what a person said.

questions.source: Consultation and recourse are people's work
questions.stem: A participant in a user study gave permission for their feedback to be used, then withdrew it. Their words were quoted in a summary, added to a vector store, used as an example in an evaluation set, and captured in a backup. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Tracking which artifacts derive from a contribution makes honoring a withdrawal feasible.
statements.explanation: Without lineage, nobody knows what to find and delete.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Consent given once is irrevocable for the project's duration.
statements.explanation: Consent that is given can generally be withdrawn, and the process should plan for it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Deleting the original transcript alone does not honor the withdrawal if derived artifacts remain.
statements.explanation: The quoted summary, embedding and evaluation example still carry the participant's contribution.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An immutable backup that cannot be edited can be left out of what the participant is told.
statements.explanation: Disclosing what could not be removed is part of honest handling of a withdrawal.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A written promise to remove the data is as good as verifying that it was removed.
statements.explanation: A promise is an intention; verification checks outcomes.

questions.source: Consultation and recourse are people's work
questions.stem: A team asks an LLM to write a plain-language explanation of its workflow for people who will be affected: what it receives, what it produces, where a person decides, what is retained and how to report a problem. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The explanation need not mention retention, because retention is a technical detail.
statements.explanation: Retention affects people's exposure, so affected people need to know about it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Shorter and simpler wording is always more accurate.
statements.explanation: Simplification can drop caveats and change meaning.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The draft will be accurate about the real configuration as long as the assistant was given a one-line description of the workflow.
statements.explanation: A model describes what it was given; a thin description leaves gaps it fills with plausible guesses.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the draft reads smoothly, checking is unnecessary.
statements.explanation: Readability is unrelated to correctness.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A person who knows the real system must check the draft against it before sharing.
statements.explanation: Smooth simplification can omit exactly the external write or retention detail an affected person needs.

questions.source: Consultation and recourse are people's work
questions.stem: During a stakeholder interview, a student says they care less about accuracy than about being quoted without context. A maintainer says an appeals channel would create unpaid support work. An instructor separates public course material from student submissions held in the same repository. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Concerns raised in interviews should be logged but should not alter the data classes or scope that were already approved.
statements.explanation: If findings never change anything, consultation was not real input; situated concerns can change data classes, access and purpose.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A fixed list of prepared question categories captures concerns as well as open-ended listening does.
statements.explanation: Prepared categories reflect only what the team already thought to ask.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A concern not on the prepared list should be set aside as out of scope.
statements.explanation: Unexpected concerns are often the ones that change the design.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because public and student-submitted content sit in the same repository, they must share the same data class.
statements.explanation: Treatment should follow the nature and sensitivity of the content, not where it happens to be stored.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The maintainer's workload concern is a governance input, since a recourse route nobody is resourced to staff will fail.
statements.explanation: Capacity is part of whether a control works.

questions.source: Consultation and recourse are people's work
questions.stem: An LLM-assisted benefits-eligibility tool denies a claim. The claimant has only a general support e-mail address to contact. Check each statement that is true about effective recourse.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An e-mail address alone is a recourse path.
statements.explanation: It lacks acknowledgment, triage, authority to change the outcome and escalation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Explaining the model's reasoning restores an opportunity that was denied.
statements.explanation: An explanation does not undo the denial; a correction would.

statements.label: C
statements.text: There should be a second route when the original owner is conflicted.
statements.explanation: A person cannot impartially review their own decision.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The reviewer must have the power to change the result.
statements.explanation: A reviewer who can only explain and not correct gives no remedy.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A correction should reach downstream copies of the contested output.
statements.explanation: Fixing one record while copies persist leaves the harm in place.

questions.source: Consultation and recourse are people's work
questions.stem: A team reviews three kinds of harm from an AI-written summary: a displayed summary containing an error, a personal detail that already appeared in a public copy, and an opportunity that was denied on the strength of the summary. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Correcting the displayed summary does not repair a decision already made from it.
statements.explanation: The downstream decision needs its own review and remedy.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A contest route is contestable only if every challenge is upheld.
statements.explanation: Contestability means genuine reconsideration is possible, not that the person always wins.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Removing personal data from the active store does not recall a public copy.
statements.explanation: Copies outside the team's control need separate handling or disclosure.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A rejected challenge should still be acknowledged and explained.
statements.explanation: The person is owed a reasoned answer and a way to escalate.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Response times should be promised only when the team can meet them.
statements.explanation: Missed promises damage trust more than modest, honest commitments.

questions.source: Consultation and recourse are people's work
questions.stem: A team designs how contested AI-assisted decisions are handled. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The contested output, input provenance where lawful, the applicable policy and the human decision record should be preserved.
statements.explanation: Without them the reviewer cannot reconstruct what happened.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The reviewer should be the same person who made the original decision when the case is a conflict.
statements.explanation: A conflicted reviewer cannot independently reassess.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the same class of report recurs while only the reply template changes, the process is absorbing complaints without controlling the system.
statements.explanation: A response that never alters the system leaves the cause intact.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The affected person should be asked to debate the model that produced the error.
statements.explanation: The person needs an answerable human, not an argument with a system.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A recurring class of reports should lead to engineering change.
statements.explanation: Fixing the cause is the purpose of an incident process.

questions.source: Worked incident rehearsal
questions.stem: A student reports that a published summary gives a deadline different from the official schedule. On investigation the student was comparing the summary with an outdated schedule, and the published date matches the current official source. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The team should not revisit the summary's wording because the published date was correct.
statements.explanation: A correct but ambiguous summary can still mislead, so wording deserves a check.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Explaining the evidence to the reporter is unnecessary when the report turns out to be wrong.
statements.explanation: An explanation respects the reporter and keeps people willing to report.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The route should still acknowledge and investigate the report.
statements.explanation: Reports are inputs even when they turn out wrong.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A report that turns out wrong can be discarded without reply.
statements.explanation: Silence discourages future reports and gives the team nothing to learn from.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The contest route is only credible if it upholds every challenge.
statements.explanation: Credible contestability allows genuine reconsideration, not guaranteed success.

questions.source: Worked incident rehearsal
questions.stem: A summarization service cites a source identifier for every claim, and its audit checks that each cited identifier exists in the document store. The service publishes a summary with a deadline that the cited document does not state. The audit passes. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The finding means the original evaluation design was adequate and needs no revisiting.
statements.explanation: The audit passed a harmful output, which is evidence the evaluation did not test the relevant harm.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A person who checks only that each cited identifier exists in the store would catch this error.
statements.explanation: Existence does not show that the cited text states the deadline, so this check misses the error.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Making the existence check stricter, for example verifying that the identifier format is valid, would fix the problem.
statements.explanation: The failure is about meaning, not about identifier validity.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The audit passing does not show the claim is supported by the cited source.
statements.explanation: It checks that a citation exists, not that the cited text entails the claim.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Deciding governance before implementation means it should not change after launch.
statements.explanation: Design-first sets the starting point; evidence from operation can and should reopen decisions.

questions.source: Worked incident rehearsal
questions.stem: A published AI-written summary is found to be wrong. The team pauses publication of affected summaries, locates copies in the systems it controls and corrects them, and notes that it cannot reach copies outside those systems. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The team should capture the source identifiers, generated output, approvals and publication evidence before changing the system.
statements.explanation: Evidence can be overwritten by fixes if not preserved first.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The correction should go out through the same channel that carried the original.
statements.explanation: Readers who saw the error are most likely to see the correction there.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Publication of affected items should pause while the cause is investigated.
statements.explanation: Continuing to publish items of the same kind risks repeating the harm.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Copies the team cannot reach should be acknowledged as a limitation instead of being implied to be fixed.
statements.explanation: Honest scope prevents false assurance.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The reporting route should be closed once the correction is published.
statements.explanation: The correction may have missed some effect; the route lets people report that.

questions.source: Worked incident rehearsal
questions.stem: A team's service produces 150 deadline claims per day. Policy says every deadline claim must be reviewed by a person before publication. Reviewers have 2 hours per day, at 4 minutes per claim. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Narrowing the feature, such as only extracting dates with the source passage visible, can reduce the review load.
statements.explanation: Smaller scope lowers the review needed per output.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Publishing the 120 unreviewed claims while still describing every claim as reviewed would accurately represent the control.
statements.explanation: It would misstate what was done.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The unreviewed backlog grows by 120 claims per day under the stated policy.
statements.explanation: 150 produced minus 30 reviewed is 120.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A control that requires review of every claim but cannot be staffed to do so is not functioning as a control.
statements.explanation: A control's value depends on its being performed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Reviewers can examine 30 claims per day.
statements.explanation: 120 minutes divided by 4 minutes is 30.

questions.source: When deferral is the responsible output
questions.stem: A team says "a human is in the loop" for an LLM system that drafts decisions on 500 items an hour. A single reviewer clicks Approve on each item. The reviewer has no stated time budget per item, no authority to reject beyond clicking a different button, and no guidance on what to look for. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Human in the loop" does not specify a control unless the human task, evidence, authority, time budget and stop rule are defined.
statements.explanation: The phrase names a person, not what the person is positioned to do.

statements.label: B
statements.text: High volume can turn approval into a ritual without scrutiny.
statements.explanation: Fatigue and time pressure erode attention.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A person clicking Approve on each of 500 items an hour provides meaningful review.
statements.explanation: The pace, about 7 seconds per item, leaves no time to assess content.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Throughput should be capped to the capacity of review and response.
statements.explanation: Review quality depends on volume being matched to reviewer capacity.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Naming a human in the process satisfies oversight regardless of whether they can reject.
statements.explanation: Oversight requires authority and ability to act on what they see.

questions.source: When deferral is the responsible output
questions.stem: A company wants to use an LLM to rank employees for promotion. The evaluation cannot observe real career outcomes, employees have not been consulted, the data boundary is unclear, and no manager has agreed to own the decisions. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Deferring the project is a legitimate result.
statements.explanation: The preconditions for responsible use are missing.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Narrowing the tool to organizing documents instead of ranking people is a possible alternative.
statements.explanation: A lower-stakes variant can proceed while the missing preconditions are addressed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the model scores well on a proxy metric, the project should go ahead.
statements.explanation: A proxy score does not address consultation, ownership or the data boundary.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A register that can only record "go" works as a rubber stamp.
statements.explanation: Without a legitimate way to say no or narrow, review has no force.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The team should record why it deferred and what evidence or capacity would justify reconsidering.
statements.explanation: A recorded reason makes the decision reviewable and the reconsideration conditions explicit.

questions.source: When deferral is the responsible output
questions.stem: An agent can read a CRM and send e-mails to customers on its own. Leadership has concerns about errors. Check each statement that is a valid way of narrowing the workflow.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Remove high-impact actions such as refunds until outcome checks exist.
statements.explanation: Excluding what cannot be safely checked limits harm.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Shorten how long conversation traces are retained.
statements.explanation: Less retained data reduces privacy exposure.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Run the pilot on synthetic customer records instead of real ones.
statements.explanation: Synthetic data removes exposure of real people while testing behavior.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Change the agent so it drafts messages that a staff member sends.
statements.explanation: Human sending adds a review point and reversibility before external effects.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Keep the full scope and add a footer saying that e-mails may contain errors.
statements.explanation: A disclaimer shifts burden to recipients without reducing risk.

questions.source: Governance failure patterns
questions.stem: Five failure patterns can make an AI governance record look sound while the system is not governed. Hollow ownership: roles are filled with labels but nobody has accepted responsibility. Unobservable trigger: a response condition with no measurable signal. Simulated consent: model-generated reactions are presented as feedback from real people. Compliance theater: a completed internal form is treated as legal clearance. Open-ended pilot: a deployment called temporary has no end condition or review date. Check each statement in which the case is matched to the correct pattern.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A deployment announced as a one-month pilot is still running fourteen months later, collecting data, with no scheduled review: open-ended pilot.
statements.explanation: The temporary framing has no end condition, so the deployment persists unexamined.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A team cites answers produced by a language model playing affected students as the stakeholder feedback it gathered: simulated consent.
statements.explanation: Invented agreement is offered as if real people had weighed in.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A completed internal template is presented to executives as proof that the system meets regulatory requirements: compliance theater.
statements.explanation: The form's existence is treated as legal clearance it cannot provide.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A trigger written as "act when quality falls", with no metric or measurement procedure: simulated consent.
statements.explanation: That is an unobservable trigger; no one reading the record can tell whether it fired.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A named owner with explicit authority to pause the system, who has never needed to use it: hollow ownership.
statements.explanation: A person has accepted the role and holds authority; hollow ownership describes fields filled with no one accountable.

questions.source: Governance failure patterns
questions.stem: A chatbot logs users' health questions for a year. The listed harm is that retained logs could expose sensitive health information if accessed improperly. The listed mitigation is a weekly test that checks the chatbot's answers for factual accuracy. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Adding the accuracy test makes the log-exposure risk resolved.
statements.explanation: The exposure is unchanged.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Reducing retention, redacting health details before logging, or limiting access would address the mechanism more directly.
statements.explanation: These controls act on the stored data and who can see it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A mitigation should be matched to the mechanism of the harm it is meant to reduce.
statements.explanation: Otherwise the register shows a control that controls nothing relevant.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The accuracy test might be useful for another risk, yet it does not reduce log exposure.
statements.explanation: Value elsewhere does not make it relevant to this harm.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The mitigation does not address the stated harm mechanism.
statements.explanation: Answer accuracy and log exposure are different risks.

questions.source: A register makes questions inspectable
questions.stem: A team of three works on an LLM workflow and records in its register: an owner, an approver and an incident contact. Check each statement that is true about how these roles differ.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The approver is the decision route for whether a proposal or change goes ahead.
statements.explanation: Approval is a gate on specific proposals.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The owner is accountable for the workflow as a continuing system.
statements.explanation: Operation, monitoring and changes over time sit with the owner.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The three roles can legitimately be held by different people to provide independent review.
statements.explanation: Separation reduces the chance that one person's blind spot goes unchecked.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The approver and owner should always be the same person so the register has no ambiguity.
statements.explanation: Combining them removes the independence that review is meant to provide.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The incident contact is where people report problems.
statements.explanation: It is the entry point to the response path.

questions.source: Governance failure patterns
questions.stem: A team builds a summarizer that reads notes written by instructors and students, summarizes them for a portal, and routes corrections through a volunteer maintainer. Check each statement that is true about identifying who is affected.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Listing only the end users is sufficient.
statements.explanation: It leaves out quoted authors, instructors and maintainers.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The maintainer's extra work is a staffing matter and not a governance concern.
statements.explanation: Who bears the correction burden is part of who pays for errors.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Affected people include those who never use the portal, such as students whose written work is quoted.
statements.explanation: Harm can reach people who are not users.

statements.label: D
statements.text: People who cannot opt out can be given less attention, since they are not users.
statements.explanation: Lack of choice leaves them dependent on the quality of governance, which calls for more attention.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Groups absent from the development examples can be ignored if the tests show no problems.
statements.explanation: Tests built without those groups cannot reveal problems affecting them.

questions.source: Build It, Use It, Ship It
questions.stem: A developer records a decision about an AI-assisted policy change, listing what the model proposed, what context a person added or corrected, the evidence supporting the recommendation, whose interests the change serves or disadvantages, and the named person's recommendation. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A longer decision note demonstrates more diligence.
statements.explanation: Length is not evidence; specificity and independent support are.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Separating the model's proposal from the human contribution lets an auditor see where a person changed the substance.
statements.explanation: A note that merges them hides whether review happened.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Listing whose interests are disadvantaged forces the writer to consider affected people.
statements.explanation: It prevents the note from reading as pure justification.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Evidence cited should be independent of the model's fluency.
statements.explanation: The model's own claim cannot be its own support.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A sentence that merely repeats the model's wording is not evidence of human review.
statements.explanation: Repetition shows copying, not judgment.

questions.source: Governance failure patterns
questions.stem: A team completes an internal AI-use register and states in a briefing: "We are compliant." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A practice that is legal is thereby ethical.
statements.explanation: Legal and ethical are different standards; legal practices can still harm people.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A completed internal form counts as regulatory approval once management signs it.
statements.explanation: Regulatory approval comes from the regulator or the legal process, not from an organization's own sign-off.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A general internal register satisfies statutory impact-assessment requirements by design.
statements.explanation: A legal obligation is met only by performing what the law prescribes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Whether personal data is processed on a lawful basis is a legal determination, not a form field.
statements.explanation: Lawfulness depends on law, jurisdiction and facts that a register cannot decide.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the register status is green, legal review can be skipped.
statements.explanation: Status from a structural check says nothing about legal review.

questions.source: Retention is a lifecycle
questions.stem: A policy says records are deleted "30 days after the case is created." A case record was created on 10 January 2027 and last used on 20 February 2027. Another team interprets the clock as starting at last use. Check each statement that is true. Assume 2027 is not a leap year.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The ambiguity does not matter because the stated number is 30 either way.
statements.explanation: The date the data is actually deleted depends on when the clock starts.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Counting from creation, deletion is due on 9 February 2027.
statements.explanation: 30 days after 10 January is 9 February.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Counting from last use, deletion is due on 22 March 2027.
statements.explanation: 30 days after 20 February is 22 March.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A policy only needs to state the number of days.
statements.explanation: It also needs the clock start, who performs deletion and how deletion is checked.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The two readings differ by 41 days.
statements.explanation: 9 February to 22 March is 41 days.

questions.source: Retention is a lifecycle
questions.stem: A company sends customer messages to an external LLM provider's API. Its register lists "retention: 0 days" because the company's own systems store nothing. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The company can assume the provider retains nothing, since providers generally say they take privacy seriously.
statements.explanation: An assumption is not evidence; the applicable terms must be read and unknowns recorded.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Zero retention in the company's own systems establishes zero retention everywhere.
statements.explanation: The provider's handling is separate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Provider handling can be listed as verified once the provider's marketing page states a policy.
statements.explanation: A published claim by the provider is not verification by the company.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Using an external provider removes the company's responsibility for the data.
statements.explanation: The company that chose to send the data still answers to its customers.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Data sent to the provider is a copy handled under the provider's terms.
statements.explanation: The provider receives and processes it outside the company's systems.

questions.source: Build It, Use It, Ship It
questions.stem: A developer writes a register entry and asks an assistant: "Do not rewrite it. List every field that names a group instead of a person, every threshold with no observable signal, every mitigation that does not address the harm I named, and one decision I have not written down." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Findings need no verification because the assistant has the whole document.
statements.explanation: Having the text does not make the model reliable.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Asking the assistant to rewrite the entry would tend to smooth over weak lines instead of exposing them.
statements.explanation: Rewrites optimize fluency, which hides vagueness.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Each finding should be checked against the entry, since a finding that cannot be located in the text may be a plausible guess.
statements.explanation: Language models can produce confident but unfounded critiques.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the assistant lists no problems, the entry has no problems.
statements.explanation: Absence of findings is not proof of absence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Using the assistant as a challenger keeps authorship of the entry with the person.
statements.explanation: The model critiques; the person decides what to change.

questions.source: Governance failure patterns
questions.stem: An AI-assisted workflow publishes a wrong figure. Several parties made choices that mattered: the user who reported it, the content owner, the vendor of the drafting tool, the provider of the underlying model, and the institution whose data was the source. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A useful question is what change made before the incident would have prevented it.
statements.explanation: This turns the review toward actions that could have been taken.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the model provider's output was wrong, the team that deployed it carries no responsibility.
statements.explanation: Deployers choose to use the model and answer for the consequences in their setting.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The answer should be judged by whether the change is an action someone takes or only a sentence someone writes.
statements.explanation: Controls exist when they change behavior.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Responsibility for failures in socio-technical systems is commonly distributed across several parties.
statements.explanation: Each choice may be necessary without being sufficient alone.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Naming one owner does not remove dependencies on the other parties.
statements.explanation: The register should record those as dependencies that were checked or assumed.

questions.source: Governance failure patterns
